Most would call it tranquil, I suppose, if not a tad foreboding. Darkened corridors, illuminated by the light of some strange genus of flower, are interspersed between calming, wondrous caverns flowing with glimmering waters. A strange, vaguely lightbulb-shaped creature asks me what a star is. “Can you touch it? Can you eat it?”,  it inquires. “Can you kill it?” There’s a pause. “Are you a star?” The monsters of the Underground haven’t seen the stars in generations, after all, so it’s unlikely this thing would know anything about them. Littering the walls of the jewel scrawled caves of Waterfall are many plaques, inscribed with the depressing history of monsterkind. They detail the sudden attack from the humans, the one-sided massacre of a war that ensued; the mystifying nature of the SOUL. Not long after, you bump into a monster. 'Wosh u leg' the birdbath-like creature exclaims; before swiftly and dutifully beginning to wash a pizza.
And that’s the general tone that Undertale sets from the get-go.
REVIEW
Undertale
GENRE
RPG?
Developed almost entirely by award-winning Earthbound mod creator and webcomic composer Toby Fox; Undertale is a (mostly) joyous romp through the otherwise depressing yet quirky land of monsters. The opening cutscene details the legend of Mt Ebott, a forsaken mountain whose travellers are said to never return from. The year is 201X, and a small child, presumably looking for shelter from the rain, wanders into an opening at the peak. Whilst exploring the inside of the cavern, they stumble on some vines, sending them tumbling far, far down into Ebott. As luck would have it, they land on a well maintained bed of golden flowers. It just so happens that this child is you, you blundering ninny! [Why would you ever climb a mountain like that? Really!] Thus, your tale begins; your, uh, Undertale! [I tried, okay?]
Moving on from my half-hearted attempts at humor, let’s talk about Undertale’s pull; its unique combat system and genuine, heartwarming humor. Sure, it has the usual RPG ensemble of combat mechanics; fight, items, flee, etc., but what truly sets Undertale apart from other games of its genre is the ACT menu. As you’ve probably seen from the trailer, the game’s description, or the blurb that sits alongside the game’s picture; the tagline of Undertale is: ‘The friendly RPG where nobody has to die!’ True to its word, Undertale is a game where not a single creature has to die; I repeat,
[That is, unless you want to have a BAD TIME.] This is where the ACT menu plays a part. Each enemy presents their own puzzle for you to solve during combat, and as the game puts it itself: “If you ACT a certain way or FIGHT until you almost defeat them (Monsters)... they might not want to battle you anymore.”
This also ties into the game’s humor quite well, as, aside from the many fantastic puns and brick jokes, the ‘hostile’ encounters with the residents of the Underground are usually chock full of it. In the aforementioned Waterfall, there exists a monster named Aaron; a deliberately creepy literal seahorse who is muscular beyond reason. All of his dialogue ends in winky faces, even when he’s as scared out of his mind as he is ripped. On the topic of Aaron’s veterinary need for his sick pythons, the ACT menu allows you to foolishly challenge this apparent god of muscles to a flexing competition. While I say foolishly, it’s the pacifist’s way of beating this beefcake. Flex thrice and the equine epitome of energy will flex so hard that he flexes himself out of the room. Yes, I’m being serious, and that’s just one of the many interactions with the monsters of Undertale.
“But what about the defensive side of the combat?”, you’d ask. “I was just about to start on that, you impatient little nerd.”, I’d respond. Much like you’d see in a game of Touhou [Or so I’ve been told, I’ve never played Touhou.], enemy’s attacks are presented as bullethell-esque challenge. You move your SOUL around a small boxed in region while your foe throws a variety of little, white ‘friendliness pellets’ which you must avoid; unless of course you
dying. Each monster provides its own unique pattern to dodge and adding more monsters to the equation only helps to further enhance the difficulty, as the monsters will combine their attacks into a completely new one. Heck, to take it another step further, the titular boss monster encounters can sometimes change the way you control your SOUL entirely. Sometimes you’ll be affected by gravity, forcing you to jump over dangerous obstacles; other times you’ll confined to a set of three pathways which you must swap in between to evade danger. Most importantly though, remember;
So that’s the end of combat, and segues sure are hard; aren’t they? Speaking of segues, I just made a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥one into the soundtrack section of this review. Neat, right? The soundtrack of Undertale is
, and I can without a doubt say that Toby’s reputation as a composer utterly precedes him. From the subtle uneasiness of ‘Your Best Friend’ to the bombastic whimsy of ‘Nyeh Heh Heh!’, the many fantastic songs of Undertale could only be described as unique. Personally, my favorite song from the OST is ‘Dummy!’ a hyperactive remix of the uniquely Undertale ‘Ghost Fight’. [Yes, I described it as uniquely Undertale; it fits the style of the game to a T.] Each song fits its situation perfectly, and, if you’re unfortunate enough, you might just uncover a certain someone’s calling card.
Aside from the audible presentation of Undertale; the visual presentation, while not too terribly complicated, is utterly intriguing. When you encounter a monster, the world becomes monochrome, aside from your SOUL; still a warming shade of red. Color is scarcely used in combat; reserved for truly singular spectacles or small, oft unnoticed details. A dark shade of crimson can barely be seen in a particular monster’s eyes, though you
have to be looking to notice it. Outside of combat, the world is vibrant, colorful,
The lovingly-crafted pixel art paints a picture of an expansive underground community, lively and fun; although sometimes dark and ominous if need be.
And that’s the truly astonishing thing about Undertale, it knows what it wants to be;
Over the course of my journey I was thrown through a whiplash of emotions and events, each delivered with the utmost sincerity and expertise. Many a hearty laugh came from the surprises Undertale had cooked up for those expecting something they'd played before. You're expected it to play like you would any other RPG you've played, and the game decides to play
instead; to take your preconceptions and mess with their very being. I find that if you let the game take your hand, let it guide you down this archaic, joyful, tragic, melancholic, path of madness; you'll come out better for it. Not many games can make you truly
that child-like whimsy of playing your first game, of learning to love your hobby all over again; even fewer can make you truly attached to the characters of its world. I'll admit, I got a bit misty-eyed when my journey had reached its end, when I looked back at all the good times I had with these lines of code I’d come to know as friends. Undertale is a game that sets itself apart from the rest, a game that knows how to be how to be uniquely
One moment, I’m traversing a luminescent grotto; solemnly listening to the hopes and dreams of the species my kind has imprisoned for centuries.
The next, I'm getting lessons on hygiene from a washing machine and its bird.

It's okay if you don't want to play this game. But if you'd like to know about this game's quality first, hopefully I can help.
Gameplay: Undertale is an RPG where monsters' attacks are short, bullet hell sequences (think Galaga or Touhou), while your actions are either to attack or do something else entirely. The gameplay in battles aren't rewarding, and they aren't meant to be, because it's the dialogue during battles that are more interesting. If you're looking for a game where you can play really well and turn around and say, "Did you see that?", you might want to play something else.
What makes this game shine is the breadth of things you can do in battles. You can't cast magic or even attack in more than one way, but you can Hug your enemy, you can Pray to your enemy, you can even start a Flexing contest or play fetch with the enemy. In brief, the gameplay is all trying new actions and surviving bullet hell sequences.
There's also a great breadth of things to do in the overworld. The game is packed with extra dialogue and easter eggs, which you'll find if you explore (e.g. talk to NPCs multiple times, kill this enemy, spare that enemy in a certain way, etc.). Excuse me for being vague, but the game seems to "anticipate" a lot of the choices and actions you'll make. It remembers when you reload your save file, and will adjust dialogue accordingly.
Story:
You're a kid who fell into the underground world of monsters and have to travel to the castle to find a way out. Along the way, you'll meet, fight, and befriend several major monster characters, each with their own agenda, personality schtick, and recurring jokes. Undertale has moments meant to be funny, and it has moments meant to be emotional. It's subjective, but I think this game does these moments very well.
The story is deep. By which I mean, you'll probably miss quite a lot of it if you're not thinking while you play. For an indie game, Undertale has quite a lot of implicit lore and dots to connect.
Presentation:
Undertale has a mix of pixel-based art styles that, strangely enough, don't get tiring to look at. This game is based off of old RPGs like Earthbound with old graphics and simple music. But unlike Earthbound, Undertale CAN go above these graphics and low-bitrate music, and it does so at key points in the game. The sound effects are toony, but only for style. During more dramatic scenes, the sounds become as realistic as they need to be.
Replayability:
Each run of the game is 3-7 hours, depending on what you're doing. However, there are multiple "routes" you can take for very different gameplay, music, and stories, so players often play 2-4 runs. In each run, there are dialogue choices and flavor text that varies depending on what you've done in a previous run.
If you think this game sounds like a good time, you should buy it. If not, that's cool too.

Undertale in and of itself is a journey. At first I was incredibly skeptical of it because I wasn't quite sure of what the game was or how it worked. But once I started playing, I became immediately invested in the story and the characters.
As many of you know, there are different endings and different ways to play. I'm playing the 'pacifist' route, not because of the ending I want to receive, but because I truly don't want to hurt anyone. Characters in the game feel like more than just pixels, and even the little 'grunts' that you fight have little quirks (hugs, flirting, and teasing, oh my!). The fact that you don't have to fight is fascinating to me. You can act. You can have mercy. I have never seen that before in a game.
Another awesome thing about Undertale is its soundtrack and humor. The soundtrack is wonderful to listen to (makes me wish I got the game AND the soundtrack deal.....), and not truly a headache to listen to. First off, let me start by saying DayZ is a game of great potential. I picked it up a year ago, and I still think the game has a lot of great potential. Too bad it seems wasted.
I've logged quite a few hours in this game by now. I've had my ups and downs; but the negative outweighs the positive, unfortunately. I am constantly searching for a game to replace this.
I took a lot of time off, and recently came back to this game. I wasn't really impressed with how little the game has been updated. With this in mind, here are a list of pros and cons:
Pros:
Good graphics
Huge map
Lots of players
Good survival and scavenging mechanics
Great selection of weapons
Decent crafting
Good community
Cons:
Poorly optimized for older systems
No easy way to find friends, or even your bearings (which can be fun and immersive in itself, to be honest)
The animations are pathetic
Melee hitboxes are irritating, prepare to be frustrated by it
Sadly there are lots of cheaters/exploiters/hackers; prepare to get frustrated by these types of players
Zombies are few and glitchy, they walk through walls and their path finding is awful
Lots of glitches and crashes to desktop, prepare to spend 4 hours getting great gear only to lose it all next time you log
Unresponsive controls- press a button to draw your weapon, nothing happens. Press it again, you draw your weapon and then put it away. Just try to jump while running and you will see what I mean.
I want to like DayZ, but at it's current state, it still seems a hot mess. Even after taking a year off of playing the game, it feels like too little has been changed or updated. Paying $30 for this barely functional game is a rip-off.
The Dev team for DayZ has made tens of millions off this game already, but the updates don't show it. Instead of fixing game-breaking bugs, they added extremely rare vehicles and cannibalism. Cool stuff, don't get me wrong, but what I was really hoping for was major fixes to things like melee combat, zombies, and unresponsive controls.
It is still a decent game in itself. I've made sure to log enough hours to justify its price point, and I have had some fun while doing it. Still, all I can think about when I talk about this game is wasted potential. It's sad, and I do hope one day that changes; but for now I will be actively searching for this games replacement.
Thanks for reading,

The characters are wonderfully written, the tone of the game is well paced in where it shifts between highs and lows, and there is a degree of challenge to be had as well. Not a lot else I can say for now, aside it's well worth the purchase price.

The biggest surprise of 2015.
Beautiful soundtrack, awesome gameplay, great story, memorable characters, nice retro graphics, funny as hell, full of feels, a lot of cultural references, nice replayability, insanely cheap, and the most scary aspect: this videogame is "alive".
Everything developed by a single person.
Makes you wonder why are you still looking for games from big companies when ultimately all of them leave you disappointed.
NOTE: Forgot to mention, but don't avoid this game just because its fanbase is kinda toxic, the fanbase doesn't make the game whole in this case. Try it and enjoy.

Undertale isn't a game for everyone, but it has so much characters and so many little nice things. it has easter eggs, plot, references to previous moments in the game and etc. You can be nice to everyone, you can kill monsters while befriending other monsters, or you can straight up murder everyone. But remember. Your decisions are yours. It's all you.
I had a good time.

-A clever, unique twist on the JRPG genre, mixing together elements from games such as Shin Megami Tensei, Earthbound, and Iji.
-A cast of memorable, unique characters that really open up depending on your playstyle. Many of their backstories come from minor details you may not even recognize on your first playthrough, and it makes it rewarding to learn more about your favorites.
-Choices that truly feel like they matter. Whether it's something simple such as dialogue or how you choose to approach a fight, there's plenty there to encourage replayability.
-An incredibly varied and stylized soundtrack that perfectly hits the highest highs and the lowest lows. Each track never feels out of place and encapsulates whatever is happening at the moment.
-Players who aren't used to bullet-hell shooters may find Undertale quite a challenging game to go through, especially when fighting certain characters. There's no real difficulty selection for the game to change this, making it a hard recommend if you aren't a fan of the genre.
-Not enough dogs.
You may notice with the above that I'm being as ambiguous as possible, not really revealing anything about the story, gameplay elements, or anything that really makes Undertale what it is. Simply put, I feel as many people need to approach this game as blindly as possible. This was easily my favorite game of 2015, and no amount of Batmobiles or Fulton extractions will ever change that.
I urge anyone who might be interested in picking it up to not watch any Let's Plays, read any comments about it, or jump on any discussion boards, and go in with an open mind. Yes, parts of the community are dreadful (To be honest, EVERY community has them), and yes, some people herald it as the gaming equivalent of Jesus H Christ riding on a flaming T-Rex doing battle with Cthulu, but look past everyone else's opinions and give it your own. You might very well be surprised what this little indie game might do for you.
TL:DR: Undertale exists as a game because it couldn't exist as anything else.

This game is great; overall I'd give it a 9.5/10.
Pros:
- The characters are endearing and don't overstay their welcomes, and the humor is balanced with seriousness throughout the story.
- If you're going in blind, you'll definitely have your perspective on things different afterwards.
- The battles are more than just luck like most RPGs, it's 99% reliant on your ability to dodge with the bullet hell-style defense mechanic.
- The spritework in this game is near-perfect, only issues I have are when it's a serious moment and they still look like their bright and colorful selves.
- Replayability with the 4 (5?) different main endings and the many, many different decisions you can make throughout the game.
- It's $10 base price, that's cheaper than most games can say.
- Price to gameplay ratio is high, it takes about 20 hours to complete every ending and even longer if you want to find the abundance of easter eggs put into the game.
- If you're planning on doing speedruns, this game is a good pick IMO.
- The soundtrack in this game is extremely fitting, and while the boss themes are great and all, the overworld tracks are what gave the game atmosphere and made it more memorable to me.
Cons:
- There's only so much different things you can do until you've seen it all, and that's what the game mainly runs on. When you first play the game you can go "What happens if I do this?" and find an alternate piece of dialogue compared to if you chose something else.
- (Spoilers sorta?) [Warning anyways] When you complete the Genocide/No Mercy ending you can never get the full-on True Pacifist ending without editing the game files.
- Typos are in this game, one of which is right at one of the endings, which kinda ruined the experience for me.
- "Long Elevator" is considered music and is in the official soundtrack.
- This game is extremely overhyped and while the community says they're a "spoiler-free zone" it's coated in them. The game is also ruined by spoilers (backed by Con #1.)

The biggest surprise of 2015.
Beautiful soundtrack, awesome gameplay, great story, memorable characters, nice retro graphics, funny as hell, full of feels, a lot of cultural references, nice replayability, insanely cheap, and the most scary aspect: this videogame is "alive".
Everything developed by a single person.
Makes you wonder why are you still looking for games from big companies when ultimately all of them leave you disappointed.
NOTE: Forgot to mention, but don't avoid this game just because its fanbase is kinda toxic, the fanbase doesn't make the game whole in this case. Try it and enjoy.

Undertale isn't a game for everyone, but it has so much characters and so many little nice things. it has easter eggs, plot, references to previous moments in the game and etc. You can be nice to everyone, you can kill monsters while befriending other monsters, or you can straight up murder everyone. But remember. Your decisions are yours. It's all you.
I had a good time.

-A clever, unique twist on the JRPG genre, mixing together elements from games such as Shin Megami Tensei, Earthbound, and Iji.
-A cast of memorable, unique characters that really open up depending on your playstyle. Many of their backstories come from minor details you may not even recognize on your first playthrough, and it makes it rewarding to learn more about your favorites.
-Choices that truly feel like they matter. Whether it's something simple such as dialogue or how you choose to approach a fight, there's plenty there to encourage replayability.
-An incredibly varied and stylized soundtrack that perfectly hits the highest highs and the lowest lows. Each track never feels out of place and encapsulates whatever is happening at the moment.
-Players who aren't used to bullet-hell shooters may find Undertale quite a challenging game to go through, especially when fighting certain characters. There's no real difficulty selection for the game to change this, making it a hard recommend if you aren't a fan of the genre.
-Not enough dogs.
You may notice with the above that I'm being as ambiguous as possible, not really revealing anything about the story, gameplay elements, or anything that really makes Undertale what it is. Simply put, I feel as many people need to approach this game as blindly as possible. This was easily my favorite game of 2015, and no amount of Batmobiles or Fulton extractions will ever change that.
I urge anyone who might be interested in picking it up to not watch any Let's Plays, read any comments about it, or jump on any discussion boards, and go in with an open mind. Yes, parts of the community are dreadful (To be honest, EVERY community has them), and yes, some people herald it as the gaming equivalent of Jesus H Christ riding on a flaming T-Rex doing battle with Cthulu, but look past everyone else's opinions and give it your own. You might very well be surprised what this little indie game might do for you.
TL:DR: Undertale exists as a game because it couldn't exist as anything else.

This game is great; overall I'd give it a 9.5/10.
Pros:
- The characters are endearing and don't overstay their welcomes, and the humor is balanced with seriousness throughout the story.
- If you're going in blind, you'll definitely have your perspective on things different afterwards.
- The battles are more than just luck like most RPGs, it's 99% reliant on your ability to dodge with the bullet hell-style defense mechanic.
- The spritework in this game is near-perfect, only issues I have are when it's a serious moment and they still look like their bright and colorful selves.
- Replayability with the 4 (5?) different main endings and the many, many different decisions you can make throughout the game.
- It's $10 base price, that's cheaper than most games can say.
- Price to gameplay ratio is high, it takes about 20 hours to complete every ending and even longer if you want to find the abundance of easter eggs put into the game.
- If you're planning on doing speedruns, this game is a good pick IMO.
- The soundtrack in this game is extremely fitting, and while the boss themes are great and all, the overworld tracks are what gave the game atmosphere and made it more memorable to me.
Cons:
- There's only so much different things you can do until you've seen it all, and that's what the game mainly runs on. When you first play the game you can go "What happens if I do this?" and find an alternate piece of dialogue compared to if you chose something else.
- (Spoilers sorta?) [Warning anyways] When you complete the Genocide/No Mercy ending you can never get the full-on True Pacifist ending without editing the game files.
- Typos are in this game, one of which is right at one of the endings, which kinda ruined the experience for me.
- "Long Elevator" is considered music and is in the official soundtrack.
- This game is extremely overhyped and while the community says they're a "spoiler-free zone" it's coated in them. The game is also ruined by spoilers (backed by Con #1.)
If anyone could tell me how to spoiler-text things that'd be great.

Oh my goodness this game. This GAME! It's one of the best experiences that I've ever gone through, and I didn't regret any second of it (well, maybe a few...) The game offers three distictively different paths that determine how the game will impact you as the player, so I'll be reviewing each one seperately.
Neutral: Not a bad romp through the Underground if I do say so myself. It's not the most satisifing, but it'll help get a feel of how the game works!
Genocide: This is where you'll most likely not enjoy the game, and with good reason! You'll spend most of the time grinding encounters, and you will be met with "a bad time". Unless you are curious on how it goes, or want to beat the hardest boss in the game, then it's better to ignore this one entirely.
Pacifist: As obvious as it sounds, this is where you'll get the most enjoyment out of the game! All the character (even the quote "villian" of the game) are all enjoyable and likeable. It's almost as if the game wanted this route... In any case, if you want to end the game somewhere, I recommend going this route!
Overall, this is a great game for this year. My only real gripe with this is that it's too short for an RPG. Then again, in a game where you're encourage not to kill, this might be for the best. In any case, I highly recommend adding this game to your Steam libary! (Also, soundtrack's pretty good. Try to buy it when y'all get the chance!)

This game holds a special place in my heart. Or should I say soul? Heh (If the game gets to make bad puns, so can I)
If you don't want to read this wall of text, heres the gist folks:
-Solid Gameplay
-Short playtime, but has good replay value
-challenges the norm of rpgs and games in general
-Innovative 4th wall breaking
-Full of the Honey Nut Feelios (Not just the plain old Feelios this time!)
-A Great play for anyone from any walk of life
Anywho. This game is a breath of fresh air. It is an unorthodox approach to a very cut and dry genre of games. This game is the crunchy peanut butter to the originally bland peanut butter and jelly sandwhich. The RPG has been done so many times by so many people that it is hard to believe that there could be yet another innovation coming our way as consumers. This game is quite short, but honestly makes up for it decently in its replay value. It has multiple endings that can be acheived based on the player's choices throughout the story as well as in combat. It takes some universally accepted concepts in RPG's and turns them on their head. It is so innovative, and so good, and the best part is, you don't have to be a seasoned gamer to enjoy this. I have peers from all backgrounds playing this game. I have dedicated FPS players and MOBA grinders to the casual parent picking this game up and giving it a go. When I came back to find them staring blankly at the screen before glancing to me as the little dog napped away on screen, I knew the game had done it for them too. This game not only delivers great gameplay, but it leaves the player setting the controller down or walking away from their keyboard with some human growth within them that was not there before they had sat down to play something they had simply assumed to be a rehash of Pokemon or Final Fantasy. This game made a positive impact on my life and I know it is a game that will be mentioned years from now, revered for its innovation and quality.
Be a part of this experience. Don't be like that person who has to pick up Earthbound at a yardsale from a old parent who doesn't know its worth just to experience a quality game. Treat yourself to something great (and cheap too! For 10 bucks?! Come on!) This is worth your time. This is worth the 10 dollars. It will put a smile on your face and flush your cheeks with warmth each time you boot up the game and see those capital letters humbly spelling out "UNDERTALE" against a sea of black. That same warmth you will feel as you complete the game, and stare down at the small dog, sleeping below that very same letters. Please, do it. It really is wortth it.

I honestly can't believe I'm saying this... but I think this game has usurped Chrono Trigger as my #1 favorite game of all-time.
Toby Fox... you have restored my faith in the video game industry.  I thought the days of truly masterful storytelling and deep emotional investment in a game's characters died with the SNES.
This game is a testament to not just video games, but entertainment writing in general.  I've never been taken on an emotional rollercoaster like Undertale in any video game... ever.  The characters, dialog, and plot are indescribably phenomenal.
I've been playing video games since age 4.  I'm 27 now, and have never experienced anything like Undertale and likely never will again.  To hell with 4k graphics and big-name voice actors.  This is the game - no, the work of art - that all developers and creative writers, gaming industry or otherwise, should be inspired by.
My advice:
1.) Buy the game
2.) Don't kill anyone - If you are forced to fight, run
3.) Complete the True Pacifist ending

I'm a long time RPG player and I'm rarely impressed by RPG's these days and I will admit I at first brushed this off as another overrated artsy game.
I can't express how pleased I am to have been completely wrong!
It starts with a premise that sounds unworkable for a video game.  An RPG where you can go without ever killing anything and in fact the happy ending requires it?  Can't be done many say.  And from there you tell an amazing story of a child's journey through an underworld of colorful and endearing characters that make you grateful that pacifism is an option.  The battle system borrows from Earthbound yet adds it's own special touches that make it far more engaging than most menu systems.  The morality system about killing is nicely blended into the game world so as not to feel gimmicky.  In fact, many gameplay elements such as exp, lv and even saving the game are all incorporated as story elements, something I hope many other games are taking notes on.
I can't discuss the plot in more detail as spoiling would be a grave disservice to you.  Even if you don't care much for RPG's, just pay the 10$ and play this game.  You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll love it!

The game is good, but there are some huge flaws with it. I know it's still in alpha, and I only have 45 hours on record, but that's about all i can stomach. I will say that it is the best zombie survival game currently on the market, but if you are looking for a survival experience, The Long Dark or The Forest is likely a better choice. The zombies in this game have insane hitboxes and because of server instability (at least this is what i attribute it to) you don't even have to be near a zombie for it to smash your face in. That paired with the hackers that you will find on nearly every server makes this game nearly unplayable. I say nearly, because until you get decent gear, you really don't seem to run into any hackers. If you manage to stay undergeared and avoid major cities, you should be ok.
That however, makes this game incredibly boring. The map is big, and that makes it great for a large number of players, but even with a full 64 person server, you will rarely run into anyone in the wilderness. This means that if you want to pvp, you must either venture into a city, or camp up on the road and hope that someone is stupid enough to stroll on through. The graphics look good, but the constant framerate drops make it a huge buzzkill. The mod is more fun, doesn't have bad framerate drops if your machine can handle it, and has much more to offer. I would recommend passing on this game for now and going to the mod instead. I'm not saying there isn't any hacking there either, but i've killed a few hackers that forgot their godmode scripts. Of course they still killed me by nuking the city, but cmon, it was still a pretty fun sight to see.

First off, I really want to say straight off the bat that Undertale is best experienced without any spoilers, and they're very hard to avoid with the current prominence of the game practically everywhere on the internet. However, I still believe you should absolutely play it even if some of the game has been spoiled for you, because a large part of the game is its focus on your decisions.
Now onto an actual review:
Undertale is an excellent game - it frequently gets compared to Earthbound, and while there are some similarites between the two, it very much stands out as its own unique beast. It manages to balance wit with emotion most of the time (although sometimes humour dampens what would be a particularly emotional scene), and moves at a pace that means the game never becomes too tedious or lingers in one area for long.
As much as this game presents itself as an RPG, depending on how you play it can feel more like a puzzle game - this game's overworld is absolutely loaded to the brim with puzzles and traps. The puzzles don't just stay in the overworld, too; that would be far too simple. Most of the time, you won't be able to SPARE enemies right off of the bat, and will need to figure out what's troubling them. Some want a hug, some want an unhug, and yet others would like you to wash your hands. A very large part of the pacifist side of this game is experimenting with different actions to see what works.
The game also manages to pull off its musical cues perfectly: the music in the game contributes perfectly to its atmosphere, from the goofy themes for the more upbeat moments to quiet music-box tunes for its more melancholy parts. The music never feels out of place, and the fact that you can buy the soundtrack with the game is an added bonus.
I'm going to stand by my earlier statement. though, and reccommend you play the game and form your own opinions on it without the influence of other people telling you what to think and what to feel about the whole thing, because the impact of your choices is much better felt when you don't know what the concequences will be ahead of time.

My first review (skip it if you want):
I highly reccommend this game to almost anyone as long as they do not look up too much about the game before playing it (though seeing some things or just simply looking up where to go if you're not sure won't change very much). It seems really short, but it has a lot of depth that you will understand if you play all 3 of the types of runs this game has to offer. These are neutral, pacifist, and genocide. Almost everyone starts off with neutral, and I had great fun with it. It also had the most entertaining ending that caught me off guard. After playing it this way, I thought about it for a while, especially about the game being pretty short with incredibly easy battles and its extremely memorable character. I heard that the 2 other types of playthroughs, however, had a lot of differences to spice things up-including different final bosses. I decided to play this game on pacifist afterwards, the run in which I spare every single monster. I thought it was very much the same even after I finished it, but it did add some funny new scenes and another area. After even more thinking, I realized that throughout the whole experience I still got a lot out of it from doing the second run. Replaying certain things made me notice details that I passed up the first time around. I also realized that even though the earlier battles were easier, they were still fun and prepared me for the very few difficult fights. The genocide run consisted of a high amount of grinding to make sure every enemy was dead, which seemed to be a funny commentary on most RPGs. However, the scenes I had watched twice had uncanny differences that really got to me. It contained the 2 hardest fights in the game (which were the only fights I died on, too, by the way) which took me very long. I had the most fun playing through genocide because of these fights which forced me to prove my skill. I was rooting for the enemy while I played as the villain, which was another really strange part of my experience.
I imagine that the hard mode which is coming out soon will make this game exactly what I want it to be, though I did finish all of the 3 runs with satisfaction.
My new review:
I really did try to trick myself into loving this game, and despite liking many parts of it, I still don't think it was fully worth my time because of how repetitive and problematic most of the time I spent playing it was. There was also too little gameplay and too much gameplay in some places for what the game was trying to do. Neutral and pacifist were each fun where they were different, challenging, and possibly just fun. I enjoyed my first playthrough for the most part, but the enemies I was facing were far too easy and I had too many items (and possible exploits) going for me. My second playthrough was mostly me trying to find new parts of the game among the old. My third playthrough (genocide) was fun when I was in the 2 most difficult fights and NOT exploiting items. Each hour I fought them repeatedly, I sensed myself improving until I FINALLY defeated both of them. Try to limit the items you use if you still want to buy and enjoy this game. However, the rest of it was grinding. I understand the lesson genocide is trying to teach, but one shouldn't really teach it by having the player mindlessly grind through enemies. I love the story and the characters, (I still can't get over them) but despite it being very creative, the gameplay didn't appeal to me. If you're looking for a challenging indie game with a major focus on gameplay, this is DEFINITELY not the game for you. If you particularly want a bullet hell game, there's a lot more to choose from.

As I was in the woods describing what I saw I thought there was a player near me, turned out to be undead. Okay, so I headed down to the nearest building. Once They told me how to open the door(center click) I got inside. Now I had read about how zombies just teleport through walls I was watching for this to happen.  Well, he did not TP into the room but I was starting to take damage. No matter where I moved in the building it was still landing damage on me. Could not figure out how to pick up the crowbar on the shelf and was still getting hit. Now suddenly the walker was walking through the floor. Running around the inside of the house, halfway stuck out of the floor. I left the house to run for it as this was a bad situation. I was bleeding. I was told to make bandages out of my shirt. My shirt was ruined and I could not. Eventually I bled out and became unconcious. I was told to respawn. Okay, so I spawn back in and again run out of plain sight and begin to describe anything unique that I saw. They knew where I was and told me I was too far away and that I should kill myself to respawn. I could find nothing to kill me this time. No falls to drop from or anything. It was coming apparent to me that I would not find my friends and that things just were not coming together. I was really looking forward to trying and loving this game. This late in the development I do not understand why the door damage/no clip for the zombies still exists. Seems like this would be just about the highest priority for now. First off, I really want to say straight off the bat that Undertale is best experienced without any spoilers, and they're very hard to avoid with the current prominence of the game practically everywhere on the internet. However, I still believe you should absolutely play it even if some of the game has been spoiled for you, because a large part of the game is its focus on your decisions.
Now onto an actual review:
Undertale is an excellent game - it frequently gets compared to Earthbound, and while there are some similarites between the two, it very much stands out as its own unique beast. It manages to balance wit with emotion most of the time (although sometimes humour dampens what would be a particularly emotional scene), and moves at a pace that means the game never becomes too tedious or lingers in one area for long.
As much as this game presents itself as an RPG, depending on how you play it can feel more like a puzzle game - this game's overworld is absolutely loaded to the brim with puzzles and traps. The puzzles don't just stay in the overworld, too; that would be far too simple. Most of the time, you won't be able to SPARE enemies right off of the bat, and will need to figure out what's troubling them. Some want a hug, some want an unhug, and yet others would like you to wash your hands. A very large part of the pacifist side of this game is experimenting with different actions to see what works.
The game also manages to pull off its musical cues perfectly: the music in the game contributes perfectly to its atmosphere, from the goofy themes for the more upbeat moments to quiet music-box tunes for its more melancholy parts. The music never feels out of place, and the fact that you can buy the soundtrack with the game is an added bonus.
I'm going to stand by my earlier statement. though, and reccommend you play the game and form your own opinions on it without the influence of other people telling you what to think and what to feel about the whole thing, because the impact of your choices is much better felt when you don't know what the concequences will be ahead of time.

So, I'm going to try to explain why this game is literally the best game I've ever played without spoiling anything:
Pros:
First, it does something that I have almost never seen doen in a video game before... fighting is optional... and has entirely different consequences either way... just that feature alone makes the game stand out from a large chunk of titles.
Second, is the art design. WIth several great artists on the credits, it's no wonder that this game is shelling out sprites that not only simplistic and charming, but also detailed enough to stand from the backgrounds and still have character and empotion flow from them... which brings me to my next point...
Thrid: Story. whether you want to be the kindest soul ever, or fill a massive cave with an even bigger murder pile, the story stays driven, engaging, and able to pull every emotion that you have... Fallout 4, as amazing as it is, can't do that. Also, the story is in no way predictable... I literally went from joy, to tears, to rage, to fear, to joy again...
And, the final piece: The soundtrack... dear god, do I suggest the shelling the extra 8 bucks for the game and soundtrack bundle? Absolutely. These songs are so good by themselves that I found myself not advacning, just to listen to the music. Is there any part of this game that was actually bad? Well, it isn't perfect.
Cons:
First, the gameplay was mediocre, at best. It wasn't repetitve, as it did try to keep you on your toes; yet, the formula was very predictable after the first bossfight. Also, the puzzles were practically fed to you...
Second: Ammount of gameplay and generally linear map design... This is, sadly.. a very short game for how amazing it is... it leaves you wanting more... it leaves you wishing that this could continue forever... but, all good things must come to an end. Although, I would not have minded a much more expansive world with a much less linear path. Even if it meant backtracking, I would have loved just more to explore.
Closing comments: This game, despite it's heavily earthbound inspired art and gameplay... is almost perfect. And, the only factor that made it not perfect is how short it is, as well as how linear and generally repetive the gameplay is. Other than that, I would recommend this game to everyone that does not care about shiny graphics. Everythign from the characters, the story, the music, and even down to the corny jokes that still manage a giggle from you is worth as much as any AAA title. Get the game while it's still 10$... I've ranted long enough... get it for yourself.

I was severely disappointed by this game. I'm not one to normally play bullet hell games, so maybe that's why I didn't like it. I am a huge RPG fan, however, and found Undertale to be severely underwhelming.
First, the good points: The game's OST and style are both fantastic. Even now I still listen to the same tracks I remember from the game, over and over.The style of this game was great too. The 8 bit world looks and feels great and it really feels reminiscent of classic RPGs like Pokemon and Mother. Even moving segments like waterfalls fit in well with the style of it all.
The combat can be decently fun too, as certain enemies require specific combinations in order to beat them without killing them. Some of these seem quite shallow (eg. Flexing several times in a row) but some are unique and fun. The game also gets bonus points for having it set up so the characters' dialogue change depending on your actions, including how you previously played the game and your previous save/load files. I felt this was a neat little tidbit to make the player feel more aware of their actions, that they would have real weight to them.
Now for the bad points.
First and foremost, this game bored me to tears. I had to force myself to finish even one run. Through every section of the game I found myself feeling the need to simply get through that section as there was no real incentive to stay within any one area. A good example is the town of Snowdin, where it might seem alive but there really is nothing to actually do there. The lava area was especially dreary, as it was tedious puzzle after puzzle that was interrupted loads of times by an annoying dinosaur and a talking robot. And what's your reward? One of the most unsatisfying battles with a talking spider. The gameplay, minus some unique Sparing battles, is garbage. You move around and press Z on things. That's it. There is no incentive to do anything besides the main quest because this game has basically zero side quests that actually benefit your gameplay in any way. The puzzles are too easy, plain, and are what you might find in early Pokemon gyms. I don't even know why the puzzles are in this game as they add nothing to it, save for the bits with Papyrus.
Combat as well is garbage if you decide to attack normally. I've heard some people say "well combat isn't a big part of the game" well if you decide to go genocide route, it's basically a third of the entire game (and that's being generous). The dialogue and characters are more hit than miss. Mettaton and Muffet, for example, felt completely out of place and would have been better left out. I understand Muffet was an extra character people paid for, which is fine, but Mettaton has no excuse considering he's in the game so much. Alphys is more tolerable because she at least has personality and reason for what she's doing, but Mettaton is basically "HA LOOK AT ME I WANNA BE FAMOUS OH BTW KEEL ALL HUMANS!!!11" What do Mettaton's constant appearances add to the atmosphere of the game? Nothing. He's basically the Jar Jar binks of the game: A character that adds nothing but is silly for the sake of silly.
The rest of the characters are sort of in the same line. Most of them are quirky for the sake of quirky and don't really fit much into the themes presented in the game. Sans, Asgore, Asriel and Toriel are really the only characters that add to the emotion the game is trying to convey. Even Papyrus, who I like as a character, was quirky for the sake of quirky, but he doesn't really add anything. He wants friends? He wants to be popular? OK great, what does that add to anything? The rest of the NPCs are even worse, throwing out stupid one-liners that don't add anything to the atmosphere trying to be portrayed. Why should I care that your library sign is misspelt? Why should I care that you like the sound of a door knock? Why are you telling you about your buyer's remorse? A lot more effort could have been put into the dialogue, especially with the NPCs who feel more stale than Pokemon NPCs. I will also mention that I didn't like the humour, but I know some people did, so I'm going to leave this as a subjective point.
Overall, Undertale is one of the most overrated games of 2015. I'm a bit disappointed by the internet for rating it so consistently highly especially when I've seen better games rated lower. I'm seriously starting to believe that the only reason people are rating this game so highly is because they were surprised by it, not because they genuinely felt it was a good game.
I know many people will thumbs down my review but instead I hope people will instead reply to it telling me why they think I'm wrong.

The greatest challenge you will face is not defeating every opponent, but sparing, and often, befriending them.
This game can be beaten without killing anyone, and this fact makes the game both heartwarming and heart wrenching, depending on your choices.
Like Earthbound, Undertale can be lighthearted and humerous and deeply disturbing, in many ways, potentially far more disturbing than the material that inspired it.
Even when you reset your game, bad descsions made in previous runs will haunt you. Some characters will become aware of the fact that you reloaded your save in various situations. The game has a minor "glitch horror" component.
Overall, I would recommend this game to everyone and their dog. Definately one of the best games I've ever played with a cast of diverse and lovable characters and a breathetaking soundtrack. So much love was put into this game.  Every time you play you're bound to have a different experience.

(Knowing that this review might get someone to buy this game... it fills you with determination.)
Undertale... oh, what a tale it was. I bought this game, already fully aware of what to expect, however it STILL managed to surprise me... in a very positive way.
You get into the game, get attacked by a flower and then instantly saved by Toriel, one of videogames' sweetest character to ever exist. She teaches you the ways of being a decent human being: DON'T try to solve everything with brute force, try to talk it out. And if you thought this only meant that you can talk your way through key moments: nope, every single fight ('cept for some boss fights) can be won without issuing a single attack-command.
Once your guardian has to leave because of unfinished business, the RUINS are yours to explore: here you might stumble across interesting creatures, such as a number of talking frogs, vegetables trying to make you eat healthy, a melancholic and adorable ghost, John Cena...
Once you're reunited with Toriel, you go ahead and move into a small house, where you have your own, fully decorated room. And let me say this: if there was a chance to STAY at that house from the very beginning... I would've taken it.
However, life can't always be awesome and so you move out to explore the world, get back to your OWN world and maybe make a few friends along the way.
The strongest point of this game -in my opinion- are it's characters. Toriel I've already mentioned, but there's also the skeleton brothers Papyrus and Sans, the adorable, albeit shy and scatterbrained Professor Alphys, the talkshow master Mettaton... there are quite a few, and ALL of them are simply awesome.
I think most people know that this game has multiple paths and whichever you end up with depends on how many 'enemies' you've killed. See, this is interesting, because it means that for me, it is flatout impossible to EVER get a 'genocide' run (you kill... essentially everything and -one) going, simply because every character is WAY to lovable to harm in any way.
Sure enough however, being pacifistic as hell is also really, really rewarding. I don't want to spoil anything, but I'll say this: the 'pacifist' ending honestly is one of the most heartwarming things I've ever witnessed. And I'm not exaggerating.
So, should you buy this game?? Yes, yes you totally should.
Should you PLAY this game?? No, you should FEEL it.
Should you♥♥♥♥♥♥off Sans?? Only if you want to have a BAD time.

This game really understands people, and understands design, and understands humor and fun.  It's an RPG with a very interesting battle system, where bullet-hell dodging mechanics come into play.
You may not like this game if you're looking for high octane action, or if you're averse to a bit of horror elements. The soundtrack is top-notch, spanning styles from retro 8-bit to pumping rock to classical ambiance.  There's something in it for most anyone.
This game is art.

is a game that came out of nowhere and captivated the hearts of many, MANY players, basicly over night. The fanbase is growing on a daily basis on every possible social and art platform, many would argue it's probably just a phenomenon or a
, but I can assure you, there is a reason for all of this hype.
The developers of Undertale dared a risky deal with this game design. You could believe that another retro-style indie game would've turned down by the community in an instant, but there is something important and
Undertale has in comparision to other recent games, even the big titles.
Heart. Soul. And character.
Let's break it down in an old fashioned pros/cons list.
is something pretty rare in most games. You're the hero, killing the bad guys for the better cause, mowing through endless henchmen and evil dudes without a second thought. You're the reaper of evil!
But what if you could look behind the characters of those you've just slain...? Would you still feel good to kill a family father who was forced to do his evil deed? Undertale does exactly that.
Murder is not fun. The game tells you from the very beginning, heck, even in the trailer, nobody has to die in this game. When you're attacking and killing, it's your choice to do so. And if you kill a character, even the monsters in random encounters, they're gone for good. Other characters will react to your murderous intentions. And all of these bad things will eventually haunt you even in new playthroughs. However, if you choose to be patient and nice, to spare your enemies and convience them to your side, you'll have way more fun on your adventure and gain new friends along the way.

First things first, I'm playing on Linux. Any persons interested in playing this one Linux or SteamOS with a future steam machine should run away now. The games concept is great, but Facepunch needs to care more about it's users.
I say that because almost every time I try to play, a new game breaking bug has been introduced. Conveniently the worst bugs appear on Linux too, likely due to a complete lack of testing (Garry has even admitted they don't test it on Linux).
What has motivated me to write this review is a bug with the Unity engine. It was introduced around the 25th of June, and causes keyboard input to allow only one press per key. I think everyone would agree that such a bug makes the game unplayable. Most would also probably say it should be a priority to fix this issue. Sadly Garry's response to such a bug was to say Linux is a second class citizen in his eyes. To add to that, a fix for the issue is weeks off because they would rather wait for the Unity devs to solve it.
For some perspective, the Cities:Skylines devs introduced the same bug with their last update a few days ago. They'd simply missed it in their quality assurance. Despite missing it the issue was fixed in a matter of hours after being reported, so there's definitely a method to work around it. Yet the Rust devs are opting to render support for a whole operating system of users obsolete.
TL:DR - Run if you use Linux or SteamOS. Facepunch and Garry don't care about you in the slightest.
Update - Over one year later. Still not recommended. Sure it looks prettier, but little has changed. It's like they're stuck in a loop of adding things, scraping what they added, then re-adding it in a different way. Doesn't help that the genre is massively over crowded either.

This game is art.

The best Post-Apocalyptic Survival FPS game round the corner is sadly not a Zombie Apocalypse Survival MMOP at all.
Any Z Apocalypse fan knows that across medias of the genre, the core interest is the bleakness of being outnumbered by the zeds, 1 vs 100 if not millions. In DayZ, you can't have more than 50 zeds on a server instance at any given time, or being chased by more than 3-4 of them, so much for being outnumbered. They don't roam in herds or swarms out of urban settings, and if you manage to meet more than 7 in a single big town, consider yourself lucky. Far worse, zombies in DayZ don't infect you. Actually they don't even bite you or try to get your flesh or innards or brain. They punch you and break your femur or bruise your ribs; because they aren't zombies: they must be some kind of mutants with a clunky animation. This is especially important because what makes the Zombie survival genre thrilling is the need to cooperate against those numerical odds. Your first instinct should be to ally with whoever living !@#$ you meet to outdo the odds, simply because it will add to your numerical power against the Living Dead; or add an edge because the guy(s) in your group can heal, or build things, or shoot better or know the area better or are good at finding caches and so on.. Of course, once you secured an area and managed to clean up some, people get bored and start shooting each other. In DayZ this does not, and can not happen, and I doubt it ever will. Since the mutants do not represent any menace, players have to turn against each other to avoid being bored, and simply because the Living Living is the actual danger here; and no bother, because the engine and the idea is around non-stop PvP; not survival in a zombie apocalypse environment.
Let's pass on there is no skills or perks; which is not a prob in itself but adds to the lack of capability to make this game a co-op (again, the base of the zed apocalypse genre); there's no end-game either (well you being dead is the end-game).
Don't get me wrong, I don't moan for a PvE only game, far from that, I love PvP. But if you want to feel like in Day by Day Armaggedon or The Walking Dead or Dawn of the Dead, look out elsewhere, it's not going to happen in DayZ. It is strikingly funny that if you want to join a group of "survivors" in this game, you need to reach out to the forums, or belong to a "clan"; there's no way you'll ever manage to create this group in-game, it can not happen. Well you can consider shooting people in the face to torture them and grab their loot as co-op considering they did the looting for you previous to you shooting thm in the face.
I don't ever recall in any Zombie Survival media people crafting fishing canes and digging for worms then going to the pond to quietly spend their Sunday afternoon tauting the carp; or looking around for berries like cavemen hunters-gatherers; or using cars to drive-bye shooting living human beings, or feeding other human beings cleaning soap. Well in DayZ you can do all of that. Meet the best and biggest PvP arena that also couples with a walking/running Sim in a Post-USSR era Czech republic backdrop. If you wish to feel the utter bleakness of being outnumbered by 99% of the population joining the ranks of the Undead, barricade yourself to feel a tempo spell of security, meet a few survivors like you to group and grow stronger (and eventually fight over the last can of beans or killing some as they get infected), progress day by day in your survival skills vs the undead, don't get this game. Hopefully H1Z1 in my wishlist will do all of that.

If you like or are good at bullet hell shooters, please disregard. If, like me, you either don't enjoy them or are terrible at them, there may be a barrier that keeps you from the same experience many other gamers are enjoying.
Every enemy in Undertale uses a bullet hell attack during the fights and there are a lot of random encounters. A challenge is one thing, but punishing me because I'm never going to be good at your core mechanic is another.
The music was nice and apparently there's a deep story if you can get to it.
I'm disappointed that I can't recommend Undertale, because what I've read about it makes it seem like it's exactly the sort of RPG I normally really like. I feel bad about only giving the game an hour, but the frustration was getting to be too much. It was either become bitter about the experience, or request a refund and give up. So I gave up.

I'll admit, first looks turned me away from the game. I wasn't exactly sure if I would like it.
Then a few dear friends suggested I get it. Some passive, other a bit more... enduring in their goal to get me to play.
After getting in some time both registered and unregistered, I gotta say:
this game is a work of art.
But what makes it so good? The simple art style of it gives it a vibe of the games of yester-year (I'm thinking NES era), and the music ranges from serene to just getting you pumped for whatever comes your way. But the biggest selling point for it was story. Personally, I love a good heart felt story, and this is one of the best that I've encountered in my life. The character arcs, the depth of the various people you encounter in the game, the threads that tie it all together... that's what makes it so memorable. I'm certain even the most stone-hearted of individuals would feel something stir after playing through the whole thing. It's an experience you just don't forget at all.
My only lament is the multiple paths. After doing a certain heart warming run through, it's almost too painful to turn that entire world upside down after what you've been through. some of my friends have actually admitted they could not go for the other ending. After everything, it is really hard to even make that choice. You just wanna keep going the main route over and over to just enjoy those heart felt moments, savour them down to the last bit of warmth they can muster.
But my lament is only short lived. Even with its potential for a darker path, the entire game shines with the knd of polish main stream game titles could even HOPE and DREAM of. And for that, we thank you.

Undertale is a game that was funded by a low-key Kickstarter campaign that raised about $50,000. It was released about a year later than initially promised. The creater, Toby Fox, didn't even expect the game to be reviewed by the mainstream press. Since release, word of mouth, streams, and Youtube let's plays made Undertale one of 2015's most talked about games.
Unfortunately, the popularity has also meant (in about equal measure) fandom circlejerking and people disliking the game out of principle. I think Undertale will be in the same boat as Portal, so profoundly  influential in story and gameplay that people will get sick of hearing about it, even though Portal's popularity was well deserved.
I say this because no matter if you're reading this review at the time of writing or years after the game was released, Undertale is worth your time. You might already know a few of the twists and there may be a dozen copycats with similiar humor and art, but playing this game beginning to end is still something special. Your first playthrough will be brisk but fun with a few surprises in store. Your second and third playthrough will flip all of your expecations, then flip 'em again for good measure.

It's hard to write a review of a game like Undertale, because a game that is this good, this well written... this heartwrenching... is hard to come by. Not many games can tug at the heartstrings in so many ways and offer so many possibilities as you go through the adventure. Though the graphics are basic and pixellated, it adds a charm and sweetness to the game overall (except in the case of a certain yellow flower wherin it becomes absolutely batshit terrifying).
The story is simple. You play as an unnamed child (gender is unknown) who fell down a mountain into the Underground where monsters dwell. From there you have a choice. Spare all the monsters and get their help to escape or kill everything in your path to get away. The choice is up to you, but what you decide affects the ending you get. There are three specific endings or "routes" you can take: Neutral (the most common), Genocide (the most evil), and True Pacifist (the most good). Each one has a different ending and depending on which you get first, also affects subsequent playthroughs. By having your choices affect what happens not just in the story, but as part of the game's structure it makes choices much more meaningful, much more difficult.
There isn't really a villain in the game per se, unless you count Flowey - the yellow flower who will haunt your goddamn dreams and make your nightmares♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves. However there is much more to the creepy flower than meets the eye, and you'll find out his true secret only if you achieve the True Pacifiist ending.
As with most RPG style games, there are some puzzles and sidequests to play with too. Again your choices will come into play here. You will answer questions, make decisions, and meet several memorable characters along the way. Toriel, Sans, Undyne, Papyrus, and Sans are the most popular by far but there are plenty of fun moments to be had just with other NPCs and some of the monsters you encounter as well. Each battle is different and all of them are a lot of fun, and sometimes infuriating as all hell (Mettaton and Flowey, I'm looking at you two).
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. This is a game all fans of RPG and fantasy genres should get a chance to play. Don't overlook its simplistic appearance, its truly what is on the inside that counts here. Oh, and the music. Toby Fox is a fantastic composer and his music is wonderful to listen to throughout the game. Some of the battle themes are truly epic.
As for my own experience, I couldn't begin to tell you how my journey went because doing so would spoil the story. I suppose what I can say, is that I achieved both of the good endings (Neutral and True Pacifist) and had my heart ripped out in the process. It says something when even the 'good' ending can tear your heart into a bazillion pieces and then put it back together with feels and tears.

The best Post-Apocalyptic Survival FPS game round the corner is sadly not a Zombie Apocalypse Survival MMOP at all.
Any Z Apocalypse fan knows that across medias of the genre, the core interest is the bleakness of being outnumbered by the zeds, 1 vs 100 if not millions. In DayZ, you can't have more than 50 zeds on a server instance at any given time, or being chased by more than 3-4 of them, so much for being outnumbered. They don't roam in herds or swarms out of urban settings, and if you manage to meet more than 7 in a single big town, consider yourself lucky. Far worse, zombies in DayZ don't infect you. Actually they don't even bite you or try to get your flesh or innards or brain. They punch you and break your femur or bruise your ribs; because they aren't zombies: they must be some kind of mutants with a clunky animation. This is especially important because what makes the Zombie survival genre thrilling is the need to cooperate against those numerical odds. Your first instinct should be to ally with whoever living !@#$ you meet to outdo the odds, simply because it will add to your numerical power against the Living Dead; or add an edge because the guy(s) in your group can heal, or build things, or shoot better or know the area better or are good at finding caches and so on.. Of course, once you secured an area and managed to clean up some, people get bored and start shooting each other. In DayZ this does not, and can not happen, and I doubt it ever will. Since the mutants do not represent any menace, players have to turn against each other to avoid being bored, and simply because the Living Living is the actual danger here; and no bother, because the engine and the idea is around non-stop PvP; not survival in a zombie apocalypse environment.
Let's pass on there is no skills or perks; which is not a prob in itself but adds to the lack of capability to make this game a co-op (again, the base of the zed apocalypse genre); there's no end-game either (well you being dead is the end-game).
Don't get me wrong, I don't moan for a PvE only game, far from that, I love PvP. But if you want to feel like in Day by Day Armaggedon or The Walking Dead or Dawn of the Dead, look out elsewhere, it's not going to happen in DayZ. It is strikingly funny that if you want to join a group of "survivors" in this game, you need to reach out to the forums, or belong to a "clan"; there's no way you'll ever manage to create this group in-game, it can not happen. Well you can consider shooting people in the face to torture them and grab their loot as co-op considering they did the looting for you previous to you shooting thm in the face.
I don't ever recall in any Zombie Survival media people crafting fishing canes and digging for worms then going to the pond to quietly spend their Sunday afternoon tauting the carp; or looking around for berries like cavemen hunters-gatherers; or using cars to drive-bye shooting living human beings, or feeding other human beings cleaning soap. Well in DayZ you can do all of that. Meet the best and biggest PvP arena that also couples with a walking/running Sim in a Post-USSR era Czech republic backdrop. If you wish to feel the utter bleakness of being outnumbered by 99% of the population joining the ranks of the Undead, barricade yourself to feel a tempo spell of security, meet a few survivors like you to group and grow stronger (and eventually fight over the last can of beans or killing some as they get infected), progress day by day in your survival skills vs the undead, don't get this game. Hopefully H1Z1 in my wishlist will do all of that.

I'll admit, first looks turned me away from the game. I wasn't exactly sure if I would like it.
Then a few dear friends suggested I get it. Some passive, other a bit more... enduring in their goal to get me to play.
After getting in some time both registered and unregistered, I gotta say:
this game is a work of art.
But what makes it so good? The simple art style of it gives it a vibe of the games of yester-year (I'm thinking NES era), and the music ranges from serene to just getting you pumped for whatever comes your way. But the biggest selling point for it was story. Personally, I love a good heart felt story, and this is one of the best that I've encountered in my life. The character arcs, the depth of the various people you encounter in the game, the threads that tie it all together... that's what makes it so memorable. I'm certain even the most stone-hearted of individuals would feel something stir after playing through the whole thing. It's an experience you just don't forget at all.
My only lament is the multiple paths. After doing a certain heart warming run through, it's almost too painful to turn that entire world upside down after what you've been through. some of my friends have actually admitted they could not go for the other ending. After everything, it is really hard to even make that choice. You just wanna keep going the main route over and over to just enjoy those heart felt moments, savour them down to the last bit of warmth they can muster.
But my lament is only short lived. Even with its potential for a darker path, the entire game shines with the knd of polish main stream game titles could even HOPE and DREAM of. And for that, we thank you.

One of the best games I've ever played. Undertale has an

soundtrack. When I first heard about Undertale, I didn't really wanna play it, because of all the hype, but I bought the game anyway, and I'm very glad I did. Undertale is a
enjoyable game. If you don't own this game yet, I highly recommend you buy it, because you'll love it.

Undertale is a game that was funded by a low-key Kickstarter campaign that raised about $50,000. It was released about a year later than initially promised. The creater, Toby Fox, didn't even expect the game to be reviewed by the mainstream press. Since release, word of mouth, streams, and Youtube let's plays made Undertale one of 2015's most talked about games.
Unfortunately, the popularity has also meant (in about equal measure) fandom circlejerking and people disliking the game out of principle. I think Undertale will be in the same boat as Portal, so profoundly  influential in story and gameplay that people will get sick of hearing about it, even though Portal's popularity was well deserved.
I say this because no matter if you're reading this review at the time of writing or years after the game was released, Undertale is worth your time. You might already know a few of the twists and there may be a dozen copycats with similiar humor and art, but playing this game beginning to end is still something special. Your first playthrough will be brisk but fun with a few surprises in store. Your second and third playthrough will flip all of your expecations, then flip 'em again for good measure.

Out of reaction I shot the man in the head and ran off. The female began to chase with her machete. The whistle of her machete swinging in the rain was crystal clear as I hopped over a fence and up the hill. Spaghetti and Meatballs
INGREDIENTS
Sauce:
2 28-ounce cans whole peeled tomatoes in juice, drained, juice reserved, tomatoes finely chopped
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
2 medium onions, peeled, halved through root end
1/2 teaspoon (or more) salt
Meatballs:
1 cup fresh breadcrumbs made from crustless French or country-style bread
1/3 cup whole milk
8 ounces ground beef (15% fat)
8 ounces ground pork
1 cup finely ground (not grated) Parmesan cheese
1/3 cup finely chopped Italian parsley
1 teaspoon salt
1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
2 large eggs
2 large garlic cloves, pressed
1 pound spaghetti
Freshly grated Parmesan cheese (for serving)
PREPARATION
For sauce:
Combine tomatoes with juice, butter, onions, and salt in large wide pot. Bring to simmer over medium heat. Reduce heat; simmer uncovered 45 minutes, stirring occasionally. Discard onions. Using immersion blender, process sauce briefly to break up any large pieces of tomato (texture should be even but not completely smooth). Season sauce with more salt and freshly ground black pepper. Remove from heat.
For meatballs:
Combine breadcrumbs and milk in small bowl; stir until breadcrumbs are evenly moistened. Let stand 10 minutes.
Place beef and pork in large bowl and break up into small chunks. Add 1 cup ground Parmesan, parsley, salt, and pepper.
Whisk eggs to blend in small bowl; whisk in garlic. Add to meat mixture.
Using hands, squeeze milk from breadcrumbs, reserving milk. Add breadcrumbs to meat mixture. Using hands, quickly and gently mix meat mixture just until all ingredients are evenly combined (do not overmix). Chill mixture at least 15 minutes and up to 1 hour.
Moisten hands with some of reserved milk from breadcrumbs, then roll meat mixture between palms into golf-ball-size balls, occasionally moistening hands with milk as needed and arranging meatballs in single layer in sauce in pot. Bring to simmer.
Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until meatballs are cooked through, 15 to 20 minutes. DO AHEAD: Can be made 2 days ahead. Cool slightly. Chill uncovered until cold, then cover and keep chilled. Rewarm before continuing.
Cook spaghetti in large pot of boiling salted water until just tender but still firm to bite, stirring occasionally. Drain.
Using slotted spoon, transfer meatballs to platter. Add pasta to sauce in pot and toss to coat. Divide pasta among 6 plates. Top each serving with meatballs. Sprinkle meatballs with freshly grated Parmesan cheese and serve.

What can be said about Undertale that hasn't already said? This is the formula to making an old game play like new again. Take the classic JRPG style and bring it into the modern era using a bullet hell formula. I was surprised how much I enjoyed the game. But, to look at this critically, we have to assess both the pros and the cons to this game.
PROS
-Wonderful story. Playing through the Pacifist Run was a joy. It was great to meet the interesting, quirky characters (though a couple get annoying) and play through the game the way that Toby Fox intended.
-Nostalgic graphics. I love the old school-style of graphics, so this game was awesome to look at. If you love old games, you'll love the look of this one.
-Humor. There is tons of it in this game. It's hilarious, and you'll love even the absolute worst of puns the game throws at you. The humor was something that drove me to keep playing Undertale.
-Soundtrack is badass. Seriously. Almost every track is worth listening to on its own without playing the game. I've been listening to it nonstop.
-Mostly fair gameplay. Bullet hells are NOT for everyone. That needs to be known before you buy this game. However, they really only punish you for mistakes. There isn't a lot of blatantly unfair BS (save for the final boss in Genocide), and you'll learn to play the game very quickly.
-Price. A cheap, fun, and enjoyable game makes for a happy consumer. For $10, you'll be getting a game of excellent quality.
-Replay value. There are lots of endings and other fun things to uncover throughout the game, so you probably won't do just one run.
CONS
-Genocide Run. Pretty much the entire thing. If you're interested in doing it just to see how the other half lives, prepare yourself for a lot of frustration and anger. This is where the game becomes unforgiving and a bit unfair, especially when you start taking damage when you're selecting an action in the final boss fight. It's extremely difficult, so be warned.
-Length. Though this game is excellent, it's so short that it's kind of disappointing. I beat the entirety of the Pacificst Run in almost one sitting. Just be prepared.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to fans of JRPGs such as Earthbound, as well as fans of bullet hell games, or people that just love to feel warm and fuzzy inside (or like a genocidal murderer, whatever floats your boat). The few cons to this game really don't outweigh the pros, and you really won't regret playing through this gem at least once.
