Take the classic JRPG style and bring it into the modern era using a bullet hell formula. I was surprised how much I enjoyed the game. But, to look at this critically, we have to assess both the pros and the cons to this game.
PROS
-Wonderful story. Playing through the Pacifist Run was a joy. It was great to meet the interesting, quirky characters (though a couple get annoying) and play through the game the way that Toby Fox intended.
-Nostalgic graphics. I love the old school-style of graphics, so this game was awesome to look at. If you love old games, you'll love the look of this one.
-Humor. There is tons of it in this game. It's hilarious, and you'll love even the absolute worst of puns the game throws at you. The humor was something that drove me to keep playing Undertale.
-Soundtrack is badass. Seriously. Almost every track is worth listening to on its own without playing the game. I've been listening to it nonstop.
-Mostly fair gameplay. Bullet hells are NOT for everyone. That needs to be known before you buy this game. However, they really only punish you for mistakes. There isn't a lot of blatantly unfair BS (save for the final boss in Genocide), and you'll learn to play the game very quickly.
-Price. A cheap, fun, and enjoyable game makes for a happy consumer. For $10, you'll be getting a game of excellent quality.
-Replay value. There are lots of endings and other fun things to uncover throughout the game, so you probably won't do just one run.
CONS
-Genocide Run. Pretty much the entire thing. If you're interested in doing it just to see how the other half lives, prepare yourself for a lot of frustration and anger. This is where the game becomes unforgiving and a bit unfair, especially when you start taking damage when you're selecting an action in the final boss fight. It's extremely difficult, so be warned.
-Length. Though this game is excellent, it's so short that it's kind of disappointing. I beat the entirety of the Pacificst Run in almost one sitting. Just be prepared.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to fans of JRPGs such as Earthbound, as well as fans of bullet hell games, or people that just love to feel warm and fuzzy inside (or like a genocidal murderer, whatever floats your boat). The few cons to this game really don't outweigh the pros, and you really won't regret playing through this gem at least once.

I approach this review with an objective. Can I recommend DayZ?
Objective is the word. I have to admit to being an original DayZ Mod Alpha player, and fan. Can I be objective from this standpoint? With difficulty. And under one massive caveat: DayZ Standalone is a work in progress and should not be viewed as a final and polished product.
The DayZ Mod was a breath of fresh air. It chimed a bell within me that hadn't been rung in a long time. It resonated louder than Fallout 3, louder than Grand Theft Auto San Andreas, louder than many full title games from the past. I found myself immersed more completely in Chernarus through DayZ than I did with ARMA II. And ARMA II, like it's predecessors, was one hell of a game. It gave me all the freedoms I wanted from a game. An open world, a sense of realism many games cannot muster, and a lack of nagging narrative. All these things drove me forward to find the next upgrade for my kit, to live on the boundaries, survive unchallenged.
For all these gripping positives, I still felt it was incomplete. And so it was. After all, it is a modification to an existing title.
When they announced the DayZ Standalone game, I was excited. I read the devblogs, garnered details, and found myself wondering if this would live up to its' obvious potential.
I bought the Standalone relatively late. I found myself resisting the temptation to dive in too early. I didn't crave disappointment.
When I played my first session, I found myself disoriented. I think that was a good sign, having spawned in the north end of the map, as it gave me the instant impression that things had expanded and improved from the Mod. And I was not disappointed. I found the graphics to be sharp, I was impressed with the character model and movement. A lot of that had been tidied up and tweaked to a satisfying level. The amount of enterable building made me smile, as too the loot placement. A lot of thought had already been implemented into tangible progress.
But it does lack quite a bit from the Mod.
That is not a point of detraction. At all times, it has to be remembered that it is Early Access. (This is a concept that was unimaginable 10 years ago.) There is a development roadmap that is being diligently followed. As things are implemented and successive builds are released, things will improve, more content will become available. This is the Early Access model. A lot of people are very happy to be a living part of the development of this title. I am.
And that is the point where a decision on recommendation must be made. I can recommend this to anyone who understands what they are getting into here. The purchase of this title right now allows you to play a work in progress, to contribute to a living development process, and best of all, it's fun.

Game is great! Nothing quite like it! From the morality system to the game mechanics. This game is the product of Toby Fox's DETERMINATION to make the best game out there. Don't let the simple graphics deter you for the gaming market has proven time and time again that not all good games have good graphics.
At first it plays like any JRPG, walking in an overworld until an encounter happens. One thing that set this game apart is it's added opportunity to hopefully spare everyone and gain gold. You might not get EXP doing them but the game doesn't even need it anyway. It's PERFECTLY doable to finish the game at LV 1.
Now for the enemy "phase" of the game. This is where the it's charm got me. Instead of a classic "Enemy uses X", the game will immediately transform itself into a state akin to a "bullet hell" game giving you an opportunity to dodge their attack completely. That isn't even the only thing the enemy can do during it's "phase". Some enemies may turn the "defense phase" into a platformer, a timing-based mode, even a shooter version of the bullet-hell mode.
Characters are well thoughtout. Every NPC and even the encounter monsters and bosses have a story to them if you give them the time talk instead of blantantly murdering them >:T
Story is dependant upon every action you make. From sparing every monster to murdering everything in your path, they heavily impact the game in a way that even persist through other gameplays. The game will keep track of your every action even if you reset the save file. The game will remember.
The soundtrack is just beautiful. From silly to intense, the music complements to game very well.
EDIT: One thing I forgot to mention. This game is best enjoyed when you have absolutely no knowledge of what's to come. If you're planning to get the game, avoid spoilers like the plague.

Undertale wears the trappings of an early 90s JRPG, but exploits the potential of that medium to the hilt.
The graphics are dated. You probably already know that. Keep in mind, that's because of aesthetic and money, not because of technical limitations. That means there's room for exceptions. You'll probably encounter a few of those exceptions if you get far enough.
The music is something special. The game's developer made much of his name as a soundtrack composer, and it shows. Themes fit characters and situations. The mood is appropriately set. Leitmotifs resurface at just the right times. The soundtrack is interwoven with the story at a level that very few games manage to reach.
The combat system is, superficially, very JRPG, but there are enough twists on the standard recipe to make combat interesting no matter your style of play. Tactical and exploratory depth can be found in the Act system, while execution and twitch reflexes are rewarded on attack and defense. Every monster comes with their own special mechanics, and most equipment (weapons especially) has an effect beyond just boosting ATK and DEF. And as long as an option exists on the in-battle menu, it has the potential to be important; especially in boss fights, sometimes the action you need to take is an action whose usual mechanical effect belies what it'd mean in that fight's context.
Speaking of menu options: you will occasionally feel frustrated by a lack of nuance in your dialog options during out-of-combat conversations. I felt that frustration too, once or twice. But like everything else in this game, it's like that for a reason.
Let's emphasize that. Everything in this game is the way it is for a reason, even if that reason is sometimes just "because it's funny" or "because it's cool". Sometimes, that reason is the way you played. And for people rolling their eyes at the apparent triteness of "Fight or Spare" as a game concept, while "the way you played" includes that variable, it also goes far beyond it.
Everything in this game is the way it is for a reason, and sometimes that reason is "there's something going on here that you don't yet understand."
The characters have hidden depths, no matter how simple they might seem at first. You will be mistaken about them, just as you will be mistaken about the world you're exploring, and its past, and its future. But as the story unfolds, many of those things become clear.
Undertale is one of the best RPG video games I've ever played. Possibly *the* best, and I say that as someone who grew up with FF6 and Secret of Mana, and then discovered Earthbound as an adult. If you've played a few JRPGs in your time, and are familiar with the way one normally plays them, then there's some things in Undertale that are there especially for you. But the game stands on its own merits, too. It's a story about engaging with the world around you and the people around you. What it means to do that, and what it means when you don't do that.
It's good stuff. And as much as I realize why it had to be as short as it was, I still wish there was more of it.

Although in a somewhat buggy alpha state, many things being somewhat glitchy and combat also feeling sluggish and buggy, it does help deliver what I expected it to. It gave me a true sense of "survival." Should I get that can of beans and risk getting shot? or try another place with the risk of starving before then? You make many choices in this game, and I felt that it really helped deliver the decision making, atleast to some level, in a surival situation.
It was fun as I would constantly discover new items of interest and it created a incentive to constantly move around.
Helped make the game feel more open and free as compared to a smaller map which would feel cramped, repetitive, and would make for a terrible cluster eff on popular servers.
Although not technically a game mechanic, this game is able to make you feel fear. Whether its the fear of dying or the feel of losing everything. Everytime I fought someone, or thought someone was there, it was extremely stressful, in a good way.
This game is plagued with many bugs, though not all game-breaking, the mass amount of bugs really hampers the experience by quite a bit. Especially when you randomly die or lose you character due to it.
This game isnt really THAT well optimized, though not terrible. Many times it feels just there were too many frame drops even though i'm using a GTX 780Ti.
Though fun espcially being able to use both first and third person, the combat honestly felt extremely buggy, unpolished, and often broken. Many times I would be really close and have my scope on someone, but it would magically miss. And many times it felt that the bullets just were registering a hit or the enemy would be able to magically not get hit by it. This is probably due to some server to player issues, but  it is still quite annoying.
Although the game has many bugs hampering it, this is mainly due to the alpha state or "early access" state of the game. I'm sure all the problem will get patched eventually, and even at this point the bugs are merely hampering and annoying, but never really game breaking for me. The plus sides to this game greatly outweigh the negatives, and it also feels good to be apart of creating a game through providing feedbacks. DayZ helps provide a semi-authentic experience on survival and although hampered by many bugs, it shows great promise through constant updates and a solid game underneath the bugs.

If you don't know anything about this game yet...I'm surprised.
It's blown up everywhere, and for a good reason. I saw it on steam when it first came out, but had zero interest in playing it due to the graphics. However, I later saw fanart of when Sans stacks hotdogs on your head, and that was when I knew I had to play it.
I don't own the game myself, just played it through a shared library, but I would definitely buy this game like fifty times if I had the money, if only to support Toby Fox.
One final thing before jumping into the actual review: Few games have made me cry - and I think all of them are from Telltale - but this game made tears stream down my face at least twice.
About the game:
Undertale is a game that can be played multiple times. Choices in your playthrough effect later choices in your playthrough, and some can even end up changing your NEXT playthrough. The main choice you can make in Undertale is what you do when encountering an enemy. There's a choice to fight, which will bring up what I can only describe as a meter of a sort, and you have to land your hits on the marked area. Or, instead, you can interact with the enemies. You can talk to them, pet them, hug them, flirt with them, threaten them, and more, and if you do the right thing, you are given the option to spare the enemy.
The enemies themselves will, of course, attack back no matter what you do (under most circumstances), until you spare or kill them. As other reviews say, it's sort of like a bullet hell, though as someone who is really really terrible at bullet hells, I had no problem with the fighting in this game. After the first turn or so, it's easy to see the patterns of attack. And in the chance that you do get hit, there's still health items in the game that you can use.
Another aspect of the game I love is the characters and plot, which I'd consider the most redeeming part. I went into this game knowing a few characters already, and of course I was excited when they showed up. And yet, with each character introduced, I found that I had a new favorite. "Here's a small ghost, I love him. Oh wait, this skeleton is making puns, he's the best. Wait, there's a robot, ignore everything I just said." They all have distinct personalities, too. Some negative reviews say otherwise, which I don't understand, because they each have a certain style of speech that really adds to them as characters, along with how they react, their "talking" sounds, and even just how they look. There are also negative reviews saying the humour is too dry, and I guess this is a matter of opinion. I loved the humour - it added nicely to the characters, to the world, and to the atmosphere. A lot of the jokes told in this game made me laugh out loud, which doesn't happen very often. But all of these things tie in to the plot.
I am someone who will get very attached to plots. I love stories; I love writing stories, I love reading stories, I love playing story based games.
The plot of this game is definitely in my top five plots in games. The initial "Monsters and Humans" is given details and explanations. The history that is told through the game all leads up to the finale, and depending on the ending you get, and how many times you've played it, everything ties together in a fantastic way.
A few more minor parts of this game that I really enjoyed were the soundtrack and the secrets. I never really listened to VGM as background music up until I played Dragon Age Inquisition, but that had been the only game I had ever listened to the complete soundtrack at least twice, up until this game. Undertale's music fits its graphics, but the soundtrack really helps the characters and atmosphere. Each area in the game has a couple songs that play on repeat, and each character has their own theme. Each time I fought a boss, I would say "this is my favorite song in the soundtrack," only to change my mind as soon as I encountered the next boss. I love the soundtrack in this game so much that I've already arranged Bonetrousle and Spider Dance, two boss themes, for a string quartet, even though I'd never tried to figure out a song from a game for multiple instruments before.
There's no shortage of secrets in this game, also. Be it interacting with hidden things, solving certain puzzles, waiting in certain rooms, backtracking, reloading your game, or just naming your character a certain thing, there will be little surprises that, although have no affect on your game, are a cute (or heartbreaking) addition anyways.
In conclusion, this game was 100000 times better than expected. I fell in love with everything about it; only a few things have ever completely taken over my life like Undertale has. It's best to play if you haven't already seen any videos or pictures, but regardless, if you haven't played it yet, find ten dollars and buy this now, because it'll last you a while.
And even when you're done, it'll still stick with you for a long, long time.

This is Rust; Where headshots make a sweet little crunch, No base is safe from a couple anti-noob engineers. And if you hear a beeping sound, you're about to be evicted.
Rust is an open world survival, shooting, building, crafting and raiding game that is updated weekly and made by Facepunch.
Before I get you little tribal savages assembled for a war party and send you to your guarenteed deaths. I want you to ask yourself one question. How angry have you been at a video game? If the answer is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ then multiply that number by 5, carry the 10, and you're still no where near the rage Rust induces. Something about losing your home, farm and life activates a special part of the lizard brain that most games can't touch.
Spawning:
Immediatly spawning on the coast like a ship-wreaked sailor with a rock and a torch, the map you are most likely on is a precedually generated map unique from every server,similar to minecraft. Although the map is unique, there are preloaded points of intrest i.e ( The dome, Radiation Towns, Water Treatment Plant, and soon the Rocket Factory) They are all connected by roads. The map itslef has biomes too. Early game Rust is the most brutal becuase you are the most vurnrable to players, animals and the enviroment, since you are un armed and homeless. For the majority of your early game (Day 1-4) you WILL be out-gunned. You have the best chance of survival scavenging scraps of bases you find.
Once you build a base, this will be your head quarters, you will hoard materials for your big stable base. You will struggle to find food and clothing but being in the right biome will help you tremendously. Dont head for the snow withot clothes becasue you will freeze.
Raiding:
Now with your epic base and tons of recourses, what do you do? You Raid other people of course. SInce raiding is considered an offensive approuch to Rust, be sure to have the materials to supply explosives and gear neccisary for raiding. Solo Raiding in Rust is very difficult, it is recommended that you bring some friends along. The defender has built their base to go against raiders, the have sniper towers that never see action until your poor soul happens to come to raid. They have hours upon hours of work and you will take that away within minutes. If you're raiding solo, raid the defender while they are offline, this will put the odds more in your favor. This is the safest raid to do solo. Most players think of raiding as an investment, hoping to get more resources out then you put in. Online raiding can be one of the most envirgorating experiences the game as to offer. When you get your friends togther to raid a base while the owners try to kill you, when you have c4 and all your guns on you is an experience like no other game has to offer.  Some of the most epic moments in Rust is when the Raid you are conducting is being talked about throught the whole server, nakeds come to watch or take scraps, looters run towards the comotion, everyoone holds their breath to see which side will win.
Rust will be a challenging but rewarding experience, enjoy your adult Minecraft

TL;DR Good concept, crappy gameplay, horridly optimized.
This game is an amazing idea, with a mediocre implementation, and a terrible developer team. I have 90 hours in the game, and have been playing since the start. I have also been an active community member and tester since then. However, Garry (the developer), in his infinite arrogance, has decided to stop properly supporting Linux, though support is still advertised. The game was totally broken on Linux for weeks, until a Unity update fixed Garry's mistakes.
For Windows and Mac OS users, the game will technically work, but it is very poorly optimized. I have a GTX 680 and a 4.5 GHz 4th generation Intel i5, and I can barely get 25 FPS at full settings. Fine, whatever. The problem is that I have to set everything to minimum to come anywhere close to 60FPS, and even then the framerate is highly unstable.
Now, about the gameplay. Crafting and loot spawning is illogical (empty cans are more valuable than full ones, and more useful; full cans don't turn into empty ones when emptied; animals all produce wolf meat, even chickens; pistol bullets cost as much as 5.56 ammo; and many other problems). While the game is very much an endless grind occasionally punctuated with excitement, those moments of excitement can be quite gratifying.
Basically, if you run on Linux, you cannot rely on being able to play this game; Garry might break it at any time. If you run on Windows with anything but a top-of-the-line machine, you can barely play this game. In either case, this game is not worth $20. Buy ARK: Survival Evolved or DayZ instead.

This game is hard to get started on. The number one thing I can tell you to do is, video record your first few lives. Not only can you learn from your early mistakes, but they make great memoirs a long time from now.
Read the wikis and forums, they will be your greatest aid. If you can't figure out what tools you can use to open that can of beans, or how to throw punches, you won't get far from the coast. Despite all those shiny new buildings you can enter, very few have useful amounts and/or types of inventory. Use maps like
or iZurvive to figure out how to maximize your loot vs time ratio. Food does you the best amount of good in your stomach so eat it all if you need space, but don't cause yourself to vomit unless you have a LOT of spare food on hand (And you aren't freezing to death).
If someone contacts you in direct chat, just assume you are F**ked and in a trap, do what they ask and you might survive. Don't get cocky until you feel reeeeaaal experienced with the game (and have good internet connection), as you will probably lose.
Final opinion, this game is what I would call a zombie sandbox that is made by the players (Devs just do us the hard work of putting it in, make sure to kiss the chef next time your favorite gun is added). It is fun to play, but requires time to invest in the best characters that, without skill, is a waste of time and will get sent back to the coast immediately. I love the ever-changing scenarios and the development process, it gives you something to explore and have fun in.

I'm not really an RPG guy, but I've been hearing/seeing a lot about this game, and it has been testing my interest, and so I could see why the hell everyone was going ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ over it. It took me having a friend drag me along to a fan-made sim of this game in a virtual chat game called 'Second Life' to convince me enough to try it out; what drew me into it the most was the game's nice retro indie style. I'm a fan of indie games so, of course, this was going to attract me.
I haven't played all too much of this game yet, but I have played enough to give a fair take on it in saying that I definitely really appreciate its dry quirky humor and unique style the most. I like how you can interact differently with enemy encounters instead of just battling them to the death. You can talk to them, joke to them, flirt with them, etc., depending on what the enemy is. A lot of them have cheesy puns as names, too, and they all have unique and vibrant personalities. Another thing I like is how they break the fourth wall quite a bit. So you can put a lot of diversity into this game depending on how you decide to play it.
Another thing I though that was really neat and innovative was the game's battle system. Instead of just sitting there and letting stats and chance decide if you get hit and how much damage you take, you actually have to move a heart icon around in a box and dodge a bunch of objects that are relevant to the enemy's attacks. I feel this adds more fun and immersment into the encounters.
I think the game has a pretty nice soundtrack. It also fits the quirkiness and personality spot on with certain enemy encounters I have noticed.
Well, that's my take on the game so far. I suggest it if you're wanting to play something relaxing with some humor. I have found the game pretty relaxing to play and that's usually kind of what I use it for.

I can't reccommend this game; and the reason is very simple: its very frustrating to play.
The first thing is that it is based on a leveling system - something that DOES NOT and WILL NEVER work in a survival game like this. Players starting out will be very frustrated by their inability to craft advanced weapons, armor, and gear, and be forced to spend hours grinding to be able to craft, but will be killed often by players who just want blood.
The next thing is the experienced players
to help you. They want to keep you alive long enough to laugh at you, and then dance around your dying corpse - and maybe not even that long. Even if you have good gear, you're going to lose it within 10 minutes to someone who has a better spot on the map than you, even better gear, and more people. When you walk outside your base with good loot on, you're going to lose it. And if its not the first or second encounter, it's gonna be the third or fourth.
The fun part about survival games is rarely the PVP. PVP is like the icing on the cake - the core of these games is meeting the funny and interesting people along the way - meeting your enemies, meeting friends, and meeting that Bill Cosby impersonator fresh spawn who for some reason just
leave you alone. And RUST just doesn't create that experience - the only types of people you'll meet are the blood thirsty wolves that just wanna be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and show you how much of a bigger♥♥♥♥♥♥they have than you by picking on the little guys.
RUST succeeds in its gun play, beautiful enviornment, base building mechanics, and how smooth it feels - or how clunky it doesn't feel. Even all of this, and an excellent development team at Facepunch is still not enough to make up for just how truly bad the experience is.
RUST fails in so many aspects to deliver a real survival game experience, and I truly expected more from a talented development studio.

The engine the game is built on is so poorly optimized that if you have an average gaming PC you will be very lucky to get above 30fps. For every fix that is released, 2 more are needed. I will update this review if the game ever comes out of alpha, but for now it is a good example of how flawed Steam's early access program is, with devlopers making their money, and then feeling no pressure to finish their game.

I've played this title off and on since legacy, and watched it change a lot as I've racked up the hours. An apt summary of this title would be that it resembles an (M) rated minecraft with guns and very heavy teamplay and PvP requirements.  These are coupled with gathering/building elements, with a dash of survival tossed in.  The build tools are functional and fairly robust.  The gunplay is solid.
So, why can't I reccommend it?
Well, there are still issues.  Lots of them.  Hackers are everywhere, and if you play on the official servers you'll encounter this almost right off the bat.  Headshots thru brush in the dead of night, people flying around, noclipping thru walls, it's really bad.  Private servers are better but still not immune.
Another issue is the grind.  Holy mother of grind.  I hope you like hitting rocks, son.  And trees.  For hours and hours and hours and hours and hours on end.  Seriously, 9/10 of my played time was spent hitting objects with a hatchet, pickaxe, or hammer.  And then, once you assembled the materials together, you queue up a batch of gunpowder and then alt+tab and go watch youtube for an hour.  Then you come back, see what you have, and start making stuff with the gunpowder.  Alt+tab again.
It takes over an hour of queue time to make a single C4, on top of the assembled materials and smelting.  That alone will turn many people off.
On top of the time investment required to make high-tiered goods, there is also the matter of protecting it.  Which is where the main reason I can't reccommend this title comes into play.
Rust is a social experiment.  Anything you craft in-game can, and probably will be raided and stolen, no matter the defenses.  People will add you to their friends list for the sole purpose of knowing if you're offline or not in-game, so as to determine the perfect time to steal all your items.  Rust is a soul-crushing digital manifestation of what happens when the world breaks down and guns and explosives are the only form of barter or negotiation.
It is a beautiful game.  The sunrises and sunsets are majestic.
What it does to people. however, is the exact opposite.  Rust is a more brutal, unforgiving, and relentless online arena than EvE Online - as even in EvE. you could park your assets in a neutral station and wait for the storm to pass.  Here, the storm is everywhere... right outside your door, crawling on your ceiling, while you're asleep in your bed.  Waking up to find your assets intact in Rust can be considered a major accompishment, and usually only practical for those in large clans which cross multiple time zones.
Ultimately. the game is fun, but the community makes it very difficult to enjoy for individual or small group gamers.  The mechanics are stacked so heavily towards larger groups and resource pools that banding up is a necessity.  Trust then becomes an issue.  Political conniving and intrigue and backstabbing ensues.  Hilarity sure to follow.
I would echo other players' sentiment in that this title holds one of that most atrocious, obnoxious communities in gaming that I have ever experienced first-hand, rivalling LoL and DoTA2.  This is not a problem isolated to one server or group; it is pandemic across the entire community and as of date of this writing, it still exists in spades.
The core progression curve and experience is, on paper, rewarding.  It's a shame that the actual gameplay 90% of the time is 3 guys with guns chasing you down for your rock, ad-infinitum.
Occassionally, as a solo player, you'll find a decent lowpop server which enables progression.  And the server admins will wipe your progress randomly midweek because they don't GAF about lowpop servers.
In all honesty, in spite of the many hours of immersion in this title, I think that nothing short of the mark of Cain could adequately rate this product, and of all the gaming experiences I've had in my life, this has been among the most frustrating and painful... on every level.  From random wipes, to hackers, to admin abuse, to 90 % of the community being total and utter mouthbreathing♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bags, any and all of which will destroy days or weeks of progress.  I wouldn't wish my time spent on this product upon my worst enemy, and I mean that.
Based on what I've seen on rustafied, twitter, and devbuilds, the dev team seems totally disconnected from the gameplay experience, and their focus is not being spent in areas that positively affect gameplay.  I do not have faith that it has a long-term plan that will result in a well-received title by most gamers.  People have been asking for some type of legiimate PvE activity since legacy.  What they got was an attack helicopter that flies around the map murdering freshspawns as they try to farm blueprints without a weapon that could even hit the chopper.  Oh, and did I mention that the helicopter drops unique components for building automated turrets that you can only acquire in this manner?  What this translates to is that new and solo players now have an even larger curve to overcome, and the large clans that run every server now also have automated gun turrets all over their bases.  Balance.
It should also be noted here that this latest release still contains known bugs, some of which can cause your system and internet to hang or BsoD, leading to hardware damage and data corruption over time.
If you are going to purchase this title, make sure you have a large group with a high threshold for self-inflicted injuries and a LOT of time on their hands, and a recent system restore.
For me, this game exposed a darker part of the human psyche that I haven't seen for a long time, and hoped to never see again until the wheels fall off.  It's a beautiful game, hauntingly so.  But the amount of time investment to get anywhere is preclusive for most.  And for those who invest the time to dig deep into the game, they might not like what they find in their fellow gamers within this arena.
This is one of the few PC games where I can justly declare that there are no winners.  The only way to win at Rust is not to play at all.

If you don't know anything about this game yet...I'm surprised.
It's blown up everywhere, and for a good reason. I saw it on steam when it first came out, but had zero interest in playing it due to the graphics. However, I later saw fanart of when Sans stacks hotdogs on your head, and that was when I knew I had to play it.
I don't own the game myself, just played it through a shared library, but I would definitely buy this game like fifty times if I had the money, if only to support Toby Fox.
One final thing before jumping into the actual review: Few games have made me cry - and I think all of them are from Telltale - but this game made tears stream down my face at least twice.
About the game:
Undertale is a game that can be played multiple times. Choices in your playthrough effect later choices in your playthrough, and some can even end up changing your NEXT playthrough. The main choice you can make in Undertale is what you do when encountering an enemy. There's a choice to fight, which will bring up what I can only describe as a meter of a sort, and you have to land your hits on the marked area. Or, instead, you can interact with the enemies. You can talk to them, pet them, hug them, flirt with them, threaten them, and more, and if you do the right thing, you are given the option to spare the enemy.
The enemies themselves will, of course, attack back no matter what you do (under most circumstances), until you spare or kill them. As other reviews say, it's sort of like a bullet hell, though as someone who is really really terrible at bullet hells, I had no problem with the fighting in this game. After the first turn or so, it's easy to see the patterns of attack. And in the chance that you do get hit, there's still health items in the game that you can use.
Another aspect of the game I love is the characters and plot, which I'd consider the most redeeming part. I went into this game knowing a few characters already, and of course I was excited when they showed up. And yet, with each character introduced, I found that I had a new favorite. "Here's a small ghost, I love him. Oh wait, this skeleton is making puns, he's the best. Wait, there's a robot, ignore everything I just said." They all have distinct personalities, too. Some negative reviews say otherwise, which I don't understand, because they each have a certain style of speech that really adds to them as characters, along with how they react, their "talking" sounds, and even just how they look. There are also negative reviews saying the humour is too dry, and I guess this is a matter of opinion. I loved the humour - it added nicely to the characters, to the world, and to the atmosphere. A lot of the jokes told in this game made me laugh out loud, which doesn't happen very often. But all of these things tie in to the plot.
I am someone who will get very attached to plots. I love stories; I love writing stories, I love reading stories, I love playing story based games.
The plot of this game is definitely in my top five plots in games. The initial "Monsters and Humans" is given details and explanations. The history that is told through the game all leads up to the finale, and depending on the ending you get, and how many times you've played it, everything ties together in a fantastic way.
A few more minor parts of this game that I really enjoyed were the soundtrack and the secrets. I never really listened to VGM as background music up until I played Dragon Age Inquisition, but that had been the only game I had ever listened to the complete soundtrack at least twice, up until this game. Undertale's music fits its graphics, but the soundtrack really helps the characters and atmosphere. Each area in the game has a couple songs that play on repeat, and each character has their own theme. Each time I fought a boss, I would say "this is my favorite song in the soundtrack," only to change my mind as soon as I encountered the next boss. I love the soundtrack in this game so much that I've already arranged Bonetrousle and Spider Dance, two boss themes, for a string quartet, even though I'd never tried to figure out a song from a game for multiple instruments before.
There's no shortage of secrets in this game, also. Be it interacting with hidden things, solving certain puzzles, waiting in certain rooms, backtracking, reloading your game, or just naming your character a certain thing, there will be little surprises that, although have no affect on your game, are a cute (or heartbreaking) addition anyways.
In conclusion, this game was 100000 times better than expected. I fell in love with everything about it; only a few things have ever completely taken over my life like Undertale has. It's best to play if you haven't already seen any videos or pictures, but regardless, if you haven't played it yet, find ten dollars and buy this now, because it'll last you a while.
And even when you're done, it'll still stick with you for a long, long time.

This is Rust; Where headshots make a sweet little crunch, No base is safe from a couple anti-noob engineers. And if you hear a beeping sound, you're about to be evicted.
Rust is an open world survival, shooting, building, crafting and raiding game that is updated weekly and made by Facepunch.
Before I get you little tribal savages assembled for a war party and send you to your guarenteed deaths. I want you to ask yourself one question. How angry have you been at a video game? If the answer is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ then multiply that number by 5, carry the 10, and you're still no where near the rage Rust induces. Something about losing your home, farm and life activates a special part of the lizard brain that most games can't touch.
Spawning:
Immediatly spawning on the coast like a ship-wreaked sailor with a rock and a torch, the map you are most likely on is a precedually generated map unique from every server,similar to minecraft. Although the map is unique, there are preloaded points of intrest i.e ( The dome, Radiation Towns, Water Treatment Plant, and soon the Rocket Factory) They are all connected by roads. The map itslef has biomes too. Early game Rust is the most brutal becuase you are the most vurnrable to players, animals and the enviroment, since you are un armed and homeless. For the majority of your early game (Day 1-4) you WILL be out-gunned. You have the best chance of survival scavenging scraps of bases you find.
Once you build a base, this will be your head quarters, you will hoard materials for your big stable base. You will struggle to find food and clothing but being in the right biome will help you tremendously. Dont head for the snow withot clothes becasue you will freeze.
Raiding:
Now with your epic base and tons of recourses, what do you do? You Raid other people of course. SInce raiding is considered an offensive approuch to Rust, be sure to have the materials to supply explosives and gear neccisary for raiding. Solo Raiding in Rust is very difficult, it is recommended that you bring some friends along. The defender has built their base to go against raiders, the have sniper towers that never see action until your poor soul happens to come to raid. They have hours upon hours of work and you will take that away within minutes. If you're raiding solo, raid the defender while they are offline, this will put the odds more in your favor. This is the safest raid to do solo. Most players think of raiding as an investment, hoping to get more resources out then you put in. Online raiding can be one of the most envirgorating experiences the game as to offer. When you get your friends togther to raid a base while the owners try to kill you, when you have c4 and all your guns on you is an experience like no other game has to offer.  Some of the most epic moments in Rust is when the Raid you are conducting is being talked about throught the whole server, nakeds come to watch or take scraps, looters run towards the comotion, everyoone holds their breath to see which side will win.
Rust will be a challenging but rewarding experience, enjoy your adult Minecraft

TL;DR Good concept, crappy gameplay, horridly optimized.
This game is an amazing idea, with a mediocre implementation, and a terrible developer team. I have 90 hours in the game, and have been playing since the start. I have also been an active community member and tester since then. However, Garry (the developer), in his infinite arrogance, has decided to stop properly supporting Linux, though support is still advertised. The game was totally broken on Linux for weeks, until a Unity update fixed Garry's mistakes.
For Windows and Mac OS users, the game will technically work, but it is very poorly optimized. I have a GTX 680 and a 4.5 GHz 4th generation Intel i5, and I can barely get 25 FPS at full settings. Fine, whatever. The problem is that I have to set everything to minimum to come anywhere close to 60FPS, and even then the framerate is highly unstable.
Now, about the gameplay. Crafting and loot spawning is illogical (empty cans are more valuable than full ones, and more useful; full cans don't turn into empty ones when emptied; animals all produce wolf meat, even chickens; pistol bullets cost as much as 5.56 ammo; and many other problems). While the game is very much an endless grind occasionally punctuated with excitement, those moments of excitement can be quite gratifying.
Basically, if you run on Linux, you cannot rely on being able to play this game; Garry might break it at any time. If you run on Windows with anything but a top-of-the-line machine, you can barely play this game. In either case, this game is not worth $20. Buy ARK: Survival Evolved or DayZ instead.

After some long thought I've decided to make a more detailed review of undertale since I've noticed more of late that, although the reviews for undertale generally praise the game, they really don't help potential buyers understand what the game really is, whether by being vague about its gamplay or by outright just saying nothing about the games story in general in fear of spoilers. My previous review of the game was also guilty of this, so now I plan to rectify that.
Undertale takes place in a realtiy where humans and monsters both exist, and where for a while, they both lived in relative peace. One day however, war broke out between the 2 races and, in the end, the humans won. As punishment for losing, the monsters were sealed by 7 of the humans strongest magicians behind a magical barrier underneath a giant mountain that anyone could enter, but no one could exit.
You take control of a human that has fallen into the mountain many, many years after the war, and it is up to you to navigate the land of the monsters to find your way out of the underground and return to the surface. How your journey plays out however, is entirely up to you. Like the games description points out, if you so choose, you don't have to kill anyone you encounter throughout the game. But at the same time, you could also choose to kill everyone instead, or do a mix of both; it is entirely up to you. And in doing so, the game will alter its tone and atmosphere to reflect your choices, for better or for worse.
In regards to the battles themselves, it takes great influence from turn based rpg's of old and mixes it will the bullet-hell genre to make a bit of its own, unique yet familiar hybrid of the two where on your opponents turn you dodge their attacks, and on yours you can choose between multiple different actions. You can attack, perform an act, use an item, or perform mercy. How you choose to engage in battles will determine how your game plays out, as I had mentioned earlier. Will you attack and kill every monster you fight? Or will you choose to act a certain way, making your opponent lose the desire to fight you, in turn allowing you to spare their life? Play however you wish.
In regards to how I feel about the game from my experience? I love this game. The battle system is varied enough that, depending how you choose to play, battles either don't take too long, or the acts you need to perform to get an opponent to stop fighting you doesn't overstay its welcome outside of the tutorial area and, at times, are quite entertaining to watch. The characters are simply adorable, charming and memorable, though depending on which route you choose to take alters how you interact with each of them, which is great for players who like characters that are as varied as you depending on the situation. The music is just amazing, mixing between old 8-bit tunes familar to the earthbound series, to simple instrumental peices, to upbeat songs reminesent of the era of swing. Each song in this game is made to fit the tones and atmosphere across all routes taken by the player to the point that it becomes quite difficult to not associate songs with a feeling or encounter it was played alongside to.
Overall I cannot recommend this game more, but in the end the choice of buying should be up to the persons preference in games, and how they feel overall from just looking at the games store synopsis and a few written reviews. Don't get this game simply because the internet won't stop talking about. Don't get this game simply because one of your friends really likes it.
Get this game if you are a fan of rpgs or bullet-hell games. Get this game if you enjoy a game with a great narrative and memorable characters. Get this game if you can get past the old style graphics and see the game for everything else it brings to the table. Get this game because YOU want to try it on your own, outside of the opinions of other people.
And if you do play it, have a good time with it, regardless of which route you choose to take.

(Note: This review was originally published on 28 Mar 2014 and refers to an older build.)
In this series I'll be looking at pre-release Alphas, games released for early access by developers, sometimes as a free demo but increasingly for real money.
The trend started with the release and massive success of Minecraft, which initially offered an alpha at a reduced price. The next big step in the alpha movement was the release of Arma 3 from Bohemia [TK]. I bought the alpha of Arma 3 shortly after release and put a lot of hours into it. I was a fan of the Battlefield series and really liked Arma's focus of simulation over action.
Bohemia followed the pattern with their next big release, a standalone version of the Day Z mod for Arma 2 Combined Operations. The mod had been a breakout hit, driving sales of Arma 2 and making a name for the developer Dean Hall. Bohemia released the Day Z standalone as an early access alpha through Steam. The alpha soon broke sales records and set the model for future early access releases.
I received a copy of the Day Z alpha for Christmas and to date I've put about 60 hours into playing it. My experiences with the standalone are pretty typical. I lost count of how many times I've been killed on sight or punched to death by another freshly spawned player. I tried playing in a group but quickly found I preferred to be on my own, a lone wolf survivor.
That's what I like best about the Day Z standalone, and one of the reasons it frustrates me so much. I love starting with a fresh spawn and gearing up by searching towns and cities, killing all the zombies I come across. I like the progression, moving from a small backpack to a large rucksack, moving from a rusty old splitting axe to a pristine fire axe, or building a bad♥♥♥♥♥post-apocalyptic soldier with an M4 and full Army camo. I loved exploring the landscape, finding a cool little bridge or abandoned shipwreck (not that one, another smaller one).
And then I'd run into someone who'd kill me without a word. And I'd respawn only to be beaten to death by someone in a motorcycle helmet. And the cycle would continue. Gear up, get killed, respawn.
I soon grew bored with the repetition. I used to think I'd prefer some interaction prior to death, like being robbed at gunpoint (which happened once but I ran away and survived) or having a tense shootout (which also happened a few times resulting in a 50% survival rate for me), but I realised that I don't like social interaction in Day Z.
A lot of people would argue that social interaction's the point of Day Z, that most of the fun and challenge comes from dealing with other players, but my preferred play method is lone survivor. I followed a similar path when I played World of Warcraft. I like building a character on my own terms but didn't like having to deal with other people.
I've taken a break from playing Day Z. I'm waiting for the update that'll bring improved zombies, as at the moment they're completely broken, phasing through walls and spawning in limited numbers. In its current state Day Z is a large scale slow moving deathmath and that has a certain appeal but doesn't make for particularly involving gameplay.
I am a fan of early access alphas, provided the developers are upfront about the bugs and limitations (as in the case of the Day Z standalone); these alphas offer players an opportunity to help shape development and get their hands on a game months and potentially years before an official release. However, Day Z sets a potentially dangerous precedent that could see developers shipping an unfinished game with little or no reason to complete development.
Gamers need to know what they're buying when paying into early access or risk being eaten by the alpha wolf.

I honestly can't believe how little progress this game has made since going standalone. I played over 100 hours on the Arma 2 mod and love it, even if was a buggy mess. It was excusable because it was just a mod. But now here we are over a year after the standalone release, and the game is in many ways worse.
What got better:
+ Graphics look great
+ World is more detailed
+ Much bigger variety of loot to be found and used (even if a lot of them are totally pointless)
+ UI is much easier to understand
You'll notice that all the +'s don't actually add anything tangible to the game. It's just polish, which is something you're supposed to do AFTER you get the gameplay sorted out.
What got worse:
- ZOMBIES. Literally the selling point of this game and they have been practically removed. You can count on one hand the number of zombies you'll find in each major town like Cherno or Elektro. And they're STILL buggy as hell. The supposed reasoning is that it puts too much stress on the servers, which brings me to...
- SERVERS. For some reason that I can't fathom the amount of stress that a server is under will directly influence your framerate signinifcantly. Want to play on one of those fabled 40 or 50 person servers? Hope you like playing at 10 FPS.
- VEHICLES. After a year of standalone we finally have one, single vehicle, and it's still unfinished. (can't ride in the back, blowing out the tires has no effect)
So the fundamentals of the game are the same, but most of the things that made the mod amazing aren't in the standalone. What happened to sneaking by streets filled with zombies desperately trying not to draw their attention? There's no zombies anymore! In the mod you'd be hesitant to use your guns in town because you'd draw a whole horde to you. In the standalone, that threat is completely gone. And without the threat of zombies, it's just a PvP game. If you want a scavenging deathmatch, Arma 3's Battle Royale does it a hell of a lot better.

Undertale, throughout its entire relatively short story, is a game that does everything with extreme deliberation, and is a testament that no matter how big or expensive a game is, it's love for the craft that above all else raises it above the competition. Everything from the writing, the gameplay, and even the choice in using a retro, pixelated art style has been a conscious decision (and on that note, uses the pixelated style to great effect, not just to attack the nostalgia glands). It accounts for pretty much any decision the player makes, sometimes even including in what order, and constantly subverts expectations not for the sake of making some grand, artsy statement, but for the sole purpose of making the game more surprising and enjoyable (and fun, you know, gameplay wise) for the player themselves. The witty and sometimes even cringe-worthy writing acts as a motivator for the player to keep pushing forward, not only to beat the game, but to see how far you can push certain gamey aspects before the game starts to take notice. It even uses said puntastic humor at times to hurt you and upset you profoundly. It's loaded with secrets to the brim, and choosing between the genocide and the pacifist run make it a wildly different experience which effectively doubles the replay value (although if you're like me, you're probably not gonna want to kill anyone).
Even if you end up not liking the game (which is fine), I'm sure you can at least appreciate the amount of pure love for the craft that went into the creation of this game. If you can't even appreciate it, you're probably the devil. Or worse: a shareholder.

This is Rust; Where headshots make a sweet little crunch, No base is safe from a couple anti-noob engineers. And if you hear a beeping sound, you're about to be evicted.
Rust is an open world survival, shooting, building, crafting and raiding game that is updated weekly and made by Facepunch.
Before I get you little tribal savages assembled for a war party and send you to your guarenteed deaths. I want you to ask yourself one question. How angry have you been at a video game? If the answer is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ then multiply that number by 5, carry the 10, and you're still no where near the rage Rust induces. Something about losing your home, farm and life activates a special part of the lizard brain that most games can't touch.
Spawning:
Immediatly spawning on the coast like a ship-wreaked sailor with a rock and a torch, the map you are most likely on is a precedually generated map unique from every server,similar to minecraft. Although the map is unique, there are preloaded points of intrest i.e ( The dome, Radiation Towns, Water Treatment Plant, and soon the Rocket Factory) They are all connected by roads. The map itslef has biomes too. Early game Rust is the most brutal becuase you are the most vurnrable to players, animals and the enviroment, since you are un armed and homeless. For the majority of your early game (Day 1-4) you WILL be out-gunned. You have the best chance of survival scavenging scraps of bases you find.
Once you build a base, this will be your head quarters, you will hoard materials for your big stable base. You will struggle to find food and clothing but being in the right biome will help you tremendously. Dont head for the snow withot clothes becasue you will freeze.
Raiding:
Now with your epic base and tons of recourses, what do you do? You Raid other people of course. SInce raiding is considered an offensive approuch to Rust, be sure to have the materials to supply explosives and gear neccisary for raiding. Solo Raiding in Rust is very difficult, it is recommended that you bring some friends along. The defender has built their base to go against raiders, the have sniper towers that never see action until your poor soul happens to come to raid. They have hours upon hours of work and you will take that away within minutes. If you're raiding solo, raid the defender while they are offline, this will put the odds more in your favor. This is the safest raid to do solo. Most players think of raiding as an investment, hoping to get more resources out then you put in. Online raiding can be one of the most envirgorating experiences the game as to offer. When you get your friends togther to raid a base while the owners try to kill you, when you have c4 and all your guns on you is an experience like no other game has to offer.  Some of the most epic moments in Rust is when the Raid you are conducting is being talked about throught the whole server, nakeds come to watch or take scraps, looters run towards the comotion, everyoone holds their breath to see which side will win.
Rust will be a challenging but rewarding experience, enjoy your adult Minecraft


TL;DR Good concept, crappy gameplay, horridly optimized.
This game is an amazing idea, with a mediocre implementation, and a terrible developer team. I have 90 hours in the game, and have been playing since the start. I have also been an active community member and tester since then. However, Garry (the developer), in his infinite arrogance, has decided to stop properly supporting Linux, though support is still advertised. The game was totally broken on Linux for weeks, until a Unity update fixed Garry's mistakes.
For Windows and Mac OS users, the game will technically work, but it is very poorly optimized. I have a GTX 680 and a 4.5 GHz 4th generation Intel i5, and I can barely get 25 FPS at full settings. Fine, whatever. The problem is that I have to set everything to minimum to come anywhere close to 60FPS, and even then the framerate is highly unstable.
Now, about the gameplay. Crafting and loot spawning is illogical (empty cans are more valuable than full ones, and more useful; full cans don't turn into empty ones when emptied; animals all produce wolf meat, even chickens; pistol bullets cost as much as 5.56 ammo; and many other problems). While the game is very much an endless grind occasionally punctuated with excitement, those moments of excitement can be quite gratifying.
Basically, if you run on Linux, you cannot rely on being able to play this game; Garry might break it at any time. If you run on Windows with anything but a top-of-the-line machine, you can barely play this game. In either case, this game is not worth $20. Buy ARK: Survival Evolved or DayZ instead.

Even with its bugs and everything, this an awesome freakin' game right here!
It has its ups and downs, periods of great fun and periods of long stalemates. For me, this game has been the true definition of an 'Early Acess' game. It has at times tested my patience, beyond the borders of sanity, but also at times, given me some of the best experiences, I have ever had in gaming, and for me personally, that is saying quite alot.
I will recommend this game, for the patient survivalist, who can take a beating now and then, even an unfair or unseen one, and not get too salty about it but get on with the game, or something else entirely. This game is certainly not catered for everyone, and if you're looking for a quick FPS type of game, you will not find it here. DayZ is dying in miserable and sometimes buggy, unfair ways.
DayZ is dying of Hypothermia, whilst bathed in sunlight and fully dressed, just cause it rained on you for 2 minutes. DayZ is dying of starvation, while picking apples, as they take 2 minutes each to find. DayZ is dying while walking down stairs. DayZ is getting scratched once by an infected, just to see your pristine military clothing 'Ruined' with all gear inside 'Ruined'. DayZ is getting sniped after spending 40 minutes running from city to city, loosing everything to an unseen enemy and not being able to do anything about it. DayZ is running out of a building with your newly aquired weapon/food/anything useful, or not really, just to be met by a black screen with a simple, cold message 'you are dead'. And that's just some of the fun parts :).
Personally I love DayZ. I have had great times and bad times with it, and count on having many more of both. If you are willing to support a great dev team, a great survival game, and you can hang in there through the bugs and the sometimes not so friendly players you see, or dont see...
Then this game could be one for you! Honestly there is too many mechanics and stuff to do in the game now, that it would take me forever to review it all. If you find yourself interested, and wonder if you should buy this game or not, I recommend watching some youtube videos about it. Just to get the real feeling of what its all about and how the game is played.
Best of luck!

First of all, some cons and pros between mod and Standalone:
Pros:
Amazing open world
Friendly people (sometimes....yes)
New items such as clothes
Zombies don't zigzag anymore
New animations
New Inventory system
Many fun moments with random survivors you meet in the game.
Many more features to come ( I didn't mention this, but they are adding more animals to hunt, vehicles, more items and weapons, basebuilding, etc. Lots to look forward to)

Cons:
Big FPS drops in big cities
Although they no longer zigzag, zombies are almost not a threat and they are glitchy.
Lack of zombies.
Melee weapons are buggy and don't work well.
Lack of loot.
Inventory system is a bit buggy.
Fast starvation and dehydration.
Firestation ladder glitch.

To quickly sum it up:
The game has a lot of potential. The map is great, and it is a great experience when you meet people and you go on an adventure with them. The game has many new items to find. Optimization isn't very good in big cities, and while there is a lack of zombies, glitchy zombies, barely any loot, some bugs, and a bad melee system, those can be fixed with some work. My biggest concern is optimization. I really hope they find some bugs that when fixed, will give fps boosts. With many good features to come, the game has some serious potential. I am looking forward to seeing how it evolves.

Ratings (as of the game's current state):
For a new inexperienced player: 3.5/10 - I do not recommend that you buy now. Get something else for Christmas.
For somebody who enjoyed playing the mod, but didn't play often: 5.5/10 - It depends on how much you want to play the game. It may be worth getting now to save the money.
For a fan who has played the mod for a long time and loves DayZ: 7/10 - If you have been waiting for what seems like forever for this game to come out, then I would get it. Just remember that it is an alpha and that it won't be the great zombie survival game just yet.

I have been playing this game since the first week of the first version. Rust is a great game to play with friends and overally a good take on the survival genre. It is in alpha however it is very polished with development focusing on increasing content.
Pros:
-Easy to understand
-Fun with friends
-Large community
-One of the fastest dev teams
-Community shaped
-Diverse servers (ex. survival, hunger games, battlefield, etc.)
-Amazing looking terrain and procedual generation
-Great performance (capped 60fps on highest settings with GTX1070)
Cons:
-A few bugs (nothing game breaking)
-Some players just want to see the world burn
-Animals can be derpy
-Very PvP focused (not a con?)
-Certain graphical aspects need improvement
Other notes:
-I am glad they removed the XP system they tried to implement but I wish they would add blueprints to the current component system.
-I have only seen a few hackers in hundreds of hours that I've played. I would recommend playing on community servers where there are admins who care about the server rather than the official servers with no administration.

The game came heavily recommended to the point where I believed it was overhyped. And to a certain extent, it is. HOWEVER, it far exceeded the expectations I've ever had for any indie title. While it lacks a shiny modern graphic design, it does not need it because it excels in every other aspect of its entity. The humorous dialogue stands equal to that of Earthbound's; the jokes were endless and, surprisingly, most of them were expertly delivered. New characters, unnamed and familiar, friend or foe, only added to the excitement and thrill of going onward. The music was completely addicting, the volume couldn't go high enough!  With a custom theme for each boss, it's the game that somehow keeps outdoing itself. The story and atmosphere was absorbing and could effectively set the tone of the game from whimsical and cheery to ominoius and spooky. The gameplay was fresh, new and truly something to be experienced in 'Pacifist Mode.'
I thought this game was another overhyped indie title, nearly writing it off as 'Flavor of the Month,' but it truly delivered much more than I ever expected from a small-time developer. I eagerly await another collaboration or projects from Mr. Toby Fox, Ms. Temmie Chang and the team behind Undertale

I first got Rust nearly a year ago on my birthday. First, I will tell you my first playthrough, which happened to be on my birthday;
> I spawned with a rock, a torch and some bandages.
> I decided that since I was new and knew nothing about how to survive on this game, I would just go and find some kind players to help me start off. I mean, this is an online game! I'm sure that the community would be nice!
> After wandering around for a bit, I hear two voices. I jump out into the open, so they could see that I was new and had nothing of interest. Using the text chat (I didn't know how to voice chat at the time), I told them I was friendly. They seemed okay with that answer, and acted as if I wasn't there.
> As the sun began to go down, the two players started hitting each other with rocks while laughing insanely, as I watched.
> As I saw that they were just messing around and not trying to kill each other, I decided I'd join in the fun.
> I hit one.
> The two players, who had just been hitting each other for the last five minutes as a joke, instantly turned on me for that ONE hit.
> They started clumsily lashing at me with rocks.
> I ran away, but I could hear them both chanting to me through voice chat, "You can't escape!" and "We're gonna get you!"
> One of them caught up to me and hit me a few times, and I started panicking.
> I managed to outrun them, but it seemed that they had nothing better to do than trying to catch me, so they were still looking for me.
> Their crazed voices finally drained away. I stopped running.
> I realized I was very hungry, and would die soon.
> Suddenly, I saw a bear.
> After playing Skyrim where I could kill bears with just my fists, I thought that I could take on the bear with just my rock.
> The bear killed me.
> I rage-quit.
> I vowed to never go on another official server again.
MORAL OF THE STORY: You should never, ever, trust a pair of nutcases who hit each other for fun.

I had no money at first. I waited long and long just to gather the amount in hope to play this.
Meanwhile friends were playing it and the whole internet was talking about it. I thought I wouldn't have the chance to play this game/
One day , I finally had the money. The excitment couldn't hold me. I started playing it.
At first I was very confused and scared. Then as the game continued I found recomfort and safety.
Although I knew it wouldn't last. I started to feel guilt and fear. My hands were shaking as I was battling when I didn't wanted to hurt anyone.
I got sad shortly after , knowing that I had to leave the only place that would offer me recomfort and safety , that I would maybe never see the only person that helped me.
I had to carry on meeting other characters , some funny , some epic. I was filled with determination to move forward. I started to feel anger and frustration as I couldn't advance. But I stayed calm and tried again and again.
After a while I got melancolic. It still pained me , not being able to see the only being that protected you. But this feeling disapeared as I made more friends along my path.
After defeating the final boss... I couldn't hold my tears , I was crying of Joy. Even after the credits I still had tears and a little smile on my face , I was feeling in such a long time : happy...
But something was stopping me from closing the game. Because I knew if I closed it. Then all this wonderful experience would come to an end.
But even after closing it I could still hear this little music box in my head , with all the good memories this game gave me.
It will be an experience I will never forget. An experience that showed me so much and reminded me of so much. For ever.... I will store it into my heart and share it.
Thank you , to all the devs that made this wonderful game.

Day Z.
DayZ is one of those games where both frustration and exhileration come together to make a video game that breaks, no smashes it's competition all the while being completely broken and devoid of any real and valuable progress towards practical completion.
To complete my review i will do a pro's and con's...
Starting with the pro's.
The game allows for almost limitless freedom and promises even more in the future as vehicles and flying are brought forth via supposed updates, However the game becomes quiet linear very quickly once you get your head around what's going on and how to succeed at doing it. Basically, Spawn, Gather, Gear Up, seek a skirmish win or die and repeat.
Best played in groups the game allows for a pack/gang of players to divide and conquer as you take over towns, city's and army bases / airfileds at will be sheer force of numbers on your way to 'gearing up' your toon. Gearing up basically prescribes hours of grinding in the form of scavenging for materials, food and loadout. All the while defending yourself from the Zobie apocalypse and even more threatening - other players.
I can honestly say that the process of gearing up can often take so long that you feel attached to the toon, You work so bloody hard to gather the gear required to defend yourself and survive... So much so that when the time comes (and it inevitibly will) that you have a skirmish with another player or group of players you feel so vested in surviving that the game genuinly gives you a HUGE adrenalin rush!! Truly, It does! These skirmishes never end well... Although there are multiple things that can happen typically the end result is the same - you get killed - Only the way in which you die or how long this takes varies.
Examples of how I've been killed so far:
Shot,
Axed.
Stripped completely naked of all equipment (except underwear) and handcuffed and fed disenfectant - Die a slow painful death.
Death by Zombie,
Death by glitch.
Death by being forced to stand beside a servcie stations fuel bowser while the enemy shoot it and blow up the servo...
Death by cold.
Starved.
Electrocuted.
It goes on and on...
The cons.
My biggest gripe is with the DayZ developer's, Bohemia Interactive and Dean Hall (DayZ's founder). I feel like we are being completely and totally taken for granted and here's why...
The game is early access, We sign up for this on the promise of the games potential and we make this decision based on what the developer tells us they are doing / going to do to make this game complete.
Since DayZ standalone's early access release it has sold over 2 MILLION copies!!! Thats right TWO MILLION + because the two million mark was actually reached sometime around May of 2014.

Given that was 8 months ago... The actual current figure could now be closer to 2.5 MILLION or even 3 MILLION copies sold...
So here's my point - lets assume it's 2.5MILLION copies at an average of say $28 per copy accounting for periods of reduced cost to buy to average out Steam Sales special's  ... 2.5 million times $28 = $70 MILLION in sales for this game and it hasn't even left ALPHA.
!!! $70 odd MILLION in sales !!!
So the issue for me and many others is not the money, It's the lack of meaningful progress in the games development cycle. At writing I have just over 400 hours of game time logged. In 12 months I have seen a slow and infrequent update cycle where no real beneficial or meaningful upgrades happen... For example;
: One gun gets removed and replaced with another gun. The new guns is useless until the next patch because there is no ammo in the game for it.
: The guys dutifully upgraded the textures of some objects - Things like Zuchini's (food) and so forth that make no difference to the game what so ever other than visual. Really? Can't the polish wait till a little later in the dev cycle?
: The melee is essentially completely broken. Hitting a zombie usually finds you flailing madly trying to move the cursor around the zombie's body to find that small area where the hit can be registered. all the while, it never misses you with every attack.
: Clipping. Clipping everywhere! And... yup you guessed it.... it's not being fixed.
: Teddy Bears? They gave us teddy Bears in the .52 update, Yay!!! Why? Why when I still can't cook food or fly a chopper? Why?
You see the thing is.... after taking 70 MILLION odd in sales Bohemia and Dean Hall are currently laying on thier beds at night making money angels in the layers upon layers of $$$$ bills.
All the while taking us, and you the prospective buyer completely for granted. Why push to complete the game - In thier eyes clearly they don't need too!!
Seriously considering making a facebook page where we (the paying community of end users) can lobby for improved progress and frequency of meaningful updates because at the rate these guys are 'pfaffing' around changing textures on Zuchini's and adding Teddy Bears in four different colors this game will never be completed in a reasonably acceptable gestation period.
What's the average norm for a game these days, start to release it's normally around about a 2 year cycle afaik... Yeah.... well we are well on the way to eclipsing that date and we are still playing an alpha game with more things broken then are fixed, more proposed content and fuctionality missing than in game and... no real direction on when we will see it.
My advice, H1Z1 is coming to Steam very soon... Suggest you check it out before you buy this, because I suspect it will take the crown from DayZ very quickly once released because... you guessed it, It has a active team developing the game under the guide and watchful eye of Sony.
So with the knowledge the game's development is almost non existent - well thats not exactly true... More that the development not being meaningful to improving the game is leaps and bounds and knowing they have raised over $70 million from it, I ask where is the investment in the game?
Why hasn't the development team expanded, new expereinced people brought in in large numbers to get the thing moving - accellorating productivity and the quality of the output.
Like I said - it all points to a developer who is taking the Intelectual Property for granted - harvesting it for all it can without putting in the development $$$ what they know they should.
Well... i say you get back out of it what you put into it.
Bohemia and even more so Dean hall - You should be completely ashamed of yourselves.
Steam - You shuld too for allowing such a reputed developer (ARMA series) to take it's purchasing customers for granted in this way. You need to tighten up the EARLY ACCESS rules with a view to ensuring progressive updates are delivered on a agreed schedule (failure to meet a deadline see's a financial penalty to the studio) to protect the end user.
$70 million raised and after nearly two years it's still broken and still ALPHA.
COMPLETELY DISGUSTING.
Sincerely, Shags.

So, this game is still very glitchy, despite having come a long way.  The minor glitches (such as zombies phasing through walls, and 2' falls being lethal) are still apparent, while new content (such as seeds) have been added.
Upon speaking to a designer for the game, it was commented that "sometimes some systems are fixed and updated before others," separating problems into "General Issues" and "Core Design."
I rebutted that anything affecting the zombies, or survival, in a zombie survival game, should be considered major problems, but this view is apparently not shared with the devs.
Despite the game being designed by kids in high-school, it has infinite potential to be the premier zombie survival game out there.  It easily blows games like H1Z1 and Infestation, Survivor Stories clear out of the water, but that doesn't say much when the game itself quite literally tries to kill you, along with the zombies, and the other players.
Also, the reviews of people cuffing people, and feeding them things?  I have no idea how this occurs.  Anyone sensible shoots on sight because of idiots like that, leading to a violent and non-cooperative player base.  Rather realistic, if you ask me, as it seems half the reviews are of people trying to lend help, only to get killed by the person they helped.  The player interaction is what makes this game so thrilling, as the zombies objective is obvious, whereas the players objectives aren't.
Of the dozens and dozens of players I've encountered, I can safely say I've only parted ways with about 4% of them.  1% of them are now my Steam friends, which is great.  The other 95% are people who will shoot you on sight, or trick you into eating silly things, or steal your things and leave you in a bad scenario (cuffed, defenseless against zombies); these are the people that either killed me on sight, or I killed on sight.
So if you're looking for a thrilling, realistic zombie survival game, come no further.  However, buy it now while it's cheap, because they are needlessly raising the cost of the game but not actually fixing any bugs.  I'm sure they will in [a lot of] time, but buying it cheaper now will allow you to play what will potentially be a fantastic game when it's complete.
EDIT:  I was permanently banned from the DayZ forums for speaking out against ignorant moderators, corrupt developers, and a game that is updating itself into the dirt.  Good riddance, uninstalling and requesting a refund.

There, just wanted to get that out of the way first, before I continue on.  There is a certain air of absolute crap that hangs in the fall air this year, as certain triple A publishers are putting up their sixty dollar games, with the top of the line graphics, and cover systems, to make matters worse.
