So I've recently Just hit 200+ hours On DayZ Standalone and i thought i would write a review for the people who have not brought it yet so they can get a clear incite on what the game is about and the good and bad aspects of the game. Well to start off it is one of the best games i could have ever played it gives an experience like no other. Yeah it sounds very cliche i know but trust me there is no other survival game which plays out anything like this. When you spawn you will likely be on the coast of Chernarus. The Spawns are usually quite far from eachother meaning when you die you may well have a very different experience from your last life. Arguably the most important aspect of the game is trying to stay alive throughout the zombie apocalypse and trust me the game takes some ajusting, you may die a couple times getting to know how the game works and what is an effective method of survival. after that it's still not smooth sailing this game like no other keeps me on the edge of my seat at all times and thats what i adore about it. Zombies are a threat in this game and need to be dealt with carefully in this game without attracting too much attention to yourself. But these are not the biggest threat... People are. running into someone could easily result in death.
to be honest there is not that many friendly people in the game and thats why i would advise taking your time in high loot areas and being as careful as you possibly can. however without these people the game wouldn't be what it is today, sometimes exploring a town and then hearing loud gunshots makes the experience quite exhilirating.
this game has changed the way we look at survival games and i feel many survival new survival games base themselves of DayZ' core aspect of a Zombie apocalypse. The Best aspect for me by far in dayz standalone is you make the choices, you do what you want to do at all times. Want to go murder some people go for it! want to go explore the map and stay out of other peoples way and scavenge for food go ahead it's all in dayZ standalone. I've never played a game with som much freedom for the player. Do remember the game is in early access and there is a number of bugs in the game but hopefully that won't stop you from picking up a game that you can easily put hundreds of hours into.
Friends, Friends introduce a completely fresh new type of playstyle into the game (if you want to lone wolf go for it!) but my favorite moments in the game have been with others. don't get me wrong if you're both new to the game and you have no idea where anything is you will have to count on luck to find eachother. but once you learn where recognisable lanmarks and spawns are the game becomes alot easier to find eachother. many survival games do not support multiplayer and they're still great but with the implementaion of multiplayer it will change survival games for you. I've had experience where my friends and i have been shot at and we have mistaken our friend for the enemy. lets just say i may have lodged a 7.62mm round into his leg.
DayZ Standalone causes you to make the decisions and think fast. your life is constantly on the line in this game and your decisions will impact this significantly. People who play the game that there is two main roles (not that you have to play either) this it the Hero and the Bandit. Bandits usuallly kill on sight and will do almost anything to see a player dead or without loot. A hero is the opposite they avoid gunfights unless shot at. and will try and help out players in the land of chernarus. This role is like no other and just by giving someone food or water is rewarding in itself. however you don't have to play either of these roles. I understand that the game is not for everyone and i would advise looking at some videos of the game before buying it to see if you will enjoy it.
The Survival mechanics in this game are pretty weel dont (except for hunger imo) it's recently become alot more daunting and i have found my character gets hungry alot quicker. Whether you're hot & cold has been recently implemented and i like the system. running outside in the rain for hours on end will cause your character to become cold and they will eventually get hypothermia. A vehicle has finally been added after just about a year ( i know that sounds like a long time) for me getting to places on foot in your own time really increases your chances of survival and improves your chances of survival substantially.
And i pretty much have to cover this as the majority of negative comments are complaining how buggy the game is. for me it really isn't, it has its flaws like every other game. but bohemia have fixed zombie mapping amazingly meaning they won't for the most part run through walls. to be honest in its state at the moment it looks better optimised that assassins creed unity. haven't run into a hacker into a while which is nice, think they cleared up most of them. there is so much you can do in dayZ standalone and to be honest with 200 hours i have only explored maybe just over half of the map. i myself love running from town just surviving on whatever resorces i can find. The design of the standalone is very much different to the mod, i feel they have given it that grubby sort of overgrown look that a zombie apocalypse needs. if you want an experience where you can drive in cars and be continuously shot by 50.cal snipers go for the mod (in no way am i saying it's bad) finding guns is stupidly easy and pretty much just results in constant deathmatching in popular cities. DayZ however when you find a gun and then ammo it feels more rewarding.
to sum up this game is one of the best games i have played and i cannot wait to see what bohemia can do with it in the future, i hope my review has been helpful!

I had recently written a review on how amazing this game was - and it is very, very good. However, recently it has been ruined beyond playing by a few things that really do screw it up.
1) Hackers - they are everywhere! Playing on the official London servers, we must have encountered about 7 hackers in the space of 5 days, all of them trying to get into our base and destroy everything. The most recent attack saw all of our chests being destroyed and a lot of loot gone by being killed by noclippers.
2) Server time-outs - no, this isn't just a problem with my connection as all of my clan get it too, every day without fail, all of the London official servers have timed out. This will last for about an hour until the server comes back up. It completely ruins the gameplay, as we have to sit here waiting for a server to come back up when we could be playing other games without this stupid issue and no hackers in sight either.
3) Russians - this is a good and bad really. They are kind of good because they are a real struggle when you are trying to survive, but the quantity of them is unbelieveable. And they show no mercy either. You will be slain by every single Russian that comes across you. They are absolutely ruthless, and there is no server that escapes them. If you get a base, chances are it will be raided by a band of Russians. If you go out farming, chances are - you guessed it - you will be killed by Russians.
However, there are a load of good points about the game aswell.
1) Teamwork - building a team in this game is great. You run across someone and start talking, and next thing you know they are in your base and you are crafting together, farming and gathering more resources, and even raiding or defending against raids. It really does bring the games community to life.
2) Gameplay - every day is different. One day you wont have anything happen, the next you will be in a massive firefight or you'll be hacking at naked people. Slavers, heroes and absolute villans are everywhere in the game, and sometimes it feels like its a staged storyline, because the people you meet are so diverse and can bring some great roleplay.
One last thing - this game teaches you how to get really excited when you see a ♥♥♥♥ing barrel. Amazing.

Undertale is one of those games that can ONLY be a game. It's the epitomy of what games can do and how to do it. It's basically a comedy RPG with a HUGE friggin' heart with enough thrills and chills to make your head spin and really make you think about your choices. And when I say it makes you think I mean it, Undertale provides you with the option to kill or spare enemies and essentially be your own moral compass as you traverse the underground environment inhabited by a VERY colorful cast of monsters.
-SPEAKING OF! The story is very simple, but that isn't necassarily a bad thing! In fact, it's one of the main highlights! Undertale is about a young child who, one day while climbing "Mount Ebott", falls into a large cavern only to find that they're in a land filled with monsters and now must seek a way out. Adventure ensues. The draw to Undertale is that what you do matters, who you save matters, and how you act in a situation MATTERS! Unlike pretty much most AAA games that boast "freedom of choice" but only really amount to a slightly different scenarios, with a few changed lines, and your best friend bob now hates you. Undertale changes how EVERYTHING goes down because of how you choose to proceed. Sometimes in really obvious ways, others not so obvious.
-OH! And the music is pretty kickass too! It's one of the reasons I bought the game! It's no surprise to me that Toby Fox nailed the soundtrack considering he's a composer to start with. But this really sticks out with it's HUGE variety of songs and almost all of them are unforgettable.
-Then there's the gameplay. The overworld is like any other rpg: explore towns, talk to npcs, random encounters (with a nonenraging encounter rate) and solve puzzles! Very standard, so if you've ever played even the most basic of game you should be all good to go...unless you are bad at reaction time. Undertale has a unique battle system, a creative one, but not really for everyone. The battle system is simple, you have: Attack, Act, Items, and Mercy.
"Attack" is what it says on the tin.
"Act" is where you can check the enemy's status and talk to them.
"Items" is where you can heal, euip items mid-battle, and well that's about it.
And "Mercy" allows you to spare an anemy after the right dialogue choices and requirements have been met so you can end the battle peacefully, or just straight out flee.
The spare/attack system is really unique as sparing an enemy doesn't provide you with EXP but instead gold whereas killing an enemy gives you EXP. You'd think that this would become a problem given that it's an RPG, right? Wrong! The game counters this with a unique "Bullet Hell" battle system where you essentially have to dodge and learn the enemy's various attack patterns AND IT'S SURPRISINGLY FUN! Never does it feel like it can be too tough, challenging? Yes. Impossible? Hell no! But there were times where I just couldn't comprehend the attack properly no matter how much I trial and error through it. While I've only played this game for 41 hours it's incredibly polished for an early access game compared to its counterparts in the same genre, and who's watermark still says "alpha".
So what can one expect from Rust? From the moment you start you have only a rock and a torch. A rock helps you gather materials which can make other things, eventually you'll find yourself in a nice living quarters shacked up from the other players outside, with huge amounts of room inside. But wait - you've built your 14x14 one level shack in the open near 100's of other people's bases, and suddenly you're staring down the barrel of a thompson machinegun held by player XxX420noskopesXxX and he blasts you away mercilessly and destroys your 14x14 one level shack you spent a couple hours to find the materials and built. And now you've respawned somewhere totally different because you never made a back up sleeping bag.
Such is Rust. "tRust" no one. Eventually you will grasp some of the foundational mechanics of rust like foraging carefully, building a base in a seculded area with limited access, upgrading base walls to withstand some attacks, and preparing to survival the harsh environment.
Helpful tips:
-Never plea for mercy, it doesn't work. Accept your death.
-Build in secluded areas.
-Know the area around your base.
-Have some form of defence whether its a bow, spear, or if you're lucky enough to find the blueprints for a gun and bullet as you just start out (highly unlikely).
-Hunt for barrels - its better that when you start rust, you go for barrels only. Don't worry about a base. Hunt for barrels and get the blueprints from them.
-You will be killed many times.
PVE survival 8/10
Most survival games can't even get a pve survival because their pve mechanics are non existant or non threatening. Rust however has a few PVE mechanics that pose threats.
While animals pose no real threat to you, unless you're near one or happen to stumble across a bear (never really happens) you don't need to worry about being attacked in the night by such things. They're easy to spot and don't move that much.
Weather will kill you. The cold is, well cold. If you sit your naked self in a cold area you will eventually die.
Go in the water at night? You'll probably get hypothermia.
See that huge town over there with buildings and hangers? Don't go in it you'll get radiation poisoning.
Uncooked food, burnt food will slowly kill you. Eating your friend who you killed for food, will kill you.. unless you cook his meat.
Fire provides warmth and increases your health.
PVP survival 10/10
Rust has some of the best pvp in a survival game i've played. It's fun and engaging, the scales can tip either way and its a major driving force for people to build bases, find blueprints, build weapons and raid other people for loot. It really never gets old and offers endless replayability with the reward of base loot.
Here's to another 41 hours and more. This is a must buy if you like survival games.

Undertale is one of those games that can ONLY be a game. It's the epitomy of what games can do and how to do it. It's basically a comedy RPG with a HUGE friggin' heart with enough thrills and chills to make your head spin and really make you think about your choices. And when I say it makes you think I mean it, Undertale provides you with the option to kill or spare enemies and essentially be your own moral compass as you traverse the underground environment inhabited by a VERY colorful cast of monsters.
-SPEAKING OF! The story is very simple, but that isn't necassarily a bad thing! In fact, it's one of the main highlights! Undertale is about a young child who, one day while climbing "Mount Ebott", falls into a large cavern only to find that they're in a land filled with monsters and now must seek a way out. Adventure ensues. The draw to Undertale is that what you do matters, who you save matters, and how you act in a situation MATTERS! Unlike pretty much most AAA games that boast "freedom of choice" but only really amount to a slightly different scenarios, with a few changed lines, and your best friend bob now hates you. Undertale changes how EVERYTHING goes down because of how you choose to proceed. Sometimes in really obvious ways, others not so obvious.
-OH! And the music is pretty kickass too! It's one of the reasons I bought the game! It's no surprise to me that Toby Fox nailed the soundtrack considering he's a composer to start with. But this really sticks out with it's HUGE variety of songs and almost all of them are unforgettable.
-Then there's the gameplay. The overworld is like any other rpg: explore towns, talk to npcs, random encounters (with a nonenraging encounter rate) and solve puzzles! Very standard, so if you've ever played even the most basic of game you should be all good to go...unless you are bad at reaction time. Undertale has a unique battle system, a creative one, but not really for everyone. The battle system is simple, you have: Attack, Act, Items, and Mercy.
"Attack" is what it says on the tin.
"Act" is where you can check the enemy's status and talk to them.
"Items" is where you can heal, euip items mid-battle, and well that's about it.
And "Mercy" allows you to spare an anemy after the right dialogue choices and requirements have been met so you can end the battle peacefully, or just straight out flee.
The spare/attack system is really unique as sparing an enemy doesn't provide you with EXP but instead gold whereas killing an enemy gives you EXP. You'd think that this would become a problem given that it's an RPG, right? Wrong! The game counters this with a unique "Bullet Hell" battle system where you essentially have to dodge and learn the enemy's various attack patterns AND IT'S SURPRISINGLY FUN! Never does it feel like it can be too tough, challenging? Yes. Impossible? Hell no! But there were times where I just couldn't comprehend the attack properly no matter how much I trial and error through it. Which is why if you have bad reaction time that I don't suggest blindly jumping into this game. Play the demo, it gives you a perfect idea of how the game is!.
-Undertale isn't a very long game, it NEVER makes you grind if you don't want to. I finished the game in...ooooh I donno, twelve or so hours? I've heard six is the very least time taken to beat and I don't disagree, but the game offers so much that sometimes I wonder if that $10 price isn't TOO generous. Every character has something fun and unique to say, every environment is filled to the brim with personality, and the how much you get out of the game really depends on how you play.
Undertale isn't just any game I recommend, it's a game I feel legitimately deserves the praise it gets. I don't think it's for everyone, but I MUST STRESS that if you have ANY interest in this game then you should pick it up. $10 may or may not be a lot to you, but if you're looking for an RPG to play that isn't tediously long and grindy then this is for you. A lot of good games came out this year but this one is easily my game of the year. Don't pass up this game.

Undertale was the best impulse buy I've ever done.
If you're a fan of RPGs at all, I'd fully reccommend that you check out this game. This game deconstructs and subverts common tropes that you'd find in other RPGs and presents them in a fresh, and interesting way that will get you hooked and wanting more. The humor in this game is legitimately funny, and doesn't rely on crass jokes or low-brow humor to get you laughing. The music in this game is freaking fantastic and makes traversing through levels and fighting enemies a treat. Every single character, including minor enemies in this game, have their own personalities and the several different ways that Undetale allow you to interact with these characters will make you feel very emotionally invested into their well-being.
That being said, this game isn't without its flaws. This game has a fair amount of long corridors, and since the main character you play as can't run, backtracking and walking through environments with these long corridors can get fairly tedious. The length of the game is also fairly short, with it taking 5-6 hours to get through the story. So if you're expected a 30-40 hour playthrough, think again. Luckily, Undertale is meant to be played over the course of multiple playthroughs, with each playthrough being significantly different from the one before. So if you want to see everything that the game has to offer, it'll take about 20 hours of gametime.
Overall, Undertale is a fantastic RPG that's well-deserving of its praise. If you have the money, definitely check out this game and remember: Stay Determined.

Without spoiling things, Undertale is an RPG unlike any other (though most closely related to Earthbound). It's an amazing an adventure through which your actions in-and-out of battle will affect the story and the ending you receive. There's a plethora of endings, but the main 3 are:
- Pacifist (do not kill anything or anyone and help everyone you can)
- Genocide (be the embodiment of pure evil and kill everything you come across)
- and Neutral (the route with the most endings all of which do not fall under the previous 2 categories).
Here's some more good things about the game that may pique your interest:
- Story/Narrative: This is the biggest piece of the entire game. If you don't talk to every sign, pay attention to every dialogue box, and really come to love the characters by the end of the game, you will not get the same experience as most of us. Make sure you also didn't spoil the game as that will make it a lot less enjoyable to play.
- Visuals: There's actually a few art styles at play, but the main one is pixel-art. It reminds you of the NES a bit, but they never look old or dated (unless you're not a fan of pixel-art). While there is a bit that they leave up to the imagination, that's actually a lot of the charm to the game and I feel makes it even better.
- Sound: Beyond superb. The soundtrack is so amazing that I've actually bought the soundtrack (something I very rarely do). The songs don't escape my thought and they're always a delight to listen to.
- Controls: I recommend a controller for this game, but you can do it just fine with a Keyboard (mouse not used). It controls just fine. Controls are very basic anyways though (move, confirm, cancel, open menu/pause).
- Gameplay: The gameplay aspects are very interesting. It's a turn-based RPG but you only have one attack (standard, physical, attack). That said, you have to do a small QTE based on the weapon you're using, and the better you do, the more damage you inflict. It's more akin to (small-scale) DDR than QTEs though.
You can also perform certain actions that change based on who your opponent is, and this is how you go a non-lethal route to "winning" fights.
But the biggest aspect of the game is defending against attacks. You control a small red heart and move about a battlefield of a barrage of "bullets" that attack you. Some you have to not be moving to avoid and others you have to be moving for them, but the majority is to just dodge them. This is a lot easier than it sounds though as some enemies literally barrage your field with showers of bullets. Be prepared!
As for out of battle, the main gameplay aspects are talking to people and solving puzzles, much like any turn-based RPG ever.
The "bad" stuff:
- It's short: Even if you talk to literally everything for every bit of dialogue, you will finish your first playthrough in around 4-8 hours. Granted, there are multiple different endings based on your playthroughs (the game should be played at LEAST twice if not thrice by everyone to get the main 3 endings), but some are even shorter than others (Genocide for example took me around 2.5 hours). Short games aren't bad though as you don't have to commit a ton of time to it, and I still had a blast, but it left me with wanting more. Still, for only $10, it's not that bad of a duration.
- Some stuff gets repetitive: A few jokes are used a bit too much for some people, though I actually never really felt that way (just pointing it out for others to be aware of). Battles however can get a bit tedious when you know how to ACT a certain way and you just want to move on to the next bit of dialogue.
- The feels: While I'm more than ecstatic to laugh harder than I ever have at some bits of the game and even be brought to tears at the extremely upsetting moments, this game may leave you feeling things you haven't felt before. Again, not a bad thing for me, it's just something for people to know.
- You may get angry: There's two parts of the game that I feel might enrage a lot of people, so I want to spell them out immediately for anyone still considering the game:
1. On your first playthrough, be sure to do a pacifist run. That is, don't kill anyone (and I mean do not, kill, ANYONE... except the one monster who won't let you not kill them. You'll know who they are when you fight them, and they'll make you feel really upset). You will get one of the best neutral ending, and this is because you cannot get a "best" Pacifist ending on your first playthrough. However, you can load the save and then be able to go back and do a few things to get said best ending. Basically, you can do a pacifist Neutral ending as well as the actual Pacifist ending.
2. When you do the Genocide playthrough, go into the final boss fight with a positive state of mind. Laugh at the funny bits and take breaks if you need to. Don't get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off like a lot of people I know are (they're up to 40+ attempts, I beat it in ~20 because I never had a bad time).
With all of the above laid out, I give Undertale a 10/10. Some bits could be made better (like duration and stuff), but it's really amazing and definitely worthy of a GOTY award (though indie games never get them because they get overshadowed by AAA games, sadly). Be sure to play it blind because it's an amazing experience unlike you've ever played before.

While I've only played this game for 41 hours it's incredibly polished for an early access game compared to its counterparts in the same genre, and who's watermark still says "alpha".
So what can one expect from Rust? From the moment you start you have only a rock and a torch. A rock helps you gather materials which can make other things, eventually you'll find yourself in a nice living quarters shacked up from the other players outside, with huge amounts of room inside. But wait - you've built your 14x14 one level shack in the open near 100's of other people's bases, and suddenly you're staring down the barrel of a thompson machinegun held by player XxX420noskopesXxX and he blasts you away mercilessly and destroys your 14x14 one level shack you spent a couple hours to find the materials and built. And now you've respawned somewhere totally different because you never made a back up sleeping bag.
Such is Rust. "tRust" no one. Eventually you will grasp some of the foundational mechanics of rust like foraging carefully, building a base in a seculded area with limited access, upgrading base walls to withstand some attacks, and preparing to survival the harsh environment.
Helpful tips:
-Never plea for mercy, it doesn't work. Accept your death.
-Build in secluded areas.
-Know the area around your base.
-Have some form of defence whether its a bow, spear, or if you're lucky enough to find the blueprints for a gun and bullet as you just start out (highly unlikely).
-Hunt for barrels - its better that when you start rust, you go for barrels only. Don't worry about a base. Hunt for barrels and get the blueprints from them.
-You will be killed many times.
PVE survival 8/10
Most survival games can't even get a pve survival because their pve mechanics are non existant or non threatening. Rust however has a few PVE mechanics that pose threats.
While animals pose no real threat to you, unless you're near one or happen to stumble across a bear (never really happens) you don't need to worry about being attacked in the night by such things. They're easy to spot and don't move that much.
Weather will kill you. The cold is, well cold. If you sit your naked self in a cold area you will eventually die.
Go in the water at night? You'll probably get hypothermia.
See that huge town over there with buildings and hangers? Don't go in it you'll get radiation poisoning.
Uncooked food, burnt food will slowly kill you. Eating your friend who you killed for food, will kill you.. unless you cook his meat.
Fire provides warmth and increases your health.
PVP survival 10/10
Rust has some of the best pvp in a survival game i've played. It's fun and engaging, the scales can tip either way and its a major driving force for people to build bases, find blueprints, build weapons and raid other people for loot. It really never gets old and offers endless replayability with the reward of base loot.
Here's to another 41 hours and more. This is a must buy if you like survival games.

The most enjoyable game and story in a very, very long time. Brilliantly written characters, incredible soundtrack, and so much replayability.
I myself have never been interested in jrpg's. I've never liked the whole turn based mechanic, and I've always found it boring. This changes that completely. Each attack the enemy makes now turns the battlefield into a small bullet hell segment. This seemingly small change makes a massive difference making this an unbelievably fun game. It's now up to you whether you take damage or not from enemy attacks, if you have the skill.
A feature this game has that is not often mentioned is that character development is made during battle. Before the enemy begins their attack, they will often give dialouge depending on what action you take against them, completely changing how that character reacts to you in the future. It also helps you learn each character's motives and personality.
Of course, the main advertised feature being the fact that you can kill people, or spare them. Now, I am not over-exaggerating when I say everytime you kill or spare someone it completely changes the game. To keep it simple I will talk about the 3 main types. Normal, pacifist, and genocide.
Normal is if you only kill a few enemies, while keeping some alive, although your first playthrough will
be normal, even if you spare everyone or kill everyone.
Pacifist is where you don't kill or attack anyone. If you do this, you can become friends with all the main characters, resulting in a very happy and uplifting experience.
Genocide is where you kill literally everyone, including every random encounter in each area. Genocide has the most notable changes during the entire game. I won't give away any spoilers, but it makes you feel truly evil.
The boss battles are some of the best I've experienced. The set up for each boss is done perfectly, and sets the mood and context for the fight. The difficulty scales up as you go through the game, making it feel like you are truly progressing through the world the game takes place in. There is no difficultly setting; if you can't beat a boss, you have to keep trying until you can learn to beat them. I personally love this, because if you want to progress you have to prove you've become better.
The characters are, like I've said before, some of the best I've ever seen written. Depending on your play style and type, they will react and treat you differently through the whole game. Each character has great depth to them, and the game wouldn't be the same without them or how well they're written.

A game that is under constant change, but is finally taking form.
By far one of the funnest online survival games I have played, with an abundance of potential. I trust facepunch studios with my life, and they have been incredibly busy pushing very significant updates every single week. I've seen other early access games get about 1/6 of the work done these guys do in a month. I'm always reading their blog posts, and their concept art/ideas for what they want to implement in the game are simply incredible.
Resource gathering is reasonable. Making a city with fortified walls isn't out of the question, even in regular Rust servers. With quarries, it has become all the more easier to collect the resources you need for your own group's mega base. And even so, if you have enough helping hands and picks/axes, you gather thousands of resources before you know it!
The building is fantastic, it's freeform but with reasonable snap into place walls that connect to each other, and is most likely going to be heavily revamped before I know it.
Raiding is exhilirating, there is always a very real fear of death, even when you're not attacking someone's house, anyone could open fire on you at anytime
The people create the experience. Factions are formed, people work together and against each other as they feel is right. People could come around to your house declaring their landlords, asking for your rent. Or they could go door to door as a common Robin Hood, delivering goodies for all to enjoy.
No matter what way you look at it, this game is shaping up to be a godly online survival experience, and you'd be out of your mind not to pick it up before it's too late.

Rust is my all-time favorite game. It brings me the most joy, adrenaline and stress of anything I've ever played. The ability to succeed is based on experience, skill and trust. It is the ultimate PvP experience, and with the way the team over at Facepunch rolls out updates, it's only uphill from here.
Experience allows you to know which walls to hit with C4, how to sleep in that bush while you have the Airdrop on you, and how to build a near impenetrable base.
Skill is used to wield various weapons and know your limits when matching up against people. Can you kill those 4 nakeds chasing after you with only a spear and a hatchet on you? That's your call.
Trust lies in the people you surround yourself with. Rust is an almost completely unpredictable game because you have no idea how people are going to react to the way you play. Killing that silly naked who wanted some food for free may have seemed like a hilarious idea at the time, but maybe not so much when he shows up with 20 friends in full gear to your front door. And allowing that guy access to your whole base after you've only known him for 2 hours? I can tell you from experience; it's not fun to log on and find that your base is no longer yours. They let me know that loud and clear as they screamed at me over their mics ;)
Be friendly or be mean, it's your call; either way you have the ability to succeed immensely, or end up homeless.
PROTIPS: Throwing spears are op, AK is best gun, pipeshotty is best gun for the poor, don't build next to a spawn, find some friends, don't be too friendly, don't eff with a clan unless you can back it up, wall off your toolcupboard, have an "airlock" in your front entrance, pillars are 100% worth, sharing sleeping bags saves 2 hours trying to find your friend, if you wear clothes you will get shot 90% of the time; if you're naked you will get shot 50% of the time, everyone can hear you c4, people saying "friendly" almost never are, nakeds aren't always what they appear to be, hv ammo isn't worth the gp, building on rocks makes for easy defense, ladders really don't cost that much, don't keep all your loot in one place, keep up to date on glitches, craft on the run, have a ton of sleeping bags, you can never have too many doors, you can smelt/cook 4 items at a time, don't plan your house too big, salvaged tools are bad, burst fire your gun, deers come installed with vtec, don't trust beancan grenades, explosives can blow up the chests inside, geared doesn't mean good or smart, follow these tips and I'll still kill you :)
TL;DR Best $20 I've ever spent.

This game is a unique experience that can be different for everyone. It could completely immerse you into its world and make you love everything about it, or it could just be no more than a regular RPG with a somewhat new idea. For me, it was the former. It made me laugh, it made me cry, it made me feel extreme joy, it made me feel severe regret, and I feel that that is what it strives to do.
The story captured me with its intriguing and unique characters that are full of personality and how the main problem in the world is integrated into everyone's lives; seeing how every character reacts to it, either as a huge threat to just a change that they have to live with to reacting in ways that I won't spoil.
The gameplay may be somewhat simplistic, but it's how it is used that makes it work so well. In combat, you move around in a box while avoiding obstacles by moving your "heart" around. It does more with this than just as reflex-based dodging, it uses this to create emotional experiences and show how your opponent is feeling through their attack patterns.
Everyone will have their own feelings about something as different as this game, and I feel that this was an experience that has changed my outlook on what gaming could be. It has genuinely made me not want to reset and play again after beating it (which, with this game, is an absolutely great thing, and I can't say why because of spoilers). This was the best $9.99 I've spent in a long time.

Day Z is both good and bad. The game itself as an idea is actually really fun and i found myself often getting caught up in totally unscripted events that were always interesting, making it really good if you want to roleplay the 'zombie apocolypes' experience. The developers have worked hard since its initial release to give the game a wealth of content to make a more fun experience; especially with other players.
However the game is still to this day riddled with a MASSIVE amount of bugs, far more bugs than i would say are acceptible at this stage in the games lifecycle. In addition to this the game is extremely poorly optimized and full of environments that are uninspired, unimpressive and uninteresting all in one. Some of the actual environment design is at an amateur level and the objects, while well designed, are mostly mundane due to the games particular setting.
The interface will take a bit of getting used to as the actual controls for the game are terrible and often needlessly abitrary; but in the end any player can learn it with enough practice. But i cant escape the reality that even the menus in the game are a kin to something from the skillset of a first year game design student.
On balance the game itself as the realisation of an idea is great, but the way it was made is terrible. The developers never demonstrate that they're even talented enough to pull off a project like this, which makes me wonder if they were the right ones for the job. The Stand Alone feels like an attempt to merely replicate the MOD version where poorly put together mechanics and visual elements would be more acceptible.
The game is not in my opinion worth its £22.99 price tag, no where close to that mark even while being on Early Access. I cannot recommend a game that still has very basic problems at a frequent rate of occurance even after over a year of culminating vast funding from on Early Access.

It's very hard to talk about Undertale because the things that make it such a great game are all things that would make your experience worse if you knew about them beforehand. If you're even remotely interested in the game then I strongly urge you to pick it up right now because waiting will result in you learning about things you shouldn't. That's what happened to me before I played, and I still had a good time but in retrospect I really wish I hadn't done that.
But what can I say about Undertale without spoiling the experience? Both good and bad things, really. It's a bullet hell RPG where rather than simply sit and wait for opponents to do their thing you get to try and avoid taking damage by dodging bullets. On your own turn you either time your attacks for extra damage or try to talk your way out of combat. Almost every encounter in the game can be resolved peacefully so you never really have to resort to violence unless you want to.
Undertale is kind of a linear game and a fairly short one on that. Even if you dally a lot it'll probably take you no more than 10 hours to play through the game for the first time. This is actually deliberate, as the game and its story changes radically depending on your choices, encouraging if not outright demanding several playthroughs. You'll have to play the game at least 2-3 times to see all the content, The real question is will you want to?
This is where the game's story comes in, and while I'll avoid the details as to not spoil it for you I will say that Undertale does something really unique: It tells a story that could only be told by a game. There's a lot of great games with great stories out there, but most of them would also work as a movie or a comic, or maybe even a book. I'm not saying this is necessarily a bad thing, but Undertale is not one of those stories, and that is what makes it so great and so interesting in my opinion.
Another thing I'd like to mention is the game's outstanding attention to detail. The game seems to have some special dialogue for almost every single little moment where you can step out of line. Whether you're deliberatly walking into enemy fire or wearing the starter gear for the entire game, your behaviour is invariably recognized. It's hard to think that a single person could think of all these possible variables.
Lastly, the soundtrack is pretty fantastic. It puts a great focus on melodies, creating a lot of memorable tunes. I'm very bad at music and music terminology so I'm not gonna talk to much about it, but the soundtrack itself is easily worth a buy.
I did say I could mention some bad things about the game earlier one, and I can, mostly on the aesthetics. Undertale's presentation is minimalistic at best and outright ugly at worst. It never detracts from the experience, and I admire the developer's desire to handle the entire game himself as to keep his vision intact but he probably could have hired a better artist.
Undertale has come to quickly establish itself as a cult classic, much like the game that inspired it. Funny, charming and surprisingly deep, Undertale is an experience you shouldn't miss out on.

It's very hard to talk about Undertale because the things that make it such a great game are all things that would make your experience worse if you knew about them beforehand. If you're even remotely interested in the game then I strongly urge you to pick it up right now because waiting will result in you learning about things you shouldn't. That's what happened to me before I played, and I still had a good time but in retrospect I really wish I hadn't done that.
But what can I say about Undertale without spoiling the experience? Both good and bad things, really. It's a bullet hell RPG where rather than simply sit and wait for opponents to do their thing you get to try and avoid taking damage by dodging bullets. On your own turn you either time your attacks for extra damage or try to talk your way out of combat. Almost every encounter in the game can be resolved peacefully so you never really have to resort to violence unless you want to.
Undertale is kind of a linear game and a fairly short one on that. Even if you dally a lot it'll probably take you no more than 10 hours to play through the game for the first time. This is actually deliberate, as the game and its story changes radically depending on your choices, encouraging if not outright demanding several playthroughs. You'll have to play the game at least 2-3 times to see all the content, The real question is will you want to?
This is where the game's story comes in, and while I'll avoid the details as to not spoil it for you I will say that Undertale does something really unique: It tells a story that could only be told by a game. There's a lot of great games with great stories out there, but most of them would also work as a movie or a comic, or maybe even a book. I'm not saying this is necessarily a bad thing, but Undertale is not one of those stories, and that is what makes it so great and so interesting in my opinion.
Another thing I'd like to mention is the game's outstanding attention to detail. The game seems to have some special dialogue for almost every single little moment where you can step out of line. Whether you're deliberatly walking into enemy fire or wearing the starter gear for the entire game, your behaviour is invariably recognized. It's hard to think that a single person could think of all these possible variables.
Lastly, the soundtrack is pretty fantastic. It puts a great focus on melodies, creating a lot of memorable tunes. I'm very bad at music and music terminology so I'm not gonna talk to much about it, but the soundtrack itself is easily worth a buy.
I did say I could mention some bad things about the game earlier one, and I can, mostly on the aesthetics. Undertale's presentation is minimalistic at best and outright ugly at worst. It never detracts from the experience, and I admire the developer's desire to handle the entire game himself as to keep his vision intact but he probably could have hired a better artist.
Undertale has come to quickly establish itself as a cult classic, much like the game that inspired it. Funny, charming and surprisingly deep, Undertale is an experience you shouldn't miss out on.

Very rarely, and I do mean VERY rarely, will a play session pass without some sort of glaring and possibly game-breaking bug. Most of the time, you will have to fight the game itself, as it tries to destroy your experience with everything it has at its disposal. From glitchy zombies, to below average performance (though, admittedly, it is a lot better now), to the violent and toxic community that plagues its servers, everything is out to get you. However, when the game does what it's best at, there is absolutely nothing out there that can replicate that feeling of unbridled adrenaline as you spend thirty minutes in an intense, nerveracking stand off, fighting to keep your life and all the high-tier loot you've spent hours or even days getting. That is a feeling no other game can replicate.
The question still stands, though. Should you buy DayZ?
The answer to that is quite simple. Yes, but not right now. Follow the devblogs, the updates and its development. Buy it when its in a better state. After that, you're on your own against the ruthless brutality of Chernarus.

I think this game breeds the type of community it has (notoriously ♥♥♥♥♥♥). As a new player, you won't have much room to breathe and experience the game mechanics without being attacked and killed often enough to make that initial "oohhhh I smash the rock with my rock to get stuff to get a hatchet!" stage enjoyable, which I think is sad. You can always join a PvE server or an empty server to give yourself room to learn, but to what end? Staying on a PvE server would get incredibly dull, unless simply building a large base satisfies you. Once you grasp the crafting, blueprint hunting, and base building systems, what other reason do you have to keep playing?
Heading to a PvP server means dealing with everything you've worked for being constantly in danger because you aren't online 24/7. You could log in any time to find that you have to start from scratch again, which is incredibly frustrating. And, when you are online, every single player you see is a potential threat, and they will view you as such. Being someone who wants to say hi and not murder every new person you meet puts you at a serious disadvantage. I think thats where the "breeds toxicity" idea comes from, and it makes the game unenjoyable to me. OH NO, THIS GAME IS MEETING ALL MY STANDARDS.
Seriously though, allow me to try and communicate something here - something complex which I lack the vocabulary or understanding to do easily.  Do you know how certain stories or works of art choose a medium, and sometimes they are released in two mediums?  For example, many popular books are made into movies and often we say that the book is better for some reason or another - but truly great films use the filmed medium.
I mention that because I want to talk about video games as a medium.  Many people my age remember bygone classics like Breath of Fire or classic Final Fantasy titles or Earthbound or Chrono Trigger with a specific fondness, and that fondness came in large part from them using the MEDIUM of a role-playing game to create a world and tell a story that suits the medium.
So what characterized those games?  First and foremost, music was used as the primary means to emote.  Without voice-acting and will limited graphical capabilities, music was what the game designers could use to communicate emotion, and that's what they did use.  We remember the music from those games because that's where the emotion existed.  Besides emotive (and, frankly, great) music, those games are also characterized by a certain quirkiness and light-heartedness.
There is a type of humor, a type of bizarre world, a type of strangeness that only works in text-based RPGs.  You're running around from place to place and NPCs shout stuff at you, and the villains have to be cartoony and ridiculous.  We all remember "Son of a Submariner" and "Spoony" and the Phantom Train and Norstein Bekkler's lab and fighting all 6 third-strongest moles and a few Developer's rooms and the crossdressing squat game.  This kind of humor and world, often called "quirkiness," suits the medium well - look at FF13 of an example of a game that was arguably forced to take itself seriously because of the voice-acting and graphical capability of the system, or the worries about the cross-dressing scene in the FF7 remake.  There's something important there, something I struggle to explain.
But Toby Fox understands.  Toby Fox has made one of my favorite video games of all time.  I love this game with every fiber of my being, and I love it because it shows Toby understands something about the RPG medium that I can only barely manage to put into words vaguely.  It jumps from serious to silly in the same way that Earthbound did.  As far as I'm concerned, Toby Fox is a genius.

It's pretty hard to sum up Undertale in words. All I can really say for starters is I wasn't prepared for how awesome it was! I don't play games nearly as often as I did when I was a kid, and really, nowadays it's only games with an "oldschool charm" which draw me in. That, combined with the fact I don't really actively seek stuff out anymore is why just last week, it had probably been a year and a half since I was actually playing any kind of single-player story-based game. For me, games had just become stuff like Mario Party or Super Smash Bros to play with others who came over once in a blue moon, and things like that.
But then, out of nowhere I start hearing everyone talking about Undertale. I'm also warned by a friend of mine to look up nothing about the game before playing it.. and I heed his advice, only really looking at the Steam Store page for it. The graphics look interesting, and the concept of not having to kill anyone seemed both relevant to me as a person and really intriguing just to see how it would work out. So I took the plunge and got it, and haven't regretted it at all. Undertale is an emotional journey, and one I'm glad I took a chance on.
The story, aesthetics, soundtrack, and most of all, characters, are pretty much flawless. This game really restored my hope for new games, and I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to try something new, and likes that old-school feel as well. Undertale is not part of any cookie-cutter category, it's in a league all its own. The only nitpicks I have are very minor.. the encounter rate, at times, seems slightly low in certain areas, but it's really no issue. And the other one is.. wish the game was longer! Haha.
In conclusion, of the hundreds of games I've played in my life it's definitely one of the best, and is in my Top 5, for sure. Undertale really touched me, and I couldn't recommend it more. 5/5 Stars, 100%, A++++++ And all that!

I loved the content and the concept, but patch after patch, they've failed to make the game _remotely_ playable. DayZ is a fantastic idea built on a flight, vehicle, and "human" simulator. There is no fluidity to movement mechanics making for herky-jerky gameplay that _should no longer exist_ in modern games.
This, and very poor netcode and prediction, make for a frustrating game when dealing with anything close quarters. Zombies that run past you and hit at the air ten feet behind you ... and suddenly you start bleeding. Hitbox detection with rogue netcode is nearly impossible.
But hey, they got crafting in there... and you can handcuff someone and put a bag over their heads.
The lack of priority on actual gameplay reminds me that this is continues to be a mod that will never change the engine it rests on. If they ever work on gameplay... and not on the game content, maybe I'll come back and review it, but there are no indications that this will ever happen. It's up to you to decide if you want to spend the price that's never dropped less than $25 and going up continually... to play a human simulator that can be a lot of fun while you explore and run across the map, but suddenly drops to a frustrating clickfest when you encounter a zombie or a well equipped player.
Sorry Bohemian. Sorry Dean. This game will die on the vine if you don't fix the gameplay and netcode. Alternatives are coming ... and I expect they've learned these lessons.

TL;DR: A wonderfully made RPG, with unique enemies, areas, and story. More than worth full price.
Undertale is one of those games that is really hard to review, because the most amazing moments in the game are either spoilers, or require build up to them. I liken it to an amazing comedian, where by the end of his show you are laughing your♥♥♥♥♥off, but if you tell those last jokes to a friend afterward, its not nearly as funny because they weren't there for the appropriate build up. A good game, comedian, movie, etc, can lead you in, build you up, and give you a great whole experience. Undertale is such a game. I would liken it to Cowboy Bebop and other pieces that are likable by people who normally don't even like the genre. Not that if you are only into hardcore multiplayer FPSs will this be the one game that changes your mind...but if you just love good games, this is one of the best I have played.
Gameplay wise, combat is far from the normal turn based 'I attack, you attack' system most RPGs have. While it is turn based, enemies attack by doing a facsimile of a bullet-hell game, where you must dodge their attacks with your heart. You act by either attacking, or talking to the enemies to convince them to stop fighting. Each enemy has unique bullet patterns and commands to get them to stop fighting, and bosses take it one step further by changing gameplay up with the mechanics of how your heart moves, and all bosses have many, many bullet patterns. Since most of the time you aren't wanting to kill the bosses, you have to survive through progressively harder and harder bullet combos to get to the point where you can get them to a point where you don't have to kill them. There are random encounters with enemies that can repeat, but every area has unique enemies, no sprite swaps, and it varies depending on if they are alone or with friends on how their bullets work. This system is superb, and really should inform others on how to make RPG combat interesting.
The overworld is mainly based on walking through set areas, and it is pretty linear. There are puzzles to solve, which are unique to each area and place, but never too onerous. The areas are diverse, well made, and thematic to what is going on in the story.
The game itself is beautiful. While it gives off a  bit of lo-fi appearance, bosses especially have very well done animation that makes the fight feel more epic than it already is. Nothing is overused or repeated without reason, and every enemy or character has unique sprites and actions. A lot of work went into making everything feel unique, and it shows.
The music is awesome, so much so I wish I bought the soundtrack bundle. I would reccomend just going and listening to the soundtrack on youtube, but it does include some spoilers, and some of the tracks may not have the same meaning without going through the boss fights. The overworld themes are a bit forgettable, but they serve to set the mood, not override the story going on.
The story itself is well told, with great characters that make you honestly care about what is going on. At one point you get a device to talk to certain characters for advice. It tends to be you not calling it for advice though, but to get more story from the characters, as almost every room in the game has them say something unique that adds to the story or their characterization. Every personality in the game is well written and adds to the feeling of the world itself, so much so I will find it hard to kill any of them for one of the endings.
Final verdict: If you like games with good stories, buy it and play it, you won't regret it at all.

I loved the content and the concept, but patch after patch, they've failed to make the game _remotely_ playable. DayZ is a fantastic idea built on a flight, vehicle, and "human" simulator. There is no fluidity to movement mechanics making for herky-jerky gameplay that _should no longer exist_ in modern games.
This, and very poor netcode and prediction, make for a frustrating game when dealing with anything close quarters. Zombies that run past you and hit at the air ten feet behind you ... and suddenly you start bleeding. Hitbox detection with rogue netcode is nearly impossible.
But hey, they got crafting in there... and you can handcuff someone and put a bag over their heads.
The lack of priority on actual gameplay reminds me that this is continues to be a mod that will never change the engine it rests on. If they ever work on gameplay... and not on the game content, maybe I'll come back and review it, but there are no indications that this will ever happen. It's up to you to decide if you want to spend the price that's never dropped less than $25 and going up continually... to play a human simulator that can be a lot of fun while you explore and run across the map, but suddenly drops to a frustrating clickfest when you encounter a zombie or a well equipped player.
Sorry Bohemian. Sorry Dean. This game will die on the vine if you don't fix the gameplay and netcode. Alternatives are coming ... and I expect they've learned these lessons.

Undertale may not be perfect, but with its varied cast of characters, fantastic music, and engaging story, it comes out pretty dang good.
Pros:
- Likeable characters (There's going to be at least one!)
- Great music
- The bullet hell segments are a lot of fun
- The boss battles are great, and can be pretty challenging too
- The game has good replay value--resetting can reveal some pretty neat secrets
- The humour is actually pretty funny sometimes, especially on the first playthrough
Cons:
- Random encounters become too easy once you've adjusted to them
- The game can be a little tedious upon replay (Really noticeable with unskippable segments, like the RG battle)
- There is a "cutscene" (of sorts) towards the end of the "good" routes which is unskippable and annoyingly long
Overall though, I have to recommend giving Undertale a shot. While it does have its problems, most of those lie within replaying it and not the mandatory experience. Undertale's got a lot of charm, and it'd be a shame to not at least try it once.

After seeing many posts regarding fanart, memes, and audio/video of Undertale through my Tumblr dash, I'd decided to go ahead and try watching a walkthrough of the game...
Now, as someone who didn't have a steam at the time, I usually would have been very satisfied with that alone..
However, about midway through the let's play, I had seen talk of various endings, mutiple easter eggs, and very lovable characters.... and--- I got curious.

That was it. That was all it took for me to secure a Steam account and nab myself a digital copy of this game that had been spoken so highly of.  And thoughts?
First of all, the characters:
There is nothing more pleasing for someone like me, who's pretty much fallen into skeleton hell, than meeting a couple of absolutely WONDERFUL skeleton brothers nearly right off the bat. Honestly, my favourite is the hoodie-wearing, pun-telling Sans, who's knack for humor as well as seeming awareness to the player's ability to SAVE and LOAD had simply won my heart the moment I'd met him.
Of course, you can't forget the younger-acting, 'cool dude' brother, Papyrus, who loves to yell and cook spaghetti, and whom sounds 100% correct in a Waluigi-esque voice.
They're possibly one of the best video game duos I've ever had the pleasure of encountering.
Secondly, there is Flowey.
He's your guide through the Undertale world! The smiling, chipper, ever-happy intro to the Monsters' realm,
a little yellow sunflower who will teach you all about LOVE and EXP--

And then Goat Mom, or Toriel,
who is perfect not only for her visual play on words name ( TU-Toriel ), but for her sweeter than butterscotch-cinnamon pie personality.
On top of these four examples, there are plenty of other FANTASTIC, well-rounded and relatable characters that'll probably leave you in tears by the End Credits, no matter the ending you get.  ( Sniffle... sniffle--- I'm not crying... I just caught a tear in my eye! )
Secondly, and do forgive me for this review being WAY longer than necessary,
THE STORY--!

In my opinion, some of the best games in the world revolve around a story... and not just any story.
It's for the same reason that I love Last of Us that I find myself drawn to Undertale, time and time again, to replay it over and over and over:
The laughter, the heartbreak, and the journey.
Had it been a non-linear sort of game, I can't say I'd enjoy it as much as I did...
While it allows the player time and room to explore areas on their own, fight enemies to their heart's content, and simply goof around until picking up the story again,  Undertale follows a wonderful plotline that draws the player in and bases its end on the player's own choice.
And when I say that, I don't mean 'here's your choice, no matter what you decide you'll still get the same end but with different characters alive--',  no... I mean entirely DIFFERENT ENDS, based off of the way YOU PLAY.
Granted, it doesn't exactly depend on whether or not you answer Junior Jumble/Crossword for being the harder kind of puzzle,  but it does rely on who you decide to befriend, who you decide to fight..
whether you leave the monsters ALIVE, or DEAD.

In the end, I've ended up completing the game with the Pacifist End twice-- I haven't been able to pull myself down the darker route,  because as much fun experimenting as it'd be, I can't kill the characters I've grown to love...
or live with the knowledge that the game will remember my choices, well after a reset.
To try and wrap it up here,
( because honestly.... this is getting horrendously long - I'm so sorry! ),
despite the basic feel of its pixilated world, Undertale does a fanstastic job of bringing to life comical, serious and touching characters; it holds within it, a captivating storyline, a charming world, the nostalgia of an old RPG game like Pokemon or Earthbound, and wonderful lore to not only the endings, but everything and everyone in it.
( Don't even get me STARTED on what a great soundtrack it has!! )

It'll leave you with plenty of laughs, plenty of tears, and plenty of secrets and endings to uncover....
Toby Fox, my hat's off to you!
Undertale is my Game of the Year by a longshot...
and I will definitely reccomend it to any and all who game!

There's an initial draw with DayZ that really hooks you in. You'll play marathon sessions and later share your stories of Chernarus with work chums. And then there's the growing disappointment when you realise how broken it is, and how much potential is missed.
DayZ is a complex, open-world survival FPS. Explore Chernarus: Wander the lovely sprawling countryside and attempt to pronounce the names of the towns.
There's tension like nothing I've ever experienced here. The first few days of playing will glue you to the keyboard and make your heart leap out of your chest when you catch a glimpse of movement in the corner of your screen.

You hide. You watch. You wait.
You've been gathering equipment for the last hour and desperately don't want to lose your rare weapon. But you're running low on bandages. Maybe this person will trade you some for a can of beans.
Did they see you? Maybe it was just a different-coloured patch of grass. Or maybe a harmless zombie. But no, there they are. It's a player. Is that a gun? They're coming towards you. What do you do? You have to decide quickly. You raise your weapon and hover the iron sights over your target. You ready your finger over the trigger and hit the push-to-talk key...
And then the server crashes.
It's then that you start noticing the irredeemable problems with DayZ. Problems that are so ingrained into the game that they probably won't ever get fixed.
It's then that you start noticing all the hats.
Why are there only hats lying around? Because people don't care about hats. They only take the useful items. Without a system of loot spawns/despawns, servers quickly become populated by hats and players wearing only one hat. And yet the developers keep on adding hats, diluting the loot even further. The servers have to shut down and restart every hour just to generate something other than hats.
Until they do something drastic with loot spawns, the chances are you'll be passing shelves filled with hats, gas stoves and bags of seeds, finding nothing useful until you get sniped by someone who spent hours on a farming server before switching to this one.
Server switching. That’s another problem. One that’s been solved by locking you out of the game for an amount of time if your connection (or the server’s) goes down. Okay. So you wait out the timer, staring at a black screen and then, after it reaches zero: “
” Okay… “
” Hmm… “
” No. I’ve got other games in my library that don’t lock me out of them.
I own games that:
Yes, it’s early access. Yes, some of the problems may be solved. Yes, I had fun with it. But no, I can’t recommend it.
I’m not sure the ArmA engine can really support this kind of game. I’m not sure that I can enjoy trying to survive at 20fps before being killed for the nothing that I own. And I’m not sure the devs will ever get over their thing for hats.

The story! Dear god, the story. What starts out as a pretty standard retro themed little-kid-in-a-scary-world RPG quickly turns into genuine care for well designed characters, some of which are downright hilarious and all of which are memorable. The complete lack of a fourth wall is played to perfection in each of the three available endings, and there are a number of twists and turns to surprise even the most jaded gamer. (Indeed, that's the whole point!)
The music is nothing short of phenomenal, and there will absolutely be tunes you catch yourself humming (or trying to get out of your head) weeks later.
Undertale has a very unique battle system - rather than the usual final-fantasy-esque bit where you swing a sword at someone from 10 feet away and they take damage, you actually dodge various bullets in a touhou/danmaku-esque game of skill. This means that if you're good enough, you can take no damage whatsoever. This means that careful play is rewarded, and there is no grinding required to make meaningful progression.
Undertale is short - an amateur speedrunner can complete the game from start to finish in two hours, and a normal human in 3-4 hours. This may or may not be a bad thing, though, since you must play through the game at least three times to experience everything it has to offer.
It's hard to read anything about the game online without running into spoilers. Given how much story and care is packed into its short time frame, any spoilers you find will be *disastrous* to your enjoyment.
Realizing that the creator of this masterpiece, Toby Fox, is so burned out on the hype and subsequent positive reaction that there will probably never be a sequel or a usage of these characters ever again.
RPG of the year 2015. You owe it to yourself to pick this game up, and then after you've beaten it, to go pick up the soundtrack. Damn near flawless, and the most memorable game in a long time. Highly, highly recommended!

Starting with the good things:
- The maps are huge and randomly generated for the most part. There is a decent amount of order in how the map is generated, which makes it easy to find out if your friends are near you. Landmarks like Lighthouses or other buildings can also help with this.
- Exploring is fun. Finding a rad town or walking along the road and breaking the barrels and finding items you want is very exciting.
- The crafting system is complex, but pretty easy to figure out. You don't need to go on a wiki to find the crafting recpies, although the rust wiki can be very helpful for things.
- Building is fun but expect to run out of materials fairly fast.
- The game is a grind, but is for the most part fun if you're patient.
Now for the bad things:
- Raiders. Pretty much if you have a life outside of this game, you are going to get raided frequently. You better have a large group to play with if you are playing on any server that regularly has players. Yes, you can protect your base, but there are always ways to get in.
- Being a fresh spawn is VERY hard, If someone who has anything sees you, you are probably going to die. 99% of the time, other players are hostile and unforgiving. They don't care if you're new. They don't care that you have absolutely no way of fighting back, or even that you have nothing on you but a rock and a torch. They kill you just to kill you and for no other reason.
- Very toxic community. If you even dare to ask how to start off as a noob, you will get bombarded with rudeness (for the most part) or people saying you're butthurt or "cry more lol" if you so even respond to them killing you. I really dislike the "This is rust, be good or get out" mentality of the community as if because it's hard, you're supposed to just suck it up and deal with it.
Suggestions for the game
- Singleplayer mode - This would be very useful for people who just want to get some practice in before playing on large servers.
- Nerf the raiders - It is far too easy to raid small bases. Anyone with some C4 can raid an offline player. It should be more of a challenge to raid small bases, even if you are further ahead than the people who built those bases. It's also impossible to protect yourself even if they have guns unless they have terrible aim and you can somehow kill them with your axe or rock. It should be possible to protect yourself as a newish player against enemies.
Overall right now, expect an early access quality game. It's buggy as of now because it's still in alpha.

As I close in on 3,000 hours of Rust, I thought it wise to augment and expand upon my original review.
TL:DR - This game is crazy, and you might be for playing it, but you should play this game!
What even is Rust?? - RUST IS IN EARLY ACCESS, AND CHANGES WEEKLY! In its current (and by far BEST) iteration, the game can be broken down into a few stages.  First, you will spawn naked on a beach with nothing but a rock and torch.  You will use your rock to gather resources such as wood, stone, metal ore, and sulfur ore.  The wood and stone will allow you to craft early tools and weapons like the stone hatchet, stone pick axe, and spear.  Along the way, you will want to gather the hemp plants for cloth to make clothes, and a hunting bow.  Finding and eating mushrooms, corn, and pumpkin so you don't starve to death is also a bonus!  Second, gathering enough wood and stone to build a structure is key.  You will need a base to be in when you log off, and to store all the goodies you'll be coming across as you explore the island.  After your base is up, you'll search for junk piles containing barrels, and crates.  In these you will find useful items and components which u can return to your base, or recycle for scrap, the marrow of the game.  Scrap is life.  It allows you to research found items, so you can craft them, and can be a valuable trade commodity.  Without scrap, the revolver you found can't be replaced without some luck if you die with it,  as you would not have researched it, and thus, can not craft a new one once you've re-spawned.
Spawn, gather, build, collect.  That's the rhythm of the game.
What to expect - This can depend greatly on where you start playing.  If you jump right into a high population server, you can expect zero mercy.  You will be hunted down moments after spawning while still naked, carrying nothing but your rock and torch.  Chances are, the person killing you will be talking trash about you being a newb, and telling you to "git gud".  If you enjoy trial by fire, this will be up your alley.  You could also choose to start on a low population server, or find and empty server, to get your legs under you.  In any case, Rust is ruthless, and every person you see should be viewed as the enemy.  Hide, shoot first, or die.
There are also PvE (player vs environment) servers where you're unable to kill people, or destroy their buildings.  These can be good for getting your feet wet, but will certainly give you an unrealistic expectation of what the game really is.
Finally, expect that once you've spent hours building your nice little base hidden off in some corner of the woods, hours collecting resources and materials to expand your arsenal, and hours enjoying yourself, that you will log in one day and find some one has blown into your base with explosives, killed your sleeping body, and taken all your possessions.  That is Rust.  If you can't handle it, this game isn't for you.
So is it even worth it? - The shortest and best answer I can think of, is, ABSOLUTELY.  The satisfaction of finally finding that item you've been looking for, from getting your first air drop, from killing your first tormentor, to narrowly evading the patrol helicopter as you scurry home with a full inventory, to taking out the Bradley IFV patrolling the launch site, to your first big score on a raid, is unmatched in any game I've played.  Sure, the low points can make you question your sanity for putting yourself through this, and question the very foundations of humanity and morality, but in the end, it's a game, and triumph can take many forms, and there are many paths with which to achieve it.
In conclusion - I recommend this game to anyone.  Never played a FPS?  Doesn't matter.  Aren't big on survival games?  Doesn't matter.  Aren't an insane sociopath?  Doesn't matter.  In Rust, you will find a niche modded server, a worthy adversary, a despicable villain, or a true friend.  You will discover the joys and art of creating structures, painting signs and pictures, or exploring.  You may take pride in playing fair and being noble, or revel in playing the profligate.  In any case, you will find something to love about this game.

I'm usually not a huge fan of indie games because most of it is genuinely terrible. There's some saying... "most of anything will be♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, and it's true; but Undertale falls into the minority - the good games! The game itself isn't very long, but as for the impression it made on me, I can honestly say that it's something that will stick with me for a while. First of all, the cast is great! Lastly, the gameplay is something I've never seen before in an RPG: bullet hell-esque dodging and sparing your enemies? I gotta say, the feeling of imminent death and dopamine skyrocketing was something I hadn't experienced in a really long time, I seriously felt like I lost a few years of my life due to a certain... encounter. Anyways, overall, I'd say the game design is very strong which is pretty hard to find nowadays!

The survival may not be entirely realistic, but the human element poses a big enough challenge this early in development.  Updates come regularly and always bring more for the player to do.  It's addicting, it's fun, and it's worth supporting.

Where do I even begin to describe how awesome this game is?
Undertale is a new spin on the classic RPGs like Earthbound, throwing you into a bullet-hell minigame during the enemy's turn so that you can actively dodge or counterattack, and several bosses throw in new easy to figure out gimmicks, like Mettaton whose final boss fight turns into one of those clasic space shooters.
However, there is one thing that the game and it's players want you to remember always: Violence is not always the answer. There are several endings in the game that change depending on your actions: Pacifist, Neutral, Genocide and TRUE Pacifist. Each ending (except for TRUE Pacifist) gets progressively worse and worse depending on how many monsters you kill, rather than befriend.
As someone who hasn't even touched the Neutral or Genocide routes yet, I can safely say that I don't even want to decide which bosses to kill, all of the characters, even those you're supposed to hate, are far too likeable: Asgore, Undyne, Sans and so on.
To end this short review, let me give you some advice: Unless you want a bad time, pick the pacifist route for your first playthrough, or at the very least neutral if you've already killed a generic monster (yes those count too, believe it or not).

As a warning if you DO decide to genocide do it AFTER a pacifist run, or itll ruin things. in a bad way. This game is amazing, so many feels, so much loves, so many cries, so many dogs, such good music, such great chars, such great gameplay, some puzzles, and ♥♥♥♥ing flowey.
