This is the one game in which you can work for hours on end to acquire the rarest and most sought-after gear, only to get shot in the back of the head. This wonderful game if a hassle for a lot of computers, but if you really love the game, you get used to it, and it dosen't really matter. This game single-handedly immerses the player without even using a story. As it states in the trailer, it is really "your story". After spending hours to get geared, you must choose. WIll you become a bandit, hellbent on getting whatever you can from whoever you can whenever you can? Or will you be a hero, hardened after countless betrayals and unsuspected deaths who makes it their mission to help whoever they can, and only kill when provoked? The game is so good, it dosen't really need a story. The player will make their own. For the player, the immersion is fueled by the interaction with other players because you never know what you'll get. The second one of your squadmates says "player! player!" your heart races with adrenaline. Will he kill you? WIll he befriend you? Will he betray you? All kinds of thoughts will run through your mind, and when the time comes, you ask that one famous question that EVERYONE who has even heard about DayZ will know. "Are you friendly?". This question will determine whether or not the person you have just come across on the massive 225sq k map of Chernarus will kill you, or become a friend. The point is, people mold the game, and everyone is molding the game for another player. You meet a guy, part of his and your story sees a new event. Another part of why so many people love this game is th loot. FInding loot is something unique in and of itself to DayZ. You simply cannot miss a building because loot spawns, for the most part, are pretty random. WIll you find something that has spawned in that house? Will you find something another plaer has left behind? A dead body? A weapon locker? Loot is very fun to find, and I've learned after countless fair and unfair deaths that after you die with something really nice, you come back only to find something better, and so the cycle continues. This game is most certainly a step in the right direction, and is very impressive for an alpha. Every update brings new loot that gets you back on the edge of your seat so that you can find it. Updates are very exciting, and I am looking forward to the next one. Unlike the mod, the standalone if SUPER easy to get used to, and know the controls, and how to use the inventory. I recommend this game to a patient person who wants a zombie game that feels like they are really in it, and that they are experiencing it like their characters. One who buys this game should be patient because of the amount of time it takes for you to run to where you want. (My friends have gotten very impatient with me when it comes to running from Kamyshovo to Balota). Tell your friends about DayZ and squad up. Like most games, this game is best played with friends, as there are funny, happy and sad moments to be had in the vast land of Chernarus.

I just finished playing through the game on the True Pacifist Route, and I just have to say that it immediately became my favorite game on Steam (that I've played). The game's overall plot and the fact that you get to choose whether to spare monsters or not is an interesting feature that makes the game more enjoyable and thought-provoking. I was also impressed by the amount of backstory they put into everything, not to mention all the different monsters, the battle sequences for every "boss", the puzzles, and the unique personality and dialogue they gave to each main character. The graphics are also nice, as they don't feel that they are trying to hard nor does it feel like the game was poorly funded.
It's hard to find a unique game out there nowadays, and while I have seen a couple elements of Undertale in other games, the combination and the way it was presented made for a pleasantly surprising experience. I, personally, become very attached to things in video games, so it may not effect everyone the same, but if you become emotionally attached or enveloped in plots, this will definitely suck you in. And in a good way, even though I cried about fifteen or so times throughout it, it was worth it in the end.
I definitely recommend it for everyone. Even if you think it isn't the kind of game you're looking for, try it. You won't regret it.

I'm not going to attempt to write one of those Really Good reviews that end up as, like, the first review on the store page or whatever, but I'll try to be honest with how I felt about this game.
But... if you don't care about that, here's the short version: if you're interested in a compelling, funny, and genuine story, with lots of what I can only accurately describe as "internet humor", then get the game, dude. It's also got a cool battle system. And more!!!
...Uh, yeah. Okay, moving on. This game is a rare experience, to be sure. And, honestly? I don't think the words I could say regarding what that "experience" was for me would do it justice. But it was certainly something that I enjoyed thoroughly, and I'm glad I bought the game when I did.
If I were to condense it to a single point, I would say that what this game does best is that it subverts the expectations of its player. And it does this straight from the very beginning, messing around even with concepts as standard to the JRPG genre as the turn-based battle system (where, along with the introduction of a "mercy" option, the deaths of monsters now take on a very *real* toll on the world). This, along with many other interesting takes on the JRPG genre, gives the mechanics of the game a fresh look in a sea of otherwise similarly designed games.
The story is fantastic as well, don't get me wrong, I just don't know what I can really say without spoiling anything. I'd definitely say the story itself is what has kept me interested in the series even now, though, weeks after I've completed the game. I love these friggin' characters, dude. Take my word for it? Or don't. I mean the game is literally like, 10 dollars, man. That's not even that much.
Basically, if you're considering it and think you might like the humor, then just give it a shot! 10 dollars ain't much, my dude. You won't miss those dollars, I promise.

Starting with the good things:
- The maps are huge and randomly generated for the most part. There is a decent amount of order in how the map is generated, which makes it easy to find out if your friends are near you. Landmarks like Lighthouses or other buildings can also help with this.
- Exploring is fun. Finding a rad town or walking along the road and breaking the barrels and finding items you want is very exciting.
- The crafting system is complex, but pretty easy to figure out. You don't need to go on a wiki to find the crafting recpies, although the rust wiki can be very helpful for things.
- Building is fun but expect to run out of materials fairly fast.
- The game is a grind, but is for the most part fun if you're patient.
Now for the bad things:
- Raiders. Pretty much if you have a life outside of this game, you are going to get raided frequently. You better have a large group to play with if you are playing on any server that regularly has players. Yes, you can protect your base, but there are always ways to get in.
- Being a fresh spawn is VERY hard, If someone who has anything sees you, you are probably going to die. 99% of the time, other players are hostile and unforgiving. They don't care if you're new. They don't care that you have absolutely no way of fighting back, or even that you have nothing on you but a rock and a torch. They kill you just to kill you and for no other reason.
- Very toxic community. If you even dare to ask how to start off as a noob, you will get bombarded with rudeness (for the most part) or people saying you're butthurt or "cry more lol" if you so even respond to them killing you. I really dislike the "This is rust, be good or get out" mentality of the community as if because it's hard, you're supposed to just suck it up and deal with it.
Suggestions for the game
- Singleplayer mode - This would be very useful for people who just want to get some practice in before playing on large servers.
- Nerf the raiders - It is far too easy to raid small bases. Anyone with some C4 can raid an offline player. It should be more of a challenge to raid small bases, even if you are further ahead than the people who built those bases. It's also impossible to protect yourself even if they have guns unless they have terrible aim and you can somehow kill them with your axe or rock. It should be possible to protect yourself as a newish player against enemies.
Overall right now, expect an early access quality game. It's buggy as of now because it's still in alpha.

As I close in on 3,000 hours of Rust, I thought it wise to augment and expand upon my original review.
TL:DR - This game is crazy, and you might be for playing it, but you should play this game!
What even is Rust?? - RUST IS IN EARLY ACCESS, AND CHANGES WEEKLY! In its current (and by far BEST) iteration, the game can be broken down into a few stages.  First, you will spawn naked on a beach with nothing but a rock and torch.  You will use your rock to gather resources such as wood, stone, metal ore, and sulfur ore.  The wood and stone will allow you to craft early tools and weapons like the stone hatchet, stone pick axe, and spear.  Along the way, you will want to gather the hemp plants for cloth to make clothes, and a hunting bow.  Finding and eating mushrooms, corn, and pumpkin so you don't starve to death is also a bonus!  Second, gathering enough wood and stone to build a structure is key.  You will need a base to be in when you log off, and to store all the goodies you'll be coming across as you explore the island.  After your base is up, you'll search for junk piles containing barrels, and crates.  In these you will find useful items and components which u can return to your base, or recycle for scrap, the marrow of the game.  Scrap is life.  It allows you to research found items, so you can craft them, and can be a valuable trade commodity.  Without scrap, the revolver you found can't be replaced without some luck if you die with it,  as you would not have researched it, and thus, can not craft a new one once you've re-spawned.
Spawn, gather, build, collect.  That's the rhythm of the game.
What to expect - This can depend greatly on where you start playing.  If you jump right into a high population server, you can expect zero mercy.  You will be hunted down moments after spawning while still naked, carrying nothing but your rock and torch.  Chances are, the person killing you will be talking trash about you being a newb, and telling you to "git gud".  If you enjoy trial by fire, this will be up your alley.  You could also choose to start on a low population server, or find and empty server, to get your legs under you.  In any case, Rust is ruthless, and every person you see should be viewed as the enemy.  Hide, shoot first, or die.
There are also PvE (player vs environment) servers where you're unable to kill people, or destroy their buildings.  These can be good for getting your feet wet, but will certainly give you an unrealistic expectation of what the game really is.
Finally, expect that once you've spent hours building your nice little base hidden off in some corner of the woods, hours collecting resources and materials to expand your arsenal, and hours enjoying yourself, that you will log in one day and find some one has blown into your base with explosives, killed your sleeping body, and taken all your possessions.  That is Rust.  If you can't handle it, this game isn't for you.
So is it even worth it? - The shortest and best answer I can think of, is, ABSOLUTELY.  The satisfaction of finally finding that item you've been looking for, from getting your first air drop, from killing your first tormentor, to narrowly evading the patrol helicopter as you scurry home with a full inventory, to taking out the Bradley IFV patrolling the launch site, to your first big score on a raid, is unmatched in any game I've played.  Sure, the low points can make you question your sanity for putting yourself through this, and question the very foundations of humanity and morality, but in the end, it's a game, and triumph can take many forms, and there are many paths with which to achieve it.
In conclusion - I recommend this game to anyone.  Never played a FPS?  Doesn't matter.  Aren't big on survival games?  Doesn't matter.  Aren't an insane sociopath?  Doesn't matter.  In Rust, you will find a niche modded server, a worthy adversary, a despicable villain, or a true friend.  You will discover the joys and art of creating structures, painting signs and pictures, or exploring.  You may take pride in playing fair and being noble, or revel in playing the profligate.  In any case, you will find something to love about this game.

It's been just over a year since DayZ was released to early access on Steam. Although it's still full of bugs and game breaking glitches, DayZ is an experience unlike any other!
With the introduction of tents, persistent items and now the games first vehicle, DayZ is slowly returning to it's glory days of the original mod!
Don't get me wrong though, it still needs a LOT of work and I can't see it being finished until at least 2016.
The Good:
A massive map to explore - For those who have never played before, expect to get lost... a lot! Villages, towns and cities are dotted around the map for you to find. Military camps can also be discovered for those who dare to find them!
Player Interactions - The community are what make DayZ what it is! When you see someone, you don't know if they're friendly or hostile. Do you avoid them? Or do you talk to them and hope for the best? Sometimes the choices you make are a matter of life or death!
Active development team - Although the development has been quite a slow 1, no one can say the dev team hasn't been hard at work on this game. Updates usually come at least once a month which normally include changes to the map, new items and general tweaks to the game.
The Bad:
Bugs/Glitches: This is an early access game in it's alpha stage, and with early access comes bugs. Expect game crashes, occasional long loading times, randomly dropping dead, odd animations and item lag to name a few. It's a game that demands a lot of patience!
The Zombies: Zombies have been made gradually better over time, but they're far from perfect! They still run/hit you through walls and just seem broken overall. Also, don't expect to see more that 10 on screen at once! Which is a shame considering this is meant to be a zombie apocalypse!
Lacking Features: I've put a lot of hours into the mod and the standalone. I've explored the whole map, found all there is to find and experienced first hand countless amounts of player interactions (Funny, hostile, wierd, random, friendly). Now I find myself asking, what next? For new players this wont be a problem for quite some time, but for more experienced players I'm sure this will be a question on a lot of players minds sooner or later....

So many games advertise the possibilities of choosing the path of being either the good guy or the bad guy. That's not even Undertale's main selling point, and it does it absolutely wonderfully.
To bring you up to speed; Undertale is a traditional 8/16-bit RPG game, in which you go on a journey as a small kid to escape the Underground. What really sets this game apart from everything else in this genre is two aspects of the battles. The first is that instead of taking direct damage during a monster's turn, you are put into something of a miniature shoot-em-up style scenario where you have to avoid the various bullet-like projectiles and patterns the monsters throw at you. This really mixes up the challenge and overall fun factor of battles.
The other and arguably more important of the key differences is that, as Undertale actually advertises, this is an RPG where you can play through the entire game without ever physically harming the opposition, let alone kill them. If you choose not to harm any of the creatures, you must win your battles by instead sparing them through mercy. How do you show mercy? This is where the game really shines in both its creativity and humor. Every monster and boss has its own unique way of being "dealt" with through the pacifist route. You have to figure out what makes each of them tick through various interactive choices, until finally you earn the ability to spare them safely.
This on top of the wonderful characters and world, as well as a great story and lore that's already ripe for discussion and expanding upon makes this one of the more memorable and surprising games of this year.
Of course, there's also the option to play the traditional way; physically fighting and killing monsters. But... Well, let's just say that Undertale does -not- advertise that aspect of the game for a very good reason. It's your choice should you decide to go ahead and start ending the lives of so many by your hands.

I just finished my non-stop playthrough of Undertale. I can honestly say that no game has touched me on a level quite like this. The only other game I can think of that even comes close is Kentucky Route Zero or To The Moon, but for vastly different reasons.
First off, let me say that, as a game designer, KRZ is the prime example of how to teach a player about themselves without saying a word. To The Moon is a perfect example of how to tell a story in a game and have the player bawling their eyes out by the end of it. Undertale finds itself sweetly in the middle.
While playing Undertale, I was constantly evaluating myself and what I believe in. I can honestly say that at several moments in the game I was choked up because I was questioning my own values. Does the skill required to beat this enemy passively outweigh the cost of just killing them and being done with it? Which do I sacrifice given the choice between two beliefs? Who do I sacrifice given the choice between two loved ones? Questions like these came up a lot, not so much in the beginning, but more and more towards the end as I realized this story had to end somehow.
A second note, the humor and cleverness of this game is fabulous. There are so many hidden treasures for you to find all around, and I'm sure that in my initial playthrough I only scratched the surface. This game has incredible replayability, which is really impressive for a game as story-driven as this one is. Undertale reminded me a lot of the Stanley Parable (the end is never the end is never the end is never the end) in the sense that, yes, I was always doubting whether or not I was REALLY at the end of the game, but also in the sense that the game is very self aware, and it plays the player. The forth wall is so thin in many parts of the game (for instance, wrecking your save files and crashing your game intentionally) that it really becomes something else entirely to you. I don't know how to explain it, but it's definitely a good trait.
Finally, the emotion behind this game. Like I said above, I'm a game designer. I firmly believe that games are the ultimate artistic medium, and that no other modern or ancient technology is comparable to that of the potential that video games have for conveying personal meaning and emotion. The idea that a game can make you feel certain things strongly is obviously very personal, but I'm sure all of us had similar heartstrings pulled at certain times in this game. Toriel placing that slice of butterscotch pie on the floor was one of those moments for me, as well as realizing that I had taken that snowman to the ends of the earth. Another moment that I remember as being particularly feels-y was when I was battling the science experiments in the lab. I say feels-y because I don't really know what emotion I was feeling. I was sad, for sure, but there was more to it than that. It was a certain emptiness. This is where games (can) excel. They can make you feel things that you otherwise could never feel - they widen your emotional spectrum to places its never been - because you literally could not have these experiences in the real world, or in a play, or through a song, or by looking at a statue. These are things that have to be experienced first-hand in order to be understood.
That being said, a lot of the time, I play a game, and I think "Wow, that really should have been a movie." Or, "That would make a great book." While these are nice thoughts to have, these are not thoughts you should be having while playing a game. A game is something that needs to be specifically experienced by you, in your own way, and from your own perspective. If it could work out any other way, than it shouldn't be a game. The same kind of reasoning goes for other art forms as well.
Undertale had to be a game. It fulfilled its role beautifully.
TL;DR:
Every once in a while, a game comes around that reminds us all why we play games. Undertale is that game.
10/10, would recommend.
Thank you, Undertale Team. You are artists.

Written by Andreas
My first day on the island did not go well. Waking after some unknown calamity, it was only a few minutes before I stumbled upon a man-made structure and encountered its owner, working diligently to expand and improve his home. He was somewhat less pleased to see me, however, than I was to meet him. "Leave or I kill," he said, four short words I failed to take sufficiently seriously, and a few seconds later he hit me in the face with a hatchet, and then again, and I was dead. That's life—and death—in Rust, an open-world survival game that falls somewhere between DayZ and Minecraft and has a way of bringing out both the best and the worst in its players.
A babe in the woods
Rust's only goal is to survive, and it's always challenging. You begin with nothing but a rock, a torch, and a couple of bandages, and if you try to spend more than two nights out in the open in that condition, you will die. It's an intimidating, sink-or-swim introduction to the game, but Rust isn't a forgiving experience. Most of the game world will do its best to kill you and while epic multiplayer battles are rare, ambush murders are not. Nor are you particularly durable, unlike conventional videogame characters, and if somebody puts a few bullets in you, you will die. Yet that fragility, coupled with the near-absolute freedom offered by an open-world, no-rules arena, is exactly what makes it work. "Go forth and do whatever the hell you want" is exhilarating.There's a primal thrill to running through the jungle like some latter-day Tarzan, but if you're serious about staying alive then sooner or later you'll want to build some form of shelter. Construction options are quite limited so you won't be erecting any great architectural masterpieces, but having a relatively safe place to crash and store your stuff can extend your lifespan dramatically. Crafting is an even more important component of the game and while it's likewise neither particularly interesting nor flexible at this early stage of development, better equipment is the key to survival. The transition from prey to predator can be tedious, but once you're packing heat (and pants), the real fun begins.
The conventional fauna is bad enough, but there are also deadly zombies and radioactive hotspots that give the game a faint whiff of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Worst of all are your fellow players, who ensure that no matter how powerful you are, you're never entirely free of danger. At one point, well-armed and equipped after several hours, I was hunting zombies near some radioactive fuel tanks. Quick double-taps from my MP5 dispatched them and I was starting to feel like a real badass, which is probably why I wasn't paying as much attention to my surroundings as I should have been—while my attention was occupied by the inventory of my latest undead victim, a pair of bandits snuck up from behind and creamed me with a shotgun.That's not to say that everyone you meet is a paranoid, kill-or-be-killed social Darwinist, and in fact there's a considerable degree of cooperation to be found in some locales. But it comes cautiously, while vicious, violent death lurks everywhere. There are non-PvP servers for those who prefer less capriciously lethal entertainment, but while that cuts down on griefers, it also does away with one of the most undeniably exciting parts of the game: Random encounters with other human beings in which anything can happen. As frustrating as it is to be blown away without warning, that pervasive uncertainty is a central part of the survival experience, and Rust is vastly diminished without it.
It's not too soon
The Rust alpha test is available via Steam Early Access, and as you'd expect it's very much a work in progress. The graphics are no great shakes and you can expect wonky shadows, occasional clipping errors, and other glitches, and the sound effects don't even pretend to venture beyond minimal. Lag is sometimes a challenge, especially when you find yourself caught up in a spot of unpleasantness with your fellow island inhabitants, and simply finding someplace to play can be a hassle: Official servers tend to be crowded, while unofficial ones can be unreliable. Server wipes happen with major updates, so it's best not to get too attached to your stuff, and there are plenty of gameplay oddities: for instance, every animal you kill, from boars to bears, provides "chicken breasts" for food. (I haven't found any chickens in the game.)Rust's alpha is rough, but it's surprisingly playable. The underlying systems are essentially complete and functional (or at least appear to be, from an outside-looking-in perspective) and recent updates have dramatically improved the performance of the server browser. Rust has a ton of potential, and it's an intense and impressive experience even now.

There are no spoilers in this review:
Undertale - a game that seemingly came out of nowhere that has reviewers lauding it as the best game they've played all year. So then, time to answer: what makes the game great and is it worth playing?
The short answer is yes, it's worth playing. However, if you're like me, you were probably dissuaded by how the game looks, as it appears to be something from twenty years ago, somewhat similar to Earthbound. It's also worth mentioning that it is not the kind of game that will find universal appeal;, it's a half turn-based RPG, half bullet hell type game, and disliking either of those genres may interfere with enjoyability. If those are game types you enjoy, or at the very least tolerate, read on:
Undertale's greatest strength is in how it is written: the story is completely original and toys with ideas never before seen in any RPG while also playing mindgames with the player. If a comparison had to be made, it's as original as Bioshock was for the time. However, unlike our deep-sea shooter, Undertale shows it can be lighthearted as well, and the pacing between charming comedy and uneasy tension is perfect, making it a roller coaster of emotions from start to finish.
As a bonus, this game's got a bloody amazing soundtrack, one which always seems to play the right notes in the right situation. If I had to compare its soundtrack, I'd say it reminds me quite a bit of Freedom Planet in its quality, utilizing old chip tunes and synthesizers in tandem with normal instruments to make some incredible listening music, even outside of the game.
I can say very little ill of this game. There are tons of choices on how to play the game, and these decisions carry on in unexpected ways. There are hundreds of little secrets that allow one to end fights early, affect enemies, or even change things beyond the confines of your save file.
I would gladly rant on Undertale forever, but this game is one that is best played completely unspoiled - even learning the names of characters can be a spoiler in some ways. The best way to enjoy this game is completely blind, figuring out the game as it unfolds.
Though it is prudent to be wary of an overly hyped game, I'm happy to say that Undertale met my expectations, and I do not regret buying it at full price, even knowing that it might be discounted one day.

Hey guys, as a heavy player of the original mod for ARMA 2/ARMA 2 OA i figured id finally get around to writing a review for the Standalone version of DayZ. In case your thinking about buying the game as you are reading these reviews id suggest going and doing a test to see if you can run the game as it can be very difficult to run on older/worse machines, also dont think about if you can run it think about if you can run it and be able to enjoy it.
This game is great to have and i launch it alot when i get bored of my usual games and sometimes when a nice update comes out. The game varies a lot from the original mod of ARMA 2 and most of it is in a good way. They recently added vehicles to the game which is what alot of people were waiting for before they purchased/played the game but the game can be extremely fun without the vehicles aswell.
The game is extremely fun with friends and big groups to help get your back and you also tend to run into other groups which can either be a friendly encounter and you guys all hang out in a parking lot trading your items amongst the groups, or you can be swarming a whole town in a fire-fight between your groups, the choice is yours. Do not hop into this game expecting everyone to hand you stuff and be friendly, a lot of players will shoot you if they see you. Some just enjoy the killing aspect from the game and have fun doing that, but alot of people like myself would rather be safe than sorry if im not the only one in a town. Dont get mad if youre killed, loot is everywhere, part of the fun is finding all the cool stuff and all the stuff you need.
During the early months of the game most spawns were centered around Balota and made a hell of a lot of PvP in the spawn cities amongst the coast. Now however, the coastal cities are a lot dryer of PvP and on the off chance you see someone, theyll be a freshspawn aswell. Most armed people head inland and start going towards the airbases and bigger towns, its still a good idea to stay away from Elektro though ;)
The games inventory/gear system i find amazing, alot of the fun is finding good stuff to make your charecter look good. Ive played a hell of a lot of zombie survival games and most dont allow such diverse custumization, you can have a mask a hat a shirt a jacket pants and shoes and even more all on one guy.
The game does fall short in a couple categories that are important to the game however, the gunplay and PvP can be.... sloppy to say the least, getting a kill tends to be a matter of luck between players. Also the zombies are still a bit odd even after all the stuff theyve fixxxed about them. Dont get me wrong the zombies have gotten a lot better but still end my life due to some♥♥♥♥♥♥more times than not. Also the game graphically wise enless your running at ultra which good luck on that, you can expect a lot of rendering issues such as white trees, black lines all over the place, blocky textures. Like i said above this game is intensive to run with good graphics.
If you are looking for a great game to have a lot of fun on however do not skip out on this if youve got the money. Its a great game overall and has given almost 100 hours of fun so far.

There are no spoilers in this review:
Undertale - a game that seemingly came out of nowhere that has reviewers lauding it as the best game they've played all year. So then, time to answer: what makes the game great and is it worth playing?
The short answer is yes, it's worth playing. However, if you're like me, you were probably dissuaded by how the game looks, as it appears to be something from twenty years ago, somewhat similar to Earthbound. It's also worth mentioning that it is not the kind of game that will find universal appeal;, it's a half turn-based RPG, half bullet hell type game, and disliking either of those genres may interfere with enjoyability. If those are game types you enjoy, or at the very least tolerate, read on:
Undertale's greatest strength is in how it is written: the story is completely original and toys with ideas never before seen in any RPG while also playing mindgames with the player. If a comparison had to be made, it's as original as Bioshock was for the time. However, unlike our deep-sea shooter, Undertale shows it can be lighthearted as well, and the pacing between charming comedy and uneasy tension is perfect, making it a roller coaster of emotions from start to finish.
As a bonus, this game's got a bloody amazing soundtrack, one which always seems to play the right notes in the right situation. If I had to compare its soundtrack, I'd say it reminds me quite a bit of Freedom Planet in its quality, utilizing old chip tunes and synthesizers in tandem with normal instruments to make some incredible listening music, even outside of the game.
I can say very little ill of this game. There are tons of choices on how to play the game, and these decisions carry on in unexpected ways. There are hundreds of little secrets that allow one to end fights early, affect enemies, or even change things beyond the confines of your save file.
I would gladly rant on Undertale forever, but this game is one that is best played completely unspoiled - even learning the names of characters can be a spoiler in some ways. The best way to enjoy this game is completely blind, figuring out the game as it unfolds.
Though it is prudent to be wary of an overly hyped game, I'm happy to say that Undertale met my expectations, and I do not regret buying it at full price, even knowing that it might be discounted one day.

If you want to start playing in Rust, I would heavily recommend that you either bring a large group of people to play with you regularly (I'm thinking 4 to 5 people at least), or be prepared to spend an obscene amount of time playing if you're on your own. The reason for this is that in Rust, the overwhelming majority of players have a firm deathmatch mindset. It doesn't matter who you are, what you have or what you're doing : if a player sees you, he will either try to kill you or run away out of fear of you doing that to him.
This problem is compounded by poor communication. Text chat is server wide, and thus hardly usable to talk to the person next to you. There is no local text chat functionality, so if you want to engage neighbouring players in conversation, you'll need to have a microphone. But of course that has got its own problem too : VOIP is extremely laggy. Out of all the short conversations I had over VOIP (and none that didn't end with either party dead), only one was understandable. All others were a garbled, incomprehensible mess.
Furthermore, the community is extremely toxic. On top of the deathmatch problem, there is a general issue of rudeness and hostility : the server chat either had people begging for blueprints (plans you can find that allow you to craft an item), or hostile flaming and taunting between various groups. And of course, there's the high level roving bands of gun toting maniacs, running around the map shooting anyone for thrills, even if they have literally nothing of value.
And of course, you can't forget to mention the people who will use up lots of their time and ressources to break into your shelter, steal your keys, change your lock, leave your door open and ransack everything, meaning that the time spent building and upgrading your shelter is all for naught, because now you've got a door that's stuck open, that you can't even break down because they took all your tools and ressources. Oh and of course, they left an insulting sign indoors, and renamed your sleeping bag &quot♥♥♥♥♥quot;.
If you read TV Tropes, you will find that the community is a perfect exemplar of the Stupid Evil trope.
As a closing statement, don't even think of playing this game on your own. It would take a very special kind of masochist to do so, because unless you integrate a large group, you will never get anywhere, trust me.
If you are a part of one such group though, I guess Rust can be fun, assuming you're into griefing.

Undertale. A game made by the developer of Earthbound Halloween Hack and one of the music writers of the webcomic series of Homestuck. is one of the best RPGs i have ever played. The basic premise is you have control over who lives and dies! You can play through the entire game without killing a single creature or go onto a mass genocide and wipe out anyone that opposes you. The story is too good to ruin with a review and as such i refuse to do so.
This game has multiple endings depending on who is killed, who is saved, and who you befriend however there is three major endings to the game. The Pacifist ending (where you kill nothing and befriend all possible people.) The neutral (where you do anything you wish. saving who you want and killing who you want.) and the Genocide ending which well.. is kinda obvious.
I have only gone through the game twice. (once for my first blind run through pacifist. and the other because someone i care about finds the system a bit too overwhelming as its a bit too bullet helly for them.) and i already have 28 hours on my record. For an $11 CAD game. you really can't go wrong with this.
I recommend that if you do play this game. Expect passionate feelings from this game. I feel that this game definately has the developers "heart" and "soul" melded into it and his passion quickly filled me with the passion to enjoy and love this game.
I am however intensely surprised that gamemaker of all programs was used to make this game! I seriously never knew it had the power to do it. But this game shows just how well it can really make games!
I say if you have a few dollars laying around and are looking for an engaging and funny while still heart string plucking RPG then grab this game immediately. You will not be disappointed!

There is a huge learning curve that accompanies this game, for the first hour or so you may be completely confused on how to play, but that is the same with most games. If you do figure out how to get started quickly, it can take you maybe 30 minutes to get well established with a house etc.
This game is very dependent on a number of factors, including server, friends, and overall attitude.
Some servers that you get on in the game have more hackers than others as indicated below. It is sometimes a challenge to find a server with good staffing and admins, but once you do, this problem is almost non-existent. If you continue to have issues with it, do some research to find a good server, and try to befriend an admin or two so you know when they are on.
This game is also very heavily group-based. If you find yourself a good set of friends to play with, it deters a lot of people from attacking you, as well as making starting off easier. Try to find some people to play with and your game play will increase tenfold.
I also put attitude here, because you have to be okay with dying. If you have a problem with that it's not the game for you. People try to kill you. That's it. The game is kill or be killed, or hide long enough to get settled. If you cannot get started easily, try to find a friend or two to play with and it makes dying not as unbearable. Also, the friendlier you are to others, the friendlier they will be back to you (usually), with this in mind you can make allies and trade with others, but it all depends on what your mindset in-game is.

Being busy with school and a new relationship has put video games on the backburner of my life, unfortunately. Even when I would play a game I would lose interest within a few hours. Undertale has changed that. Right away, there are two reasons you might not want to play this game...
This game is a (excuse the cliche) gem. With an innovative combat system that allows for 2 different ways to solve conflicts (act/talking and standard attacking that requires reaction time to increase hit damage). Each monster you encounter is unique and gives a new way that they will attack/interface with your character. This can lead to some humorous or intense combat situations. There is no need to grind monsters just to complete a section, which is a nice change of pace from traditional RPG's experiences. The battle system requires skill to accomplish and every hit you take is because of your own fault and less of a RNG situation.
Characters are lovable. Even the enemies are memorable in some aspect (TsunderePlane, Jerry, Washua). Even after finishing the game I found myself wanting to explore the Underground more to see what I have missed. But you do not need to backrack if not desired.
The game provides you with 3 endings: A neutral route that must be completed first (if you kill no monsters you can just reload your save afterwards), a true pacifist ending obtained by killing no enemies throughout the game and completing additional criteria (as mentioned above you can just reload your previous save from the neutral route if you chose not to kill anyone your first time through), and lastly a genocide route where all enemies must be killed (a set amount in each area). Each ending has a different experience, with the latter leading to one of the most complicated difficult fights I've experienced.
I could go on but there are so many other reviews that you can read and get much more of the same. Play this game

To add an additional comment as of now (26/07/2015), DayZ is still the worst, still in Early Access and still limited. H1Z1 on the other hand is great. Their devs are super-supportive, they don't sensor negative comments on the forums like these nut-jobs and it is stable fun for all.

If you want to start playing in Rust, I would heavily recommend that you either bring a large group of people to play with you regularly (I'm thinking 4 to 5 people at least), or be prepared to spend an obscene amount of time playing if you're on your own. The reason for this is that in Rust, the overwhelming majority of players have a firm deathmatch mindset. It doesn't matter who you are, what you have or what you're doing : if a player sees you, he will either try to kill you or run away out of fear of you doing that to him.
This problem is compounded by poor communication. Text chat is server wide, and thus hardly usable to talk to the person next to you. There is no local text chat functionality, so if you want to engage neighbouring players in conversation, you'll need to have a microphone. But of course that has got its own problem too : VOIP is extremely laggy. Out of all the short conversations I had over VOIP (and none that didn't end with either party dead), only one was understandable. All others were a garbled, incomprehensible mess.
Furthermore, the community is extremely toxic. On top of the deathmatch problem, there is a general issue of rudeness and hostility : the server chat either had people begging for blueprints (plans you can find that allow you to craft an item), or hostile flaming and taunting between various groups. And of course, there's the high level roving bands of gun toting maniacs, running around the map shooting anyone for thrills, even if they have literally nothing of value.
And of course, you can't forget to mention the people who will use up lots of their time and ressources to break into your shelter, steal your keys, change your lock, leave your door open and ransack everything, meaning that the time spent building and upgrading your shelter is all for naught, because now you've got a door that's stuck open, that you can't even break down because they took all your tools and ressources. Oh and of course, they left an insulting sign indoors, and renamed your sleeping bag &quot♥♥♥♥♥quot;.
If you read TV Tropes, you will find that the community is a perfect exemplar of the Stupid Evil trope.
As a closing statement, don't even think of playing this game on your own. It would take a very special kind of masochist to do so, because unless you integrate a large group, you will never get anywhere, trust me.
If you are a part of one such group though, I guess Rust can be fun, assuming you're into griefing.

Being busy with school and a new relationship has put video games on the backburner of my life, unfortunately. Even when I would play a game I would lose interest within a few hours. Undertale has changed that. Right away, there are two reasons you might not want to play this game...
This game is a (excuse the cliche) gem. With an innovative combat system that allows for 2 different ways to solve conflicts (act/talking and standard attacking that requires reaction time to increase hit damage). Each monster you encounter is unique and gives a new way that they will attack/interface with your character. This can lead to some humorous or intense combat situations. There is no need to grind monsters just to complete a section, which is a nice change of pace from traditional RPG's experiences. The battle system requires skill to accomplish and every hit you take is because of your own fault and less of a RNG situation.
Characters are lovable. Even the enemies are memorable in some aspect (TsunderePlane, Jerry, Washua). Even after finishing the game I found myself wanting to explore the Underground more to see what I have missed. But you do not need to backrack if not desired.
The game provides you with 3 endings: A neutral route that must be completed first (if you kill no monsters you can just reload your save afterwards), a true pacifist ending obtained by killing no enemies throughout the game and completing additional criteria (as mentioned above you can just reload your previous save from the neutral route if you chose not to kill anyone your first time through), and lastly a genocide route where all enemies must be killed (a set amount in each area). Each ending has a different experience, with the latter leading to one of the most complicated difficult fights I've experienced.
I could go on but there are so many other reviews that you can read and get much more of the same. Play this game

In many ways, creating reviews on YouTube, or anywhere else, is rather easy. Reviewers inform the public their opinions on games, movies, TV shows, comics, while adding jokes and entertaining banter. Bad material is fun to review, as the jokes tend to write themselves, and all that's needed is a clever delivery. There's a certain joy a creator recieves when he laughs at a joke he created.
Deep down, every reviewer on YouTube is a reviewer because of one truth: They love the material. At one point, that reviewer's life was touched by the medium they now critize. And every so often, something comes along that reminds them why they care. Why they choose to call themself a nerd, or a fan, or a gamer.
I'm Sean Emery. I'm a gamer. And this is Undertale.
You are a child who fell down a hole, up in the mountains one day. You quickly find out that you've slipped into the realm of monsters, who have been imprisioned in that mountain for over a millenium, thanks to a barrier you passed through while falling down the hole. And that's all of the plot you're getting out of me, cause I'm not spoiling anything!
Undertale is a RPG that feels heavily inspired by Earthbound, in both it's graphical presentation, and it's engaging main and side characters. The thing that originally drew me to Undertale was hearing that you could clear the entire game without killing anything. That not only sounded intriguing, but also impossible. How could you progress through an RPG without gaining experience and leveling up?
This game does a fantasic job keeping the player on their toes. Any knowledge of traditional RPG tropes will be thrown out the window the minute you begin Undertale, often in a hillarious way. And that's something worth noting: The humor in Undertale is the most genuine I've seen in years. It's never crass, or in questionable taste, but rather in pure situational banter between the main characters. Even the characters in towns that you only see once managed to make me laugh a few times. It feels like all the monsters use humor to cope with their current situation, and although you laugh at the jokes (because they are the best in years), you never shake the feeling that the monsters are miserable down here.
The combat system in Undertale is rather unique. When you enter a battle, you have the choice to fight, act, item, or mercy. Acting allows you to talk or act with the monster, in an attempt to get them to stop fighting. Once you fulfil the act necessary for each monster, their name will be highlighted in yellow, indicating that granting the monster mercy will work now. Otherwise, you can attack using a timing-based counter. When enemies attack, you'll be allowed to move your "soul" around the enclosed box, avoiding the enemies attack, similar to a bullet-hell SHMUF. Each enemy's attack is different, which keeps combat fresh in every situation.
I mentioned before that this game has the appearance of a Super NES/DOS RPG, and the game does a great job in twisting what the player expects out of Undertale. Without giving anything away, you don't expect to see different styles of graphics in a game that looks like this, so when something happens that changes the graphical layout, it's effect on the player is amazing.
I dare not give anything away about the villain, but just imagine this: Psycho Mantis from Metal Gear Solid and Giygas from Earthbound in a single character. This is a fantastic villain: Everything from his intentions, his backstory, and his power is astounding. And his power stems from one of Undertale's greatest feats: It remembers everything.
Every choice you make in the game has a significant impact on the world around you. From what I've seen, there are three main ways to play Undertale: The pacifist route, where you don't kill anything. The neutral route where you kill some monsters and characters, and the genocide route where you kill everything. Your choices decide how certain characters interact with you, how a town welcomes you or not, and what kind of ending you recieve. The amazing thing about Undertale though is every choice you make, for the most part, is irreversable. If you make a decision that you regret, reload your save file, and change, it does not matter. The game remembers that first choice you made. This adds an enormus amount of weight to your decisions, especially towards the end.
On top of that, there are certain characters who seem to be aware of who you, the player, are to the world of Undertale. Some are aware that you, the player, are the most unstoppable force that world has ever seen: a being that can reset, load, and save a world in the blink of an eye, with all the other characters having no idea what you did... But some characters know.
I dare not spoil this part, for it was one of the most powerful moments in recent memory, but I will say this: I played Undertale on the pacifist route because that was the reason I became intereted in the game: winning by not killing anything. It wasn't even the ending yet, and I was driven to tears after seeing the result of my actions. It was magnificent. Knowing the weight of my decisions, aware the characters in the game could see what I did, and coming out of the other end with no sins on my back... A game has never made me feel like this before.
I can't tell you how to play this game, but after completing the pacifist run, I can tell you this will complete honesty: I will never do the genocide run. The game has created such a rich world with lovable characters that if I were to go through and kill them one by one, it would genuinely disturb me.
And the one element that ties this game, and all of it's events, humor, and drama together, is the music. The soundtrack in Undertale has to be one of the most appropriate to a game I've ever seen. Every song fits the mood of every scene perfectly. Toby Fox, the game's creator, was also the composer of all the music in Undertale, and you can feel the strength of the music. Every song feels like it was created with each scene in mind. I won't say it's the most impressive soundtrack of all time, but each song was created with a purpose: to set the mood. And it does that magnificently.
.	.	.
So here we are: the arbitrary score at the end of the review.
For me, this game reminds me not only of the incredible wave of emotions video games can provoke in a player, but why I call myself a gamer to begin with: because of experiences like this. It's only been a week since I finished this game, but I can say this with full honesty: Not only does Undertale get the biggest and loudest 10 out of 10 I can give it, but it is now my favorite game I've played in my entire life.
I'm 26 years old. I've played every Nintendo console when it was new, along with some of their competitors. I won't say that Undertale is the greatest game ever created. Lord knows if I did, people would be debating me for years on end. When I say that Undertale is the best game I've ever played, this is what I mean: Super Metroid made me feel like a badass. Ocarina Of Time made me feel like a hero. Halo made me feel like a soldier. Undertale... Undertale made me feel  human. Not a player, but a human.
No game has ever done to me what Undertale has done. And that is why it's now my favorite game of all time.

There will be desynch to horrible levels at times and  you will struggle to find the things you need when you need them (I'm looking at you matches/ammo for the weapon I've found/magazines etc).
There are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s everywhere, most players would rather put a bullet in your skull than talk to you, some may even tea bag your dead body whilst calling you rude things over the in game chat, but, for all this it is a game that continues to excite me.
I can't think of another game which gets my adrenaline going as much as this, the sound of footsteps near your building, the distant gunshots, manic laughter from a cannibal or the sound of zombie aggro (is it at me or someone else?).
It's getting better, it's actually getting better at a faster rate now than in the early months of alpha. The game is slightly more polished, it looks and runs better and has vehciles (which should hopefully quiten some areas of the fanbase).
Has the game got a long way to go? Yes, and if you are after a finished product (or something resembling one) then stay away for now. If however you want a few hours of nervousness and fun and can stomach the flaws of a developing game then I highly recommend this game.

In many ways, creating reviews on YouTube, or anywhere else, is rather easy. Reviewers inform the public their opinions on games, movies, TV shows, comics, while adding jokes and entertaining banter. Bad material is fun to review, as the jokes tend to write themselves, and all that's needed is a clever delivery. There's a certain joy a creator recieves when he laughs at a joke he created.
Deep down, every reviewer on YouTube is a reviewer because of one truth: They love the material. At one point, that reviewer's life was touched by the medium they now critize. And every so often, something comes along that reminds them why they care. Why they choose to call themself a nerd, or a fan, or a gamer.
I'm Sean Emery. I'm a gamer. And this is Undertale.
You are a child who fell down a hole, up in the mountains one day. You quickly find out that you've slipped into the realm of monsters, who have been imprisioned in that mountain for over a millenium, thanks to a barrier you passed through while falling down the hole. And that's all of the plot you're getting out of me, cause I'm not spoiling anything!
Undertale is a RPG that feels heavily inspired by Earthbound, in both it's graphical presentation, and it's engaging main and side characters. The thing that originally drew me to Undertale was hearing that you could clear the entire game without killing anything. That not only sounded intriguing, but also impossible. How could you progress through an RPG without gaining experience and leveling up?
This game does a fantasic job keeping the player on their toes. Any knowledge of traditional RPG tropes will be thrown out the window the minute you begin Undertale, often in a hillarious way. And that's something worth noting: The humor in Undertale is the most genuine I've seen in years. It's never crass, or in questionable taste, but rather in pure situational banter between the main characters. Even the characters in towns that you only see once managed to make me laugh a few times. It feels like all the monsters use humor to cope with their current situation, and although you laugh at the jokes (because they are the best in years), you never shake the feeling that the monsters are miserable down here.
The combat system in Undertale is rather unique. When you enter a battle, you have the choice to fight, act, item, or mercy. Acting allows you to talk or act with the monster, in an attempt to get them to stop fighting. Once you fulfil the act necessary for each monster, their name will be highlighted in yellow, indicating that granting the monster mercy will work now. Otherwise, you can attack using a timing-based counter. When enemies attack, you'll be allowed to move your "soul" around the enclosed box, avoiding the enemies attack, similar to a bullet-hell SHMUF. Each enemy's attack is different, which keeps combat fresh in every situation.
I mentioned before that this game has the appearance of a Super NES/DOS RPG, and the game does a great job in twisting what the player expects out of Undertale. Without giving anything away, you don't expect to see different styles of graphics in a game that looks like this, so when something happens that changes the graphical layout, it's effect on the player is amazing.
I dare not give anything away about the villain, but just imagine this: Psycho Mantis from Metal Gear Solid and Giygas from Earthbound in a single character. This is a fantastic villain: Everything from his intentions, his backstory, and his power is astounding. And his power stems from one of Undertale's greatest feats: It remembers everything.
Every choice you make in the game has a significant impact on the world around you. From what I've seen, there are three main ways to play Undertale: The pacifist route, where you don't kill anything. The neutral route where you kill some monsters and characters, and the genocide route where you kill everything. Your choices decide how certain characters interact with you, how a town welcomes you or not, and what kind of ending you recieve. The amazing thing about Undertale though is every choice you make, for the most part, is irreversable. If you make a decision that you regret, reload your save file, and change, it does not matter. The game remembers that first choice you made. This adds an enormus amount of weight to your decisions, especially towards the end.
On top of that, there are certain characters who seem to be aware of who you, the player, are to the world of Undertale. Some are aware that you, the player, are the most unstoppable force that world has ever seen: a being that can reset, load, and save a world in the blink of an eye, with all the other characters having no idea what you did... But some characters know.
I dare not spoil this part, for it was one of the most powerful moments in recent memory, but I will say this: I played Undertale on the pacifist route because that was the reason I became intereted in the game: winning by not killing anything. It wasn't even the ending yet, and I was driven to tears after seeing the result of my actions. It was magnificent. Knowing the weight of my decisions, aware the characters in the game could see what I did, and coming out of the other end with no sins on my back... A game has never made me feel like this before.
I can't tell you how to play this game, but after completing the pacifist run, I can tell you this will complete honesty: I will never do the genocide run. The game has created such a rich world with lovable characters that if I were to go through and kill them one by one, it would genuinely disturb me.
And the one element that ties this game, and all of it's events, humor, and drama together, is the music. The soundtrack in Undertale has to be one of the most appropriate to a game I've ever seen. Every song fits the mood of every scene perfectly. Toby Fox, the game's creator, was also the composer of all the music in Undertale, and you can feel the strength of the music. Every song feels like it was created with each scene in mind. I won't say it's the most impressive soundtrack of all time, but each song was created with a purpose: to set the mood. And it does that magnificently.
.	.	.
So here we are: the arbitrary score at the end of the review.
For me, this game reminds me not only of the incredible wave of emotions video games can provoke in a player, but why I call myself a gamer to begin with: because of experiences like this. It's only been a week since I finished this game, but I can say this with full honesty: Not only does Undertale get the biggest and loudest 10 out of 10 I can give it, but it is now my favorite game I've played in my entire life.
I'm 26 years old. I've played every Nintendo console when it was new, along with some of their competitors. I won't say that Undertale is the greatest game ever created. Lord knows if I did, people would be debating me for years on end. When I say that Undertale is the best game I've ever played, this is what I mean: Super Metroid made me feel like a badass. Ocarina Of Time made me feel like a hero. Halo made me feel like a soldier. Undertale... Undertale made me feel  human. Not a player, but a human.
No game has ever done to me what Undertale has done. And that is why it's now my favorite game of all time.

With only about 7 hours of playtime and my first playthrough completed, I have to say that this game is probably one of the best ones I've played in years. I like Retro-Styled RPGs like these because they've got a lot of charm to them, and Undertale would be a prime example of this.
This game is both a happy and sad one. Despite being simple gameplay-wise, it tells a story in a very complex way. Given that you played through to the Peaceful Ending, Undertale is quite the experience. All throughout these 7 hours I've played it, I've laughed (sometimes hysterically), I've cried, but most of all, I've had fun.
Undertale has a blend of basically everything. The environment and characters can be beautiful, cute, cool, and sometimes even scary. Music is also great, and tugs at your feelings during both peaceful and epic moments.
As you play this game, you start to bond with everyone you meet (given you took the Peaceful Route), and it makes it hard to leave them after completing the story.
Undertale may not be the best game mechanics-wise, but it is for sure one of the biggest RPG experiences you can get today. With that in mind, I can gladly give this game a 10/10.
Plus, it's only 10 dollars, which is so cheap compared to most games out there today.

What can I say about this game other then the fact that, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ its actually a really good game!
Fact of the matter is, it's a genuine, unique expirience to play through, especially if your the kind of guy that's into RPG Games with a focus on Story. Undertale is, in fact, a JRPG-Style game drawing influences from the Mother/Earthbound Games of the SNES Era, but adding a unique twist to it. Instead of 'kill monster to gain EXP' or 'Destroy boss to progress to next level', you can actually Befriend the Bosses and the Monsters. Yes, you're reading that right, you can litterally befriend every enemy; in lamen's terms: your befriending the living hell out of them. This unique system also adds for some unique story elements, as killing one of the bosses in the game changes the way the game feels, the atmosphere it has and the story as a whole. As you probably figured it out by now, killing a boss means it changes the story for good, as once they're dead, they stay dead throughout that time and they don't come back, leading to some unique situations that don't normally occure in other RPG Games. It's also has a 'bullet hell' system for when the monsters attack, which is actually fairly easy to learn and is not too punishing for those just getting into the game. Oh, and just to be clear:
Don't let the Fandom draw you away from this game if the fandom doesn't appeal to you, it's still a great expirience to behold
TL:DR Feel Trips, Loving the Hell out of your Enemies, Killing is Bad, and Eat lots a spaghetti.
Seriously though, get this game, you will NOT regret it.

Undertale is a game that understands what a morality system truly is. It reacts to your actions and makes you feel good or bad depending on your decisions. In my opinion, one of the best games ever.
The combat system is not based around fighting, but on talking your way out of a fight.  I think this charming detail adds a game-play mechanic unlike anything I've ever seen. You have to look at details about a character. Say the information was "lacks self confidence" you might choose to press the flirt button, to cheer them up. You can play through this game without killing a single person. Alternatively, you could ruthlessly slaughter every man woman and child you meet, but that's not my sort of thing. For now.
Although the combat system is turn-based, there is a component that requires skill. You have a heart which you control with the arrow keys, and have to dodge hundred of attacks flying across the screen each turn, which always kept me on my toes. As well as this, sometimes, the whole game-play mechanic changes with each boss/mini boss, creating some challenging new game-play.
Another thing that sets it out from the crowd is the writing. Toby Fox has made a game where when I entered a village, I went around speaking to literally everyone. And don't worry Jacksfilms fans, that wasn't a misuse of literally. The dialogue is so charming and funny that I always want more, and every character has it's own quirky charms and personality flaws.  There is an option to press X to skip dialogue, though. Due to this, there is now a small pile of untouched dust on my X key.
Great games, amazing characters and fight system. Extremely memorable and amazing soundtrack to top it all off.

This game was so engrossing, involving, and heartrending, the only time I put it down was when I absolutely needed to for irl reasons (schoolwork, sleeping, studying, etc.) I adored it. Please play this game. Though while I'd personally implore you to never, ever do the Genocide run, I also acknowledge, like the game legitimately drives home to you again and again no matter what route you play, that it's entirely up to you. You will have to live with your choices, and their repercussions, if you decide to kill everyone instead of keeping them alive, or even if you keep them alive and then decide to reset and kill everyone because you want to see what happens. Choose wisely, because killing someone will affect and change the world and the story itself. Plus, the soundtrack is amazing, and remains one of my all-time favorites even nearly 5 months since I finished the game for the first time. And only time, because, again, I personally refuse to erase everyone's memories with the True Reset just to then decide to kill them all, especially not after I worked so hard to give everyone the happy ending I feel they honestly deserve.
But that's my own bias showing here. However you choose to play this game, what Undertale brings to the table with its narrative, characters, and mechanics -- especially with the player-choice-matters-and-there-are-consequences one -- is absolutely not only important, but like others on here have said, a work of art in of itself. I can genuinely say, as well, that I've never been as affected by a game in any of the ways this one did. Not even with, say, Mass Effect, or Dragon Age. Undertale, at times, makes you feel like the world it encompasses and involves isn't just one inside a game, not entirely. No. It definitely has a life of its own.

10/10 PERFECT SCORE
Undertale. What a game... no, an experience..... this is. Undertale is the work of genius by Toby Fox with the support of Kickstarter and adoring fans. Previously, Fox was known for his Earthbound Halloween Hack and his work with the Homestuck comics. It is quite clear that Undertale takes much inspiration from the Earthbound (Mother in Japan) series, but not directly ripping it off. To my understanding, this game was also made in RPG Maker, which really goes to show just what that tool is capable of. The visual style is somewhere between NES and SNES graphically. I'd call it 12-bit. Every character from the main folks, to the smallest enemies (hOI!!!!) are loveable. The best way to describe the humor is by calling it "dad jokes," the kind that can be corny, but you're still laughing at them. Undertale will DEFINITELY elicit multiple playthroughs from players, as there are NUMEROUS endings dependent on your choices, and the True Ending is pretty tricky to get. The combat is actually optional! That's right, this is one RPG where nobody has to die! And it's how you can avoid these fights that really puts a spin on what we know from RPGs. It's goofy, it's fun, it's got its scary moments, and it WILL make you cry. There's also plenty of challenge for those who seek it, and you may regret seeking it out. This game really captures the charm Earthbound and Mother 3 carried. The kind that makes you happy to be playing, and really draws you in. The soundtrack is probably the best part of this AMAZING title. Every track carefully fits the scene (and even Toby's signature piece, Megalovania, which has appeared in every one of his major works thus far, is in here), and really brings forth the emotions you want to be feeling at that exact moment in time. Never before have I felt so engaged in a scene by the music alone! I downloaded the soundtrack as DLC and now listen to it in my car daily, and remembering where the music plays, letting the memories of my journey flow to me, it brings a smile to my face. Kids, adults, moms, dads, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, grandmothers, grandfathers, friends, family, everyone you know would love this game, and it's the first game to really win my heart over like this. I've never been so captivated by a game before, not like this. I am very very glad I was gifted this game. With that said, this gets the first ever score of 10/10 from me. It is the only game I have ever rated with a perfect score, as I typically do not believe in perfection in game design. But Undertale is, without a shadow of a doubt, my new favorite game of all-time. It is a masterpiece that Toby Fox will go down in history for, and that deserves Game of the Year  in my opinion (Sorry Metal Gear Solid V The Phantom Pain and Fallout 4, you just aren't as fun as this), and I sincerely doubt this will be leaving my heart anytime soon. If you haven't played this masterpiece yet, you are missing out on the first game of this year to get EVERYTHING about it right! Majora's Mask 3D was close, but this is right on the nose with how games SHOULD be, and it didn't need VR, motion controls, 3D, or stunning 3D graphics to pull it off. This is an absolute must-have for anyone who calls themselves a gamer, and trust me, you will not regret spending the extra $8 to get the soundtrack bundle!

What can I say about this game other then the fact that, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ its actually a really good game!
Fact of the matter is, it's a genuine, unique expirience to play through, especially if your the kind of guy that's into RPG Games with a focus on Story. Undertale is, in fact, a JRPG-Style game drawing influences from the Mother/Earthbound Games of the SNES Era, but adding a unique twist to it. Instead of 'kill monster to gain EXP' or 'Destroy boss to progress to next level', you can actually Befriend the Bosses and the Monsters. Yes, you're reading that right, you can litterally befriend every enemy; in lamen's terms: your befriending the living hell out of them. This unique system also adds for some unique story elements, as killing one of the bosses in the game changes the way the game feels, the atmosphere it has and the story as a whole. As you probably figured it out by now, killing a boss means it changes the story for good, as once they're dead, they stay dead throughout that time and they don't come back, leading to some unique situations that don't normally occure in other RPG Games. It's also has a 'bullet hell' system for when the monsters attack, which is actually fairly easy to learn and is not too punishing for those just getting into the game. Oh, and just to be clear:
Don't let the Fandom draw you away from this game if the fandom doesn't appeal to you, it's still a great expirience to behold
TL:DR Feel Trips, Loving the Hell out of your Enemies, Killing is Bad, and Eat lots a spaghetti.
Seriously though, get this game, you will NOT regret it.

Rust has a lot of potential for becoming an even more amazing game than it already is but in order to get there it's going to take time. Yes, the game has bugs. Zombies are still going through the walls, they have the worst path finding system in the world and you can break your legs by missing just one step on the stairs.
But let's get over that, and look at the other elements of the game. The game is amazing on your own, but it's even better with a friend. Yes, you spawn in the south of the map while your friend is in the north side of it, who cares? It's amazing just to talk about the loot you find on the way to his location.
Your friends refuse to buy it due to those negative reviews or don't have enough money? Doesn't matter, once you get the conecpt of the game and use a map to guide yourself in Chernarus you'll make friendsY or enemies in all the cities you across.
The game have so many amazing features, such as fishing and creating your own farm to produce food. The fight for military loot, searching for heli crash-sites and so on. But, remember one thing, DayZ is horrible and cruel. It's a hard game where in the first minutes of the game (if you are not familiar with those kind of games) you will find yourself dying of hunger, bleeding or by zombies. You will die looking through empty towns and you will give up on this game, saying "The guys saying this game sucks in the review section are so right", but it's you that suck. And you will suck until you find out that this time you are not dying of hunger anymore. You will find tips from other players and all sorts of hints and you will get to a point when you are not dying because of those things anymore. You finally have a gun and decent gear and feel like you can take any challange... you are wrong, because there are others that think just like you, and shoot you on sight... and you will start over with the game, you will start facing players more often because you know how to find your loot and where to search for players, you will be a bandit and hunt poor players, but there will be other players who hunt you as well and later on, you will be the one who will hunt people like you.
This is DayZ, a game where the weak give up and the strong finds a new opportunity after each death. Pick your servers wisely, don't go over on servers with 300 ping or with 60 players if you know  you are having troubles. Get familiar with the map and areas and start sucking less.
There will be bugs and broken legs, but it's a good game after all, and if you are up to those challanges then you will enjoy the game, besides of the bugs and optimization problems it has. The game is in Alpha for over a year now, and hidding behind the excuse of a "Early-Acces" it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ move, that's why I will never say that it's an Alpha and you should expect those things to happen, not after a year.
It's a good game and those bugs don't happen that often if you know where to play and how to play. If you are still not confident enough with the Standalone, try the mod , I just think other "DayZ ripoffs" are not that good, talking about multiplayer ones and they suck on stealing pants and over-feeding cuffed people.
Good luck.

This is the way I described it to a friend, via chat, who said the game looked like a bunch of bullet hell minigames and he lost interest 20 minuets into a gameplay video of Undertale. (Warning. I ramble. A lot.):
Well, a simple way is how I've seen Undertale described as an experience. I agree that it is an experience but not because it is a game where everything is so amazing it leaves a lasting effect, but because of how most of it is ♥♥♥♥ing mind-blowing for someone like me. Due to how big of a fan I am of J-Rpgs and J-Rpg-esque games, one of the main big companies for me is square enix, who are famous for their RPGs. They are supposed to have great characters, music and story. Other RPGs from other companies also stood out because of messages they gave, or characters and issues they tackled. Undertale is an indie game that was only made by a couple of people. They didn't do the best on gameplay when compared to games from the final fantasy series and such, but when you compare the music, characters and story. The result is something that blows my mind. A single playthrough can last several hours at best, yet they pack such amazing things into those few hours and, to me, rival the companies and games I am rambling on about in a fraction of the time final fantasy games or the persona and shin megami tensei series would use to convey the same things. The game even uses its length to its advantage with the branching path leading to genocide, neutral and pacifist endings
. Each song fits the mood, whether it is a mysterious tune for damp and dark caves,
or an epic tune for the ending fights, the music just fits it perfectly. The characters are varied and most, if not all, major characters and some simple npcs can be lovable. This game is just amazing from where I'm looking at it. The community also can create some funny videos for others that played the game. This review explanation theme was fueled by the true pacifist run final boss theme and most likely a hell of a lot of sugar. I apologise.
P.S. ♥♥♥♥ the Genocide Run. it can keep its dead people and Neutral can keep at least 1 dead person. Font-named skeletons make some of the best friends. (The characters are so good, I can't bring myself to kill anyone within the game. Basically, I am reluctant to have a bad time.)
P.S.S. Would play Pacifist or True Pacifist run again... and again... and again... and again.
