Welcome to "Raiders Are Us".
The game that has systematically evolved from a survival game to a game that focuses purely on raiding and clan warfare.
Let me be clear. If you are a player who like to solo or play with a few friends, then this game is not for you. This is a game where resources create victories. Where many grouped hands dominate the entire servers.
Over time the game has evolved from a survival game, to a game that caters to those that like to raid people there bases. Preferably those bases from solo, small or medium clans.
If you like to spend 20 hours to resource gather, stare at trees while you cut them down, refine resources and hope you are not killed in the time for your measly resources. Only to build a small base that gets destroyed every day when your asleep, and have all your resources stolen by the bigger bullies around. Still interested? Then yes, then this game is perfect for you. The raiders are looking for more fresh victims who do not know what they are getting into.
Unfortunately for most, the building aspect while "fun" is secondary to the whole destruction element of the game. The resource costs for building have systematically been going up, while the destruction tools increased in damage or more destruction tools got added to the game. Making it extreme difficult for players who have only a few hours of game play each day, to even get a good footing on a server. Unless you prefer to live as a nomad, from spawn to spawn, you will die every day. Even multiple times per day.
The game is a pure resource game and this is also its extreme weakness. Because of the focus on raiding, it allows for those who raid in group to constantly grow in resources. While those who are its victims in general become nothing but milk cows to be raided again and again for there resources.
Some will disagree with this review but it speaks to the fundamentals of the game. There is no survival aspect. Cold only kills people who are new to the game. Bears & Wolfs ( the only predators ) are a joke and spawn so few now, that you can go days without seeing them. Other people on the other hand, they will kill you without thinking twice because the game has become nothing but "survive the other humans". Take no risks. Shoot first, ask question later after you rob there bodies dry. You are a fresh spawn with only a rock? Bang .. your death. You are no threat to anybody yet but you insult the other survivors for just being "alive".
This is not a game for people with good hearts. There are some but they are few. Most people will gladly mislead other players to rob and kill them. Because that is the only way people think you can survive. Every resource is needed in hopes to stay alive and very few do so.
Be warned that building a base of any kind is a open invitation. It reads: "There be loot here".
Building bases to defend yourself becomes a futile struggle as the resource costs astronomically increases as you add defense layers. The same defense layers that the developers keep making weaker and weaker by adding new tools to destroy them, increase the damage on them or simply avoid them.
But do not trust the description of the game because its so inaccurate these days. This is a game where unless your in a 10+ player clan, you will wake up every day on the beach as somebody killed your character while it was sleeping. Your safe base not being safe at all.
This is game where you need to put in 20, 30, 40 hours of harvesting, crafting, building after every wipe ( every week or few weeks ) to have any form of defense that will scare away all but the big clans. And those big clans then look upon your mighty base as a goldmine. Because if you spend this amount of time building, you have a lot of resources for them to plunder.
Think of this game as "Battle Royal" with the illusion that you might be safe when you log off for the night.
In short, its a horrible one sided balanced game where the developers make no secret that they want people to kill each other and constantly improve the tools to do so. Many may think that they like this description but they forget that they are at the bottom of the feeding pyramid.
So buyers be warned. You are entering "Raiders Are Us". And you are not the raider.

First off, I don't mind admitting I SOLELY bought this game based on the hype it's been getting over the internet; more specifically, a couple choice Youtube channels I follow.  Born and raised in the N64 era, while I could appreciate retro games, I didn't feel the same pull as them as other gamers; I haven't played and finished many games from that era, so they hold no nostalgic value to  me. As such Undertale's graphics, musical style and battle system didn't quite draw me in; if anything, it's obvious affinity for a time before mine made me feel like it was directed to another audience and was probably not quite for me. Still it was only 12 bucks, I wasn't playing anything in particular, and the last indie project I sunk my teeth into- the Stanley Parable- was a brief, but quite enjoyable affair; that plus the aforementioned made me say 'oh, what the heck' and give it a shot.
It wasn't something that IMMEDIATELY grabbed me; the first half of my play time- only a few hours  or so- were enjoyable but spread out over a few days. The characters were endearingly quirky, the dialogue was well written, the musical score was excellent to my pleasant surprise, and the battle system was fun and unique; I had nothing bad to say about the game thus far and was enjoying myself, but I couldn't see what all the hubbub was about.
By the time my first playthough was over however, something had changed in my viewpoints; characters had gone from endearing to people (er...monsters... whatever) that I truly cared about, certain plot twists hit me out of nowhere and threw me for a loop, what I had been doing up until this had meaning that I wouldn't have expected, and the final boss (for the 'normal' or neutral' loop) was something that was quite terrifying and unexpected.
Before I knew it I was back for more; I couldn't just stop here. I needed to get to a better ending! To leave the world the way it was  would just be depressing, so I  wanted to play it and get the BEST route. Many hours later, I did; along the way however, the game had pulled me into its clutches even more, sprinkling in even more climatic and downright suspenseful moments along with a few poignant moments that  really touched my heart. By the time the end credits rolled around, I left this game feeling satisfied, enlightened, and wishing for more.
Sound a bit sappy to you? Well, there's a good reason for that; Undertale's plot, humor and allegorical  message also serves as a allegorical message that speaks directly to the player. It pokes fun at the tropes of RPGs, it impresses upon the player of the consequences of their actions in a way  few games seldom accomplish, and even speaks to- sometimes criticizing-  the reasons we play games to begin with. Whether it connects you on an emotional level as it did with me or not, if you call yourself a gamer, you'll get something out of the message the game is trying to get across.
Now, literally only one day after completing the game, I can say that this game is- without a doubt or exageration- one of my favorite games of all times . It has style and substance, a perfect blend between gameplay and story,  and is unique in a truly novel and wonderful way without ever feeling gimmicky. Ever so rarely does a game come along that almost everyone can agree is great. Games like Undertale would be one of those, but it really does make me question of video games as a pure form of entertainment, or a pure form of art.
On my journey through the Pacifist route of Undertale, I laughed, I cried, I dated a skeleton, I dated a lizard, I made lovable friends along the way, and I experienced one of the greatest games I've ever played.
Simple on paper, boundless in practice; Undertale raises the bar for me on storytelling as a genre and reads to me one of the most compelling stories I've ever heard.
This game isn't just a mindless game, it's a game that will make you question the bounds of imagination and what single minds can create with the right power. This is a game that will make you experience a journey told to its greatest potential, it's a game that I will surely gush over for a couple of months, and I will surely remember it for years to come.
In short, being one of the best games with a great concept, story, and execution, I proudly admit that reviews have never been my type of thing, I always just assume that I like or don't like a game and move on; but Undertale is a game that everyone deserves to experience. It's not just a game. It's a work of art. And much like real art, it's beauty is in the eye of the beholder, and explaining its beauty is like trying to explain what makes a song beautiful.
There's no combination of words in the dictionary that I could put together to describe why this game is great, but I gladly leave it in my heart. And if you want a nice adventure that will surely make you think of life and people in a new perspective, please, buy this game, and enjoy.

Last week a friend of mine bought me Undertale as a gift and I started playing it on Friday -- In my determination to see through to the happiest ending, this game's true majesty shined out and brought a light to my life in a time that's been somewhat dark for me.
Never in playing a game have I felt so invested... From the colorful cast of characters to the truly gripping concept of the game that judges you as a person for your actions and decisions. And it's funny because I went for the best ending first-- and now can't bring myself to reset the game because of how much it warmed my heart that these characters found such peace.
The cast themselves were what really drew me in though. If it means anything to say so.. This game reminded me a great deal of the kind of characters I've been fleshing out over the years, too.
It started back when I was three years old, when I made up an imaginary friend who to this day has been my longest enduring concept- and will always hold a big part of my heart and mind. His name is Buuku.
With how well Undertale has been received by players -- being as when I'm writing this the 4th highest acclaimed game of this year, it fills me with determination that maybe someday Buuku and all his quirky friends will be able to touch the hearts of the masses as Undertale has done.
So thank you Toby... From the bottom of my heart. Thank you and the crew behind Undertale for having graced the world with a truly memorable, heart-felt game that reminds us all of the true realities we face in our lives.

Ten dollars. Only a few hours of gameplay. 16-bit graphics compared to the flashy 1080p stuff in standard games.
But... wow. Undertale blew me away. It doesn't need flashy graphics or even fanservice to falsify its enjoyment. It just does things right, and boy that was one immensely enjoyable experience.
I think most of the magic of this game comes from knowing absolutely nothing about it. I got this game from a friend and just decided to play it since it looked very interesting and it was getting good responses. So I went in completely blind, knowing nothing but the game's name. And I'm glad I did, because everything the game presented to me was unexpected, notably dark in places, and very emotional, which would have been lost entirely if i watched someone else play it. So, if you happened to have been flooded by everything Undertale on tumblr
and the entire story's already laid out for you, the magic has been lost and the game won't be as incredible of an experience. I'm sorry.
Of course, I call Undertale an "experience", not a game, only because it does such a fantastic job at it. Following the motto on the store page, "the game where you don't have to destroy anyone", the game always tries to nudge you in that direction, taking a back seat in your mind and reminding you to "Spare them!". And of course, you answer with "Why? Why should I do that when it offers me the option to kill anyone I want right in front of me? What's in it for me?" And that's where the game literally turns into a personal experience, as everyone has a different response for the game's selling point. And boy, does it turn to black or white pretty fast from here.
Undertale's ability to completely turn the tables of its story depending on your actions is massive. Upon your game's startup, every little thing you do will be set in stone in the game's story pathing. If you're the type who immerses yourself into the game's charming music, laughs at the childish but hiliarious anctics, and is willing to hork down healing items just to prevent yourself from killing a monster just because a fight is difficult, the game rewards you. It opens up a very character-developing and world-unfolding story, along with some of the most emotionally invested boss battles I have ever experienced. You know a game is good when it breaks the fourth wall so well that you're shaking in your seat in true fear and can't stop the shivers, all while having to fight a hopelessly overpowered god of a boss. The amazing writing only starts once you beat the final few bosses, and the story doesn't stop being good from there onwards.
On the other hand, what makes this game different is that it keeps its dark side from you, and its entirely your choice to experience it. If you scoff at the game's sparing choice since you're
or
to possibly be nice to people, you can go around and intentionally sink your weapon into a monster who just wants to be a friend. And unlike many other games, this isn't just a simple moment of "Oops, I killed another unnamed enemy, let's reset the game and nothing changes"... the weight of a dark choice is huge. Nothing can be taken back, and it forever changes your playthrough. Reset the game, and the characters know. Events change. And with each curious kill, you, in turn, turn from the only human in a land of monsters into the biggest monster in a land of innocents. In the end, ignoring what Undertale sets out to do, which is to let you experience childlike innocence and fun, only makes it delibrately change the game into a quieter, more grim story. Very little character development, and the world isn't explained to you, nothing. There's very little reward for going through this route. Yet it is a choice you can do. Granted, you get two of the hardest boss battles by becoming the murderer and will be forced into Game Overs repeatedly from them, but even that is a message from the game...
It's as if you're doing deeds in an actual living, breathing world. And that's what makes it even more terrifying when you decide to become a murderer instead of a savior, because only you know that you're willingly going forward to obliterate every weakling in front of you. It's a test of your willpower, and it's your choice. The worst thing? The damage cannot be repaired. Go clean, or go home tainted. The game even gives you the choice to completely delete everyone's happiness after the most satisfying happy ending. The happiness you worked so hard to earn. And you can even become the murderer after saving the world, which will only permanently taint your game and never let you have a satisfying ending again. That's absolutely brutal, and yet that's still a choice. Amazing.
Yes, this game might not be for everyone. The humour may become dry after a while for some people, and tons of gamers nowadays like to bash at popular games instead of trying it out, just because they feel accomplished by doing it. But, if like me, you are willing to experience why everyone's been talking about this game, give it a shot. Hell, even if you hate the game to bits and want to kill everyone, buy the game, do so, and at least have your own personal experience before refunding it. This game does the morality concept so well that other games can only dream of doing the same, and it is one not to be forgotten.

Ten dollars. Only a few hours of gameplay. 16-bit graphics compared to the flashy 1080p stuff in standard games.
But... wow. Undertale blew me away. It doesn't need flashy graphics or even fanservice to falsify its enjoyment. It just does things right, and boy that was one immensely enjoyable experience.
I think most of the magic of this game comes from knowing absolutely nothing about it. I got this game from a friend and just decided to play it since it looked very interesting and it was getting good responses. So I went in completely blind, knowing nothing but the game's name. And I'm glad I did, because everything the game presented to me was unexpected, notably dark in places, and very emotional, which would have been lost entirely if i watched someone else play it. So, if you happened to have been flooded by everything Undertale on tumblr
and the entire story's already laid out for you, the magic has been lost and the game won't be as incredible of an experience. I'm sorry.
Of course, I call Undertale an "experience", not a game, only because it does such a fantastic job at it. Following the motto on the store page, "the game where you don't have to destroy anyone", the game always tries to nudge you in that direction, taking a back seat in your mind and reminding you to "Spare them!". And of course, you answer with "Why? Why should I do that when it offers me the option to kill anyone I want right in front of me? What's in it for me?" And that's where the game literally turns into a personal experience, as everyone has a different response for the game's selling point. And boy, does it turn to black or white pretty fast from here.
Undertale's ability to completely turn the tables of its story depending on your actions is massive. Upon your game's startup, every little thing you do will be set in stone in the game's story pathing. If you're the type who immerses yourself into the game's charming music, laughs at the childish but hiliarious anctics, and is willing to hork down healing items just to prevent yourself from killing a monster just because a fight is difficult, the game rewards you. It opens up a very character-developing and world-unfolding story, along with some of the most emotionally invested boss battles I have ever experienced. You know a game is good when it breaks the fourth wall so well that you're shaking in your seat in true fear and can't stop the shivers, all while having to fight a hopelessly overpowered god of a boss. The amazing writing only starts once you beat the final few bosses, and the story doesn't stop being good from there onwards.
On the other hand, what makes this game different is that it keeps its dark side from you, and its entirely your choice to experience it. If you scoff at the game's sparing choice since you're
or
to possibly be nice to people, you can go around and intentionally sink your weapon into a monster who just wants to be a friend. And unlike many other games, this isn't just a simple moment of "Oops, I killed another unnamed enemy, let's reset the game and nothing changes"... the weight of a dark choice is huge. Nothing can be taken back, and it forever changes your playthrough. Reset the game, and the characters know. Events change. And with each curious kill, you, in turn, turn from the only human in a land of monsters into the biggest monster in a land of innocents. In the end, ignoring what Undertale sets out to do, which is to let you experience childlike innocence and fun, only makes it delibrately change the game into a quieter, more grim story. Very little character development, and the world isn't explained to you, nothing. There's very little reward for going through this route. Yet it is a choice you can do. Granted, you get two of the hardest boss battles by becoming the murderer and will be forced into Game Overs repeatedly from them, but even that is a message from the game...
It's as if you're doing deeds in an actual living, breathing world. And that's what makes it even more terrifying when you decide to become a murderer instead of a savior, because only you know that you're willingly going forward to obliterate every weakling in front of you. It's a test of your willpower, and it's your choice. The worst thing? The damage cannot be repaired. Go clean, or go home tainted. The game even gives you the choice to completely delete everyone's happiness after the most satisfying happy ending. The happiness you worked so hard to earn. And you can even become the murderer after saving the world, which will only permanently taint your game and never let you have a satisfying ending again. That's absolutely brutal, and yet that's still a choice. Amazing.
Yes, this game might not be for everyone. The humour may become dry after a while for some people, and tons of gamers nowadays like to bash at popular games instead of trying it out, just because they feel accomplished by doing it. But, if like me, you are willing to experience why everyone's been talking about this game, give it a shot. Hell, even if you hate the game to bits and want to kill everyone, buy the game, do so, and at least have your own personal experience before refunding it. This game does the morality concept so well that other games can only dream of doing the same, and it is one not to be forgotten.

Oh boy. Where do I even start with this one? So much to talk about.
Undertale is an RPG game with bullet hell elements. You control a child who fell down from a hole in the mountain, far down into the Underground, where all monsters were exiled after they lost the war with humans. You journey through to the barrier that separates both worlds, meeting and fighting many interesting, weird, or downright wacky characters along your way. Ultimately it is up to you whether you will spare their lives... or kill them.
The game is obviously holding a simple 8-bit style for the most part, but it isn't afraid to drop it when needed. It's all pretty to look at despite its simplicity, but that's not what I would call the best part of the game.
Music. Almost every single piece composed for this game feels unique, done in its own style, blending perfectly into the current scenery or what's happening on the screen, giving an incredible effect. Just try to walk through the
without stopping for a moment to listen to the music. Or just downright doing nothing during a boss fight for the same reason.
The story is, for the lack of originality and better words, amazing. Depending on which path you take, you will feel a whole plethora of emotions as it progresses. You will laugh. You will cry. You will feel DETERMINED to keep on going.
Finally, the gameplay. You can explore the locations in your usual RPG fashion, and you enter a turn-based RPG-style battle when a random encounter happens. However, unlike in other games, during the monster's turn you will be thrown onto a field, controlling a red heart (called your SOUL), dodging enemy projectiles and attacks. This gives it some skill-based value and keeps it interesting - you can potentially avoid taking damage entirely if you're good enough. I will refrain from making remarks about its difficulty, as someone well-versed in bullet hell shmups, the game was rather easy for me personally. (I died maybe once or twice over the course of the whole game.)
But what the most important is, it's like there isn't exactly a fourth wall here. The gameplay rules are being altered to fit what is going on the screen at that moment. The game knows when you die and reload a save and will call you out on it. It's ready to mess with you at every occassion, making it sort of unpredictable. And so interesting.
My only complaint with the game is that it's a tad bit short. Your first playthrough will most likely be completed in less than 10 hours. I don't mind short games though, especially if it's something as great as this one.
I recommend this game... no, you HAVE to play it. There's no excuse. The game is everything that was great and even more about the old RPGs. This is an unforgettable adventure of your life.

I think it is quite unfair to say that this game is similar to Earthbound, or any game in the 'Mother' series. Not that that's bad, or anything.(I mean, Earthbound is a great game) Chances are, if you are reading this review by me, one of the many, many people who played this game, you already know, from other more acclaimed critics that this game is heart-warming, creative, innovative, emotional, etc. I'll talk about other aspects of the game, and not its plot, innovation, characters and dialogue, because everyone else will do a better job than me at that.
Firstly, soundtrack. Amazing. Nowadays, music in gaming is mostly walls upon walls of sounds, where it is hard to tell what is the melody. The music in this game is actually similar to music back then, where restrictions forced music composers to come up with memorable melodies. Not that the current gaming music is bad, mind you, I'm saying that this music stands out from music of this gaming generation. And it is fantastic. (And I didn't grow up playing games in the 8-bit era either, I started gaming  in the GBA era)
Secondly, the art style. This is the second reason people compare this game to the 'Mother' series (especially Earthbound, and the first is the characters and dialogue). I can see where they are coming from. I've played Earthbound myself since I wanted to experience the best of the 8-bit era awhile back and played the game from start to finish. I will admit that this game has lots of 'Earthbound' vibes. The art style is simplistic and does not have all the pointy bits and shiny texturees, but this art style is enough. It does a great job of conveying story. And that's really all art needs to do in games. Convey story and emotions(of which, the second I said I will not talk about in this review), nothing more, nothing less.
Lastly, the mechanics in this game. This game has a mercy system in place that has more impact on the game than initially thought by many when they first play this game. It will affect your ending, your relationships, and in the long run, you could say everytime you fight, you make a decision, like in those choose your own adventure books. Except unlike a book, this game REMEMBERS your choices, almost like it is self-aware. Toby, the creator of this game, accounted for 99.99% of player shenanigans(Is that how you spell it?) and created dialogue to specifically react to those actions. Like repeatedly petting a certain Dog. Oh boy, that one is great. And that's only the mercy system. There is also receiving attacks. You play a QTE-esque minigame to determine damage taken in battle.
Overall, even outside of its strong points, the story, characters and dialogue, it is still very strong. Not many weak points in the game. Not perfect, but this game may have been the closest to what anyone might call perfection in these past few years of gaming. After all, what game on this flat Earth allows you to date a skeleton?

If the planets align for an hour or two this game can be outstanding. You'll be playing with friends, hitting the right balance between dangerous situations and rewarding finds, and think, "Wow. You'll then spend another 30 hours slogging through one of the most unfun, fundamentally busted and exploited games ever sold, desperately trying to get that hour back.
If nothing else, this game is an accurate simulation of what it's like to be an addict chasing a high. Everyone giving this game a positive review is either reviewing the idea of DayZ, or they may, in fact, actually be high.
The developers have slowly doled out a handful of superficial updates so that they can fall back on the excuse of early access when dodging criticism, but make no mistake--this game is just as half baked as it was when first released. Don't let the ever increasing price fool you either.
Simply put: this game will never be finished. And why should it be? The devs were able to release a proof-of-concept and sell millions of copies while taking home a handful of awards. Who else do they have to sell it to? Those millions of consumers won't be repurchasing the game. This industry is bananas.

Once you get more than 5 minutes into it though, you realize that you can only trust 1 in 20 people who claim to be friendly, people will hack/ghost into your house, steal all of your 10's of hours of hard earned materials and gear and leave you naked and with 5hp(out of 100) all while locked inside your own house with no way to escape or even to kill yourself and respawn.
It was interesting and mildly annoying the first time it happened. it's F****** infuriating the second time. there is NO sense of accomplishment when the rug can so easily be pulled out from under you. I have had it with this 'Game'.
To be perfectly clear, I have no problem with a game being hard; in fact, I play permadeath games whenever possible, I love the dark souls series, and I only play skyrim with a super difficult and realistic Requiem mod set.
What I have a problem with in Rust is the utter lack of anything resembling a community, the chat is constantly filled with some of the most racist and hateful crap that I've ever seen in text form, there almost never seems to be a mod watching chat, the fact that you can spend hours and hours and hours working to make yourself as safe as possible before you log out to use the bathroom, and when you come back, it's all down the toilet...
This was a total waste of my money and for the first time ever, I'm going to search for a way to permanently remove 'Rust' from my games list. This crap is why I used to torrent games before buying them.
-10/10 (I've never given a game a negative score before)

2. Every update seems to halve my Framerate even further while not actually seeming to provide anything useful.
******EDIT: After thinking about it, I'me going to try a foriegn server. One where English is likely not spoken often. Hopefully by doing this I can evade the 'hate chat' and maybe by building my house in the middle of nowhere and build it very small, I can stay below a hackers notice?... sigh... I spent good money on this, and I WANT to like it.... Ging to give it another shot...
*****2ND EDIT:   Tried it again, received some VERY rare kindness from a fellow with a house near mine. Paid it forward by supplying a noob with useful tips and basic tool and food, made a secure stone home, logged for the night, and was house hacked AGAIN and locked inside with no way to escape or respawn or kill myself or anything.
My initial review was done in the heat of the moment and I was rather upset at the time, but I'm crystal clear now and stand by everything I said previously. I gave Rust its second chance. I think it is quite unfair to say that this game is similar to Earthbound, or any game in the 'Mother' series. Not that that's bad, or anything.(I mean, Earthbound is a great game) Chances are, if you are reading this review by me, one of the many, many people who played this game, you already know, from other more acclaimed critics that this game is heart-warming, creative, innovative, emotional, etc. I'll talk about other aspects of the game, and not its plot, innovation, characters and dialogue, because everyone else will do a better job than me at that.
Firstly, soundtrack. Amazing. Nowadays, music in gaming is mostly walls upon walls of sounds, where it is hard to tell what is the melody. The music in this game is actually similar to music back then, where restrictions forced music composers to come up with memorable melodies. Not that the current gaming music is bad, mind you, I'm saying that this music stands out from music of this gaming generation. And it is fantastic. (And I didn't grow up playing games in the 8-bit era either, I started gaming  in the GBA era)
Secondly, the art style. This is the second reason people compare this game to the 'Mother' series (especially Earthbound, and the first is the characters and dialogue). I can see where they are coming from. I've played Earthbound myself since I wanted to experience the best of the 8-bit era awhile back and played the game from start to finish. I will admit that this game has lots of 'Earthbound' vibes. The art style is simplistic and does not have all the pointy bits and shiny texturees, but this art style is enough. It does a great job of conveying story. And that's really all art needs to do in games. Convey story and emotions(of which, the second I said I will not talk about in this review), nothing more, nothing less.
Lastly, the mechanics in this game. This game has a mercy system in place that has more impact on the game than initially thought by many when they first play this game. It will affect your ending, your relationships, and in the long run, you could say everytime you fight, you make a decision, like in those choose your own adventure books. Except unlike a book, this game REMEMBERS your choices, almost like it is self-aware. Toby, the creator of this game, accounted for 99.99% of player shenanigans(Is that how you spell it?) and created dialogue to specifically react to those actions. Like repeatedly petting a certain Dog. Oh boy, that one is great. And that's only the mercy system. There is also receiving attacks. You play a QTE-esque minigame to determine damage taken in battle.
Overall, even outside of its strong points, the story, characters and dialogue, it is still very strong. Not many weak points in the game. Not perfect, but this game may have been the closest to what anyone might call perfection in these past few years of gaming. After all, what game on this flat Earth allows you to date a skeleton?

If the planets align for an hour or two this game can be outstanding. You'll be playing with friends, hitting the right balance between dangerous situations and rewarding finds, and think, "Wow. You'll then spend another 30 hours slogging through one of the most unfun, fundamentally busted and exploited games ever sold, desperately trying to get that hour back.
If nothing else, this game is an accurate simulation of what it's like to be an addict chasing a high. Everyone giving this game a positive review is either reviewing the idea of DayZ, or they may, in fact, actually be high.
The developers have slowly doled out a handful of superficial updates so that they can fall back on the excuse of early access when dodging criticism, but make no mistake--this game is just as half baked as it was when first released. Don't let the ever increasing price fool you either.
Simply put: this game will never be finished. And why should it be? The devs were able to release a proof-of-concept and sell millions of copies while taking home a handful of awards. Who else do they have to sell it to? Those millions of consumers won't be repurchasing the game. This industry is bananas.

Oh, Undertale?
I guess the best way to explain it to you is this:
It's a top-notch game. Hands-down game of the year for me. Why?
Have you ever been able to flirt with your enemy?
To laugh with your enemy?
To have your enemy cleanse your body of all the filth and stains that lay all over you?
Have you ever played a game where hilarious jokes and references are hinted at almost every area in the game without it being repetitively uninteresting?
Have you ever played a game where random and seemingly unnecessary events/items pop in at unforeseen points in the story that, instead of ruining the immersion, assist in the cooling and comfort of your mind?
Have you ever been able to run through a turn-based game and NOT destroy anyone?
No..?
That's why this game is a diamond in the rough.
This game is includes all these features. You're able to not murder anyone, you're able to uncover the history of the game's story at YOUR pace, and you, overall, have the ability to create YOUR story, which is all done through retro, 8-bit  graphics. Undertale has multiple endings, which make you want to return to the game to uncover the many different routes that you can take within the story.
The soundtrack is riveting and gripping in the idea that it fits with every situation it's placed in. If you spare an enemy, the music fits. If you take them down with brutal force, the music changes so it can fit. For example, murdering everyone will change the mood of an area, as they will most likely fear you. If not, then the music is going to be very "happy-go-lucky."
The characters were not scrapped from petty ideas that popped in the developers' minds. They were ALL very well thought of and they were ALL very well contrasted to the monster's predicament as a race. (I can't go that far in depth without spoiling something, so I'll leave this review for now.)
You can even date a skeleton.
This game will forever remain near and dear to my heart. It's touched my feelings in ways that I thought would never have been moved for a long time. I recommend this game to everyone who has the patience and time to want to actually listen to one talk about their deep and innermost feelings.
Overall,
it's a 10/10.

Oh, Undertale?
I guess the best way to explain it to you is this:
It's a top-notch game. Hands-down game of the year for me. Why?
Have you ever been able to flirt with your enemy?
To laugh with your enemy?
To have your enemy cleanse your body of all the filth and stains that lay all over you?
Have you ever played a game where hilarious jokes and references are hinted at almost every area in the game without it being repetitively uninteresting?
Have you ever played a game where random and seemingly unnecessary events/items pop in at unforeseen points in the story that, instead of ruining the immersion, assist in the cooling and comfort of your mind?
Have you ever been able to run through a turn-based game and NOT destroy anyone?
No..?
That's why this game is a diamond in the rough.
This game is includes all these features. You're able to not murder anyone, you're able to uncover the history of the game's story at YOUR pace, and you, overall, have the ability to create YOUR story, which is all done through retro, 8-bit  graphics. Undertale has multiple endings, which make you want to return to the game to uncover the many different routes that you can take within the story.
The soundtrack is riveting and gripping in the idea that it fits with every situation it's placed in. If you spare an enemy, the music fits. If you take them down with brutal force, the music changes so it can fit. For example, murdering everyone will change the mood of an area, as they will most likely fear you. If not, then the music is going to be very "happy-go-lucky."
The characters were not scrapped from petty ideas that popped in the developers' minds. They were ALL very well thought of and they were ALL very well contrasted to the monster's predicament as a race. (I can't go that far in depth without spoiling something, so I'll leave this review for now.)
You can even date a skeleton.
This game will forever remain near and dear to my heart. It's touched my feelings in ways that I thought would never have been moved for a long time. I recommend this game to everyone who has the patience and time to want to actually listen to one talk about their deep and innermost feelings.
Overall,
it's a 10/10.
P.S. - Yes, my favorite character is Napstablook. :)

If you ever find yourself arguing with someone that doesn't think that video games are an artistic medium, this should be your go-to example.
It isn't just that the game has more care, skill, and thought put into it than any other you're likely to play this year.  It isn't just that it's superbly written, or that it's self-aware enough to be both hilarious and downright terrifying, sometimes at the same time.  It isn't even all of the subtle details and variations that make the prospect of multiple playthroughs something to look forward to, instead of a chore.
It's that the entire time your playing, regardless of HOW you play, Toby Fox is presenting an experience that manages to feel tailor-made for YOU; the game is astoundingly good at predicting what the player will try, and the experience of seeing how the game reacts - as a singular entity, not just as something presenting you with the next challenge - is something that no other medium can offer in quite the same way.
I'm not writing this review to convince people to buy it; I'm writing this review because this is a game that well and truly deserves to be celebrated.
Something very special.

Undertale will not be forgotten by gaming history. It might be a little heavy on the pop-culture references at times, but at the core, it asks a very relevant question of our time:
Do we really need to kill stuff to be entertained? Can we go through a whole world filled with "monsters" without ever slaying one? And can we still be the hero at the end?
Explore these feelings yourself and get touched by a game that rarely uses more than 16 colors in one scene, but can be more beautiful than any Ultra settings can ever achieve.

Full disclosure: I've never played the Dayz mod, and have less than 10 hours on this game.
All in all, a $40 regret. After taking a break from Rust I thought I would give Dayz a try since I always saw it on the Top 10 seller list. Maybe my expectations were different, but I really found myself bored in Dayz. First of all, the server populations are all less than 50 players (more often 20 or less), yet the map is huge. This makes for very infrequent player interactions, and almost becomes a single player exploration game. That's fine if you like single player games, but those generally aren't for me.
To add to this, the game requires that you stay hydrated and eat often. That's fine too, but it can often be very difficult finding areas of the game that have these items available to loot... let alone finding a weapon.
After a while, I found myself visitng the same style housing environments opening doors and going to the next one... and it was just.. BORING. The movement, and aiming all felt very weird too. I never played Arma or the mod, so I can't compare... but it almost had a Rainbow Six feel to it. Seemed sluggish, and awkward.
Maybe things will be different closer to release, but I can't recommend this game to anyone right now.

Updated Review for DayZ (Dec 2017):
I was a genuine fan of the Arma 2 DayZ Mod. My brother introduced me to it and I put around 500-600 hours into it. It was one of the most fun multiplayer experiences I've ever had with games. My experience with DayZ Standalone started very similarly. I met some people in the game who I rolled with for a while and it was fun. However, the lack of content and things to do made it extremely boring. After around 100-150 hours, both the people I played with and I stopped playing DayZ. We came back occasionaly and would play for about a week and stop again wondering if the game would ever get better, but it didn't. I would hope that once the game reaches Beta and they can start pushing out content for it with the new engine that they put a massive sale on the game for something like $5-$10. This would help rebuild the dying community and playercount as well as generate interest for the game, I would also hope they add modding very soon after Beta. This is wishful thinking though, considering the game has never gone below $25 I don't think they would do some sort of mega-sale. Unless the playercounts increase, basebuilding and vehicles are a thing, and the game is cheaper, don't buy this.
Rest in peace DayZ, I will miss you.

This game really strikes a love / hate relationship with it's player base. There is so much potential behind the concepts here, but the time it is taking for the devs to deliver is really heartbreaking. Having taken a seven month break from this game I was really hoping for it to be in better shape, but while playing my character was erased not once, but twice while changing servers, quickly wiping out 6 hours or so of my time.
That said, this game makes your heart race unlike any other. The pvp is pure adrenaline pumping action, where you truely feel you have much to lose, because you do. And I like that sense of danger. The level of realism devs are striving for on this game is wonderful, even ground breaking, but it's just taking a long time to hit their goal.
So, that said, if you're on the fence about this game, wait for more of the bugs to be worked out. If you can't wait to do alittle highway robbery, looting military bases, or exploring a vast world, go ahead and splurge alittle. This game, in it's current state, is still an incredibly fun game, and possibly the most frustrating game I've played in my life.

This early-access game is kind of like "modern society simulator". Finding the right server and community to play with, being part of that community, getting friends, getting betrayed, and a lot more is included in this game.
The company developing this game, Facepunch, developer of Garry's Mod, keeps the game updated, and it contains loads of fun, especially if taking into consideration the fact that it's still in alpha-stage. Bugs and such do exist in the game, though usually they are minor, and the most major ones are fixed by the team in few weeks, even days.
Getting started in Rust is going to be a long journey if you have no knowledge of the game. Gathering enough resources to craft your very first Stone Hatchet is a satisfying trip to learning more about the game, and what you might find when proceeding closer to the end-game gear. Got your base ready, set of Kevlar equipped, enough weaponry to beat anyone who comes at you? Go and blast a wall of another player. Grab all the loot you can. Get the hell out. Developed better tactics for... Whatever you might need. Raiding, building, surviving, trading, there are several things where you can develop.
if you have any doubt if you should buy this or not, I recommend to do so. The game is still unfinished, but still great.

Long, looong ago there was a time when the ony objective to Rust was to survive. whether it be from zombies, crippling weather, or OP bears and wolves a new type of survival emerged: your fellow man (and/or woman).
The game turning from a caveman survival to a Hunger Games survival really turned the tide tide and the direction of the game for me. Crafting, building and hunting were fun but since then has turned into a pvp shooter game really drew the last straw with me this past year. So there for I don't like it anymore, as there are plenty of other titles that focus on crafing and actual survival and i encourage you to search for them before considering buying this game.
So is it a bad game? No, certainly not for people who like to hone their pvp gun skills for other games but I just believe Rust lost it's true intentions years ago, but it isn't my style of game anymore.

"No crying until the ending. Guaranteed Masterpiece"
That's one of the first things that came to mind when I played this game through the first time. It was re-affirmed the second time, the third time, and the fourth.
This game has tons of replay value, and Toby Fox really outdid himself on this. I think it will be hard for him to top this in any future endeavors. It also tears apart the notion that a modern game can only be successful if it has bleeding-edge graphics, a full symphonic orchestra, and a cast of all-star voice actors. Undertale does the two core things a game should do: immerse the player and provide a temporary escape from reality. It happens to do this very well.
If you like RPGs, bullet-hells, and emotional rollercoasters, this game is definitely for you. Even if you don't like any of the above, this game is still worth a try. You may even warm up to the above!
I'd also recommend picking up the soundtrack while you're at it. Totally worth it.

I am officially changing my review, as I have racked up quiet a few more hour on this game.
Pro's:
- The core mechanics of this game are extremely enjoyable and I had many hours of fun exploring the world and building up a base, from the resources I had collected. The crafting feels really smooth and enjoyable and is really nice when setting up foundation's/walls/ceilings/etc. for your base/home. Additionally, the visuals on this game are amazing and not to mention the gun-play, which is some of the best I have seen in any game.
Con's:
- Now this is where things start getting annoying and start to ruin the game. Firstly, the community is completely toxic. You think DayZ has a bad community, well then look no further than Rust's. No matter if you join a dedicated, full server or an almost empty modded server (which is PvE or has no KOS), you can expect people to go out of their way to raid you and kill you on sight. You will end up taking a long time (i.e 10 hours) building up a base and gathering resources, which will be completely gone after logging off for and hour or so. Also, if you then respawn on the beach and try getting some materials (to make tools) and some barrels, you will be lucky if you don't get the geared KOS players surrounding the spawns, so expect to die pretty quickly.
I will admit that I have made a few close friends on this game, through the community, however this does not count for the other 90% of the community, who wont even give two about you or any of your progress, that you have made through the game (Base building, material gathering, exploring, etc.).
TL;DR:
If you can stand a game where the community is worse than DayZ's, you don't mind the countless times you will die to people who are more geared than you (after you fresh spawn) and restarting up your base from scratch, everytime you log out and come back, then this is the perfect game for you. If not, then I would highly recommend staying away from this game.

Strange kinda game this is really.
It's definately a survival game, but more surviving the other survivers then worrying about zombies.
Everybody is KOS, even your friends, just in case they're thinking the same thing.
You can(you will) spend hours and hours running accross the map for loot. If you manage to gear up you then have to decide if you want to risk losing all your gear in an instant by comming into contact with other survivers who will kill you for a can of beans, let alone a full military setup, or do you want to just hide in the woods.
Hermit style game play is ok for a while, you'll get to hold onto your sweet gear for a few extra hours, or as long as you want really, just be a hermit and hide...making all your awesome gear kinda useless and wasted.
Or you can head into a city and be killed by..well you won't know as there is no info to tell you how you died, just a black screen saying "you are dead".
Then it's back to running for hours and hours again.
Unless you play with a group of friends at all times the game is pretty much a running simulator with brief interuptions to your running while you eat your beans.
The game does however have alot of mechanics to support roleplaying(idealy on a private server), and if thats your thing, this game will only get better for you.
I'm sure once the game gets ALOT more zombies(both more types and numbers) it will start to morph into a more coop type game but atm unless you're roleplaying it's totally a KOS PvP sandbox with a few zombies.
As far as bugs and glitches, yeah theres a few, but the game has been overall very stable on my PC (i7 2600k with 670GTX) at max settings. Hackers havn't been a problem for me...yet. So far i've only played on low pop servers though as i want to feel confidant of the controls and have a basic knowledge of which building are worth searching etc. Going by other reviews they are a big problem on higher pop servers but i guess if you join a clan and play on a private server it probably shouldn't be such an issue.
Overall the game is very playable, wether you'll love it or hate it depends on what you want in a game but theres enough review/videos/live streams/etc to make a pretty informed decision.
Give it a go, or just wait for H1Z1 in a few weeks.

Undertale has been gaining quite a bit of popularity as of late, and for good reason; IT'S GODLIKE. Allow me to give you a quick rundown of why this is.
As far as the gameplay goes, Undertale is a retro style, Earthbound-ish RPG with some bullet-hell thrown in. It's pretty delicious. But where the game really goes BEAST MODE, is in it's dialogue, humor, Characters, and story.
This all gets even JUICIER when they throw in some cause-and-effect decision making into the mix. Depending on the choices you make throughout the game, even small ones like choosing to either kill a random monster or spare its life, will affect the game in some way. This leads to bunch of different endings and changes to the story that you can witness, and it also leads to a ton of replayability.
Sounds pretty sick, huh? Well, you're dang right.
The soundtrack, especially the boss themes, is comparable to a 5 star steak sauce marinade, which is to say, it is quite good. Speaking of boss fights, Undertale has some of the SICKEST ones i've seen in some time. Many of them put unique twists on the combat style and they are DANG GOOD.
When all is said and done, this game reminds me a lot of that Horse Egg Casserole I ate last week: It looks a little weird at first, but once you get a taste, it gives you a warm satisfying joy in your belly that sticks around for days to come. This is surely a slam dunk worth experiencing.
If Undertale was an earthquake, it would have a magnitude rating in the 7.1-7.9 range, "Major earthquake. Serious damage." Thank you for reading this review.

Minor spoilers in the review, I suggest you buy the game, although don't expect to get a lot more than ten hours of play out of those ten bucks, the game made me feel kinda bad for wanting to restart the game after I got the perfect ending.
Fun game Even if you know the story already: Primarily because of the gameplay, and tunes.
What this game has is a good, healthy amount of replay value for the price. There are three major ways to play, Genocide, Neutral, and Pacifist. Each with its own ending, although playing as a pacifist you have to go through the neutral ending anyway.
Well one of the neutral endings anyway. There are lot's of them, every possible thing you can do differently will change something about the end(or nearly so minor mooks are noteworthy only in that they raise your murder-count).
There is never a need to kill anything in this game, except one particular boss, he'll make it clear their's no way out.
Also people call the game a Jrpg, but it adds plenty of bullet hell, ever rage at a game for having RNG dodge mechanics? Well in this game you manually dodge attacks, so it's mainly skill that decides whether you live or die, very nice.
Oh also the game has rules it sets up early, and it messes with them, not so much breaking the rules as playing legalese with them. That is to say, some enemies interact with your menu, or stretch the box you dodge in, or do a few other crazy things.
Anywho there are a few nice secrets in the game too, not going into detail in case you want to hunt them down yourself, but two of them come in as invisible paths. Fun.
Oh by the way the dialog and lore in this game are really nice, shows actual effort put into making a world rather than a pass-time, and the serious bits of the game are much improved by the contrast between them and the jokes you get in between.
Also the OST is probably worth the price, if you don't feel ike getting the whole game. Wait can you buy that thing alone? I dunno, didn't check. It's  very nice chiptunes if you like the Earthbound OST I think you'll like these, they are better in context though, always fitting the mood of where they're placed.

I am officially changing my review, as I have racked up quiet a few more hour on this game.
Pro's:
- The core mechanics of this game are extremely enjoyable and I had many hours of fun exploring the world and building up a base, from the resources I had collected. The crafting feels really smooth and enjoyable and is really nice when setting up foundation's/walls/ceilings/etc. for your base/home. Additionally, the visuals on this game are amazing and not to mention the gun-play, which is some of the best I have seen in any game.
Con's:
- Now this is where things start getting annoying and start to ruin the game. Firstly, the community is completely toxic. You think DayZ has a bad community, well then look no further than Rust's. No matter if you join a dedicated, full server or an almost empty modded server (which is PvE or has no KOS), you can expect people to go out of their way to raid you and kill you on sight. You will end up taking a long time (i.e 10 hours) building up a base and gathering resources, which will be completely gone after logging off for and hour or so. Also, if you then respawn on the beach and try getting some materials (to make tools) and some barrels, you will be lucky if you don't get the geared KOS players surrounding the spawns, so expect to die pretty quickly.
I will admit that I have made a few close friends on this game, through the community, however this does not count for the other 90% of the community, who wont even give two about you or any of your progress, that you have made through the game (Base building, material gathering, exploring, etc.).
TL;DR:
If you can stand a game where the community is worse than DayZ's, you don't mind the countless times you will die to people who are more geared than you (after you fresh spawn) and restarting up your base from scratch, everytime you log out and come back, then this is the perfect game for you. If not, then I would highly recommend staying away from this game.

If you are a person who is tired of games as commercial products and miss the days when you would pick up something at the rental store just because the cover looked cool and then discovered those games to be some of the most memorable games you ever played even if they weren't technically better games than stuff coming out now: you deserve to play undertale. Even if you are someone who never played an Earthbound game or many JRPGs, or even if you hate turned based combat you will probably find something to love about Undertale. Its a great example of how even its flaws as an actual product, like archaic feeling controls and dated and ugly UI designs, make the experience of it as a game even better. It's a game that frustrated me at several parts but also reminded me of those old Sega Genesis games and Nintendo 64 games I use to rent with my meager allowance that have stuck with me far more than most major, modern blockbuster could hope to. Just one more piece of advice: try to go into it completely blind. Don't let yourself know what you are getting into, and STAY DETERMINED.
That's why you need to play Undertale.

If you're looking to play casually, go somewhere else. In its current state, this game is not for the faint of heart unless you can find a private server that's more your speed.
If you enjoy PvP, confrontation, and facing off against humanity's societal lows, then look no further.
Reminds me of EVE: Online where the game is dominated by older players who have already dug in and established their own footholds. Community's pretty toxic when it comes to new players, who are often referred to as "Nakeds", and the common kill-on-sight policy for Nakeds only helps to drive the point home.
Generally you'll be ganked and robbed by opponents who have better tech, more resources, and more allies (I would use the word "friend" sparingly in this game) than you do, for little more than spite or sadistic amusement. You'll need to invest quite a bit of time and either bring friends or find allies sooner than later in order to survive the community. Expect abuse and an uphill battle.
Be aware of your surroundings at all times. If you see a stranger in the distance who isn't naked, he probably has a gun. If he hasn't shot at you yet, assume he will. If you're ever in doubt, run. Run for cover. Then run until you can find a good place to hide. Never run back to your home base if you can help it. You'll tell your enemies where to raid.
Most importantly, when you log out, your character doesn't leave the game. He lies down to sleep. This is when you're most vulnerable, so plan for it.
If this sort of challenge sounds like your thing, the rest of the game isn't bad: competent survival mechanics including thirst, hunger, climates (and dressing appropriately), shelter, radiation, day/night cycle, hunting and being hunted by wild animals, scavenging, and crafting. It's still in early access, so I hope and expect the game will continue to gain depth in this regard.
All in all, the game itself has merit even if the community isn't my cup of tea.

(SPOILER FREE)
Right off the bat, I want to say that I did not go into this game completely blind. I watched about thirty minutes of beginning gamepley along side the trailer, and even that small amount, was far too much. I will always have a feeling of regret not going into this game blind, it was far too good not to be experienced that way. So as a warning to any who come across this, DON'T watch any minute of gameplay for this game til you have played a good while yourself, even the trailer alone is an iffy subject, just know, that violence is not always the answer, and be on your way into this god-sent gift of a game.
As starters I want to mention the beginning, it drops you into a world where monsters and humans have had a very bad relationship over the years and were kept underground, and you, the human, fall down into the underground, and must find your way out. It's short and cuts to the chase very quickly, and is done flawlessly.
Second, the characters. Everyone you meet, is the most enjoyable person you will have ever met, whether they're completely oblivious to everything and love you to death, or stern and outright hate you, you will feel a connection to them in some way, garunteed.
Third, the music. Never in my entire life have I heard such an amazing soundtrack, the pure ambience and feeling each single note gives is a noise to treasure and love. There are normal songs that set a sad tone, some happy, some outright goofy, and even a select few of terror and discomfort, yet each is perfect in its own way.
Any who are reading to this point without having played the game, decide now wether you are interested or not, and if you're wary, know that in my opinion, this is at least in the top 3 games I have ever played list, so I highly recommend it. This easily gets my favorite game of all time, so yes an 11/10. Now onto my final topic of discussion with this game.
(MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD)
Feeling. I loved every single character in this game. I was horrified when I saw them in danger and absolutely giddy when I saw them again or even spoke to them in a less dangerous environment. I did my best to make sure they liked me and everyone felt special. I knew they were all fake characters, yet, if I could meet them on the streets, I would be overjoyed to see their faces. They all feel so real, depending on the ending you get, It hurts painfully, or feels absolutely wonderful. I got the true ending of this game, and cried. I am not ashamed to admit that, if you do not even slightly tear up at the true ending, you have no soul. I only knew the person for a collective 3 minutes or so, yet I cried for them. Please, if you decided to read on and get to this point, just buy the game and play it yourself, its heartwarming, heartbreaking and all out a fantastic journey to experience.

I'll be honest, when my friend told me about this game I wasn't too sure about it. It was so new, I didn't think it would live up to the hype, but I humored her as she gushed about it. Just to appease her, I put it on my wishlist.
Then she bought it for me.
I know it's only ten bucks, but I didn't want that money to go to waste, so I put aside my doubts and began playing.
And I have been blown away.
When it comes to games with story, I like games with a lot of emotion and really make me think. normally, they tend to be overly complex, but this one keeps it simple while still making me feel so much for the characters. I've learned to appreciate bad jokes and puns more, and when it's over... do you really want to take the characters away from their happy ending? These characters that you've actually gotten to know and become friends with... would it really be right to rip their happiness away from them.
Well, you can if you want. Nobody is stopping you from killing everything in your path. At least not until later on, and there's no turning back even if you reset the game. You'll have actual consequences to your actions, and the game lets you know this.
I can't remember the last time I enjoyed a game so much.
A compteley different experience from what you're used to. The best way to experience this game is to go in knowing nothing about it. Enjoy.

If you're looking to play casually, go somewhere else. In its current state, this game is not for the faint of heart unless you can find a private server that's more your speed.
If you enjoy PvP, confrontation, and facing off against humanity's societal lows, then look no further.
Reminds me of EVE: Online where the game is dominated by older players who have already dug in and established their own footholds. Community's pretty toxic when it comes to new players, who are often referred to as "Nakeds", and the common kill-on-sight policy for Nakeds only helps to drive the point home.
Generally you'll be ganked and robbed by opponents who have better tech, more resources, and more allies (I would use the word "friend" sparingly in this game) than you do, for little more than spite or sadistic amusement. You'll need to invest quite a bit of time and either bring friends or find allies sooner than later in order to survive the community. Expect abuse and an uphill battle.
Be aware of your surroundings at all times. If you see a stranger in the distance who isn't naked, he probably has a gun. If he hasn't shot at you yet, assume he will. If you're ever in doubt, run. Run for cover. Then run until you can find a good place to hide. Never run back to your home base if you can help it. You'll tell your enemies where to raid.
Most importantly, when you log out, your character doesn't leave the game. He lies down to sleep. This is when you're most vulnerable, so plan for it.
If this sort of challenge sounds like your thing, the rest of the game isn't bad: competent survival mechanics including thirst, hunger, climates (and dressing appropriately), shelter, radiation, day/night cycle, hunting and being hunted by wild animals, scavenging, and crafting. It's still in early access, so I hope and expect the game will continue to gain depth in this regard.
All in all, the game itself has merit even if the community isn't my cup of tea.

Right off the bat, I want to say that I did not go into this game completely blind. I watched about thirty minutes of beginning gamepley along side the trailer, and even that small amount, was far too much. I will always have a feeling of regret not going into this game blind, it was far too good not to be experienced that way. So as a warning to any who come across this, DON'T watch any minute of gameplay for this game til you have played a good while yourself, even the trailer alone is an iffy subject, just know, that violence is not always the answer, and be on your way into this god-sent gift of a game.
As starters I want to mention the beginning, it drops you into a world where monsters and humans have had a very bad relationship over the years and were kept underground, and you, the human, fall down into the underground, and must find your way out. It's short and cuts to the chase very quickly, and is done flawlessly.
Second, the characters. Everyone you meet, is the most enjoyable person you will have ever met, whether they're completely oblivious to everything and love you to death, or stern and outright hate you, you will feel a connection to them in some way, garunteed.
Third, the music. Never in my entire life have I heard such an amazing soundtrack, the pure ambience and feeling each single note gives is a noise to treasure and love. There are normal songs that set a sad tone, some happy, some outright goofy, and even a select few of terror and discomfort, yet each is perfect in its own way.
Any who are reading to this point without having played the game, decide now wether you are interested or not, and if you're wary, know that in my opinion, this is at least in the top 3 games I have ever played list, so I highly recommend it. This easily gets my favorite game of all time, so yes an 11/10. Now onto my final topic of discussion with this game.
(MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD)
Feeling. I loved every single character in this game. I was horrified when I saw them in danger and absolutely giddy when I saw them again or even spoke to them in a less dangerous environment. I did my best to make sure they liked me and everyone felt special. I knew they were all fake characters, yet, if I could meet them on the streets, I would be overjoyed to see their faces. They all feel so real, depending on the ending you get, It hurts painfully, or feels absolutely wonderful. I got the true ending of this game, and cried. I am not ashamed to admit that, if you do not even slightly tear up at the true ending, you have no soul. I only knew the person for a collective 3 minutes or so, yet I cried for them. Please, if you decided to read on and get to this point, just buy the game and play it yourself, its heartwarming, heartbreaking and all out a fantastic journey to experience.

Then she bought it for me.

When it comes to games with story, I like games with a lot of emotion and really make me think. normally, they tend to be overly complex, but this one keeps it simple while still making me feel so much for the characters. I've learned to appreciate bad jokes and puns more, and when it's over... do you really want to take the characters away from their happy ending? I can't remember the last time I enjoyed a game so much.

Pros:
- Graphics are pretty nice, runs fairly well on my upper medium rig
- Building a base with some friends, gathering resources and getting blueprints for weapons is very satisfying
- You can occasionally meet someone who won't shoot you on sight, then maybe you'll have a laugh together
- The paintable signs are a great idea and add some much needed personal touch to the world
Cons:
- The community is toxic, ~9/10 people will kill you instantly on sight even if you are a fresh spawn, but whats worse is half of them sound like spoiled 10 yr olds over voip which is extremely annoying
- Logging in and seeing your base and all your stuff completely gone just cos you couldn't play for a day is pretty disheartening, so unless you want to be a 24/7 rusthead then don't bother, all you'll get is frustration time and again.
- Makes you hate the community, turning you into another kill on sight ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cos you're sick of getting shot for no reason, hence the community breeds it's own demise.
- Hackers (not to name names but cough *russians* cough)
Basically if you want to have a game that you have to dedicate 4 hours a day to AT LEAST then you might enjoy rust, but for me its just a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥ sitting in their towers shooting everyone they see, only going outside to shoot more people on sight.
Having said that you might want to be one of those people, and it can be really good fun don't get me wrong. I just want you to be a little more knowledgeable about what you're getting with rust, which is what a review should be.
Edit: This is the most complete early access game I've ever witnessed. While the gameplay isnt my cup of tea anymore I do recommend playing this if you have friends to play with.

I know we're in the very strict minority, but my friends (3/12 of us live in Europe, the rest in the USA) and I play DayZ together not as "Call of Duty with a Hunger Mechanic" but as if we had an opportunity to really hang out in a post-apocalyptic world. We travel, take up temporary residence in towns for a while, hunt, farm, fish, cook, and do ridiculous silly crap because it's fun.
The way I see it DayZ is not a 'game' in the traditional sense. The developers are not setting an objective, and they're not telling us who we are. DayZ is a series of tools and actions that are being made available to us so we can do whatever we want with them. Everyone who buys this game is free to play it exactly how he or she wants. For some people this is great, for others it's terrible. Your mileage may very, but I absolutely love it.

I have been wanting to grab Rust for a while now, for me the survivability mixed with building sounded amazing, not so much for the PvP aspect. Now after 40 hours and countless houses later I can say I am extremely glad I finally grabbed Rust and it is every bit worth the 20 bucks.
A good server is key to enjoying the game (in my eyes) and the server I am on has a smallish population which works out great. There is enough of a challenge through the PvP that I am not constantly getting my house destroyed, but enough people to still warrant a challenge and having to start over occasionally. I was even raided by the nicest people ever. They killed me while I tried to defend, then took only the materials while leaving me clothes and food to at least survive! Haha.
The survival aspect is great as well. You can get too hot or too cold which will kill you, as will starvation. But it is not impossible to have even the smallest amount of protection to keep you safe.
If you enjoy Minecraft but want more excitement, Rust is your game.

Alright, here is the deal with this game. This game is a fun game but that fun is very very spread out across hours and hours of playing the game. This effect is only given a solution by playing on full pop servers because of how big this game is. My review has changed over the years and for the most part was a do not recommend review. Bohemia interactive is striving ot make a survival sandbox game on a scale and intensity that has not been pulled off as of yet. As buggy and frustrating as this game is, it is the best survival game you can play, but that also depends on your personal tastes as a gamer. What I want in a survival game is micromanagement of my character; keeping them fed and hydrated, keeping them free of infection which also throws in body temperature, manage injuries which could definitely use a bit more work but things like broken limbs having to be managed and consciousness being a factor is a fantastic feature. I am, perhaps, ignorantly optimistic that these features will be completely functional at some point and will no longer be a factor by simply walking down stairs. I want tactical military simulation firefights, and this game delivers that with realistic gun mechanics including bullet drop, guns jamming, having to bolt or pump your gun manually is something that always gets overlooked and I actually thoroughly enjoy that little function.
I think it is important to also point out the things I do not want in a survival game. I don't want base building to be the main focus (Rust, H1Z1, 7 Days to Die, Ark). I don't want firefights to be the main focus and as a result they feel very arcade like with bunny hopping and quick scoping and the like (H1Z1, Ark).
Now, in my original review, the hackers were a major plague on this game. It was to the point that I was shocked if I went one day without dying to someone shooting me through buildings or looting all my stuff while I was alive and conscious and teleporting behind me. However with the last 2 large patches that went into this game, I have not encountered a single hacker. Now I'm not sure if it's BattleEye that has finally stepped up their game or if the hackers just moved on to other games where griefing is a major factor of the game. I have experienced some suspicious characters and died to them, but no one that I can actually confirm is a hacker. And it has been an extra 200 hours of playing that I have not experienced a hacker.
The bugs are still present in this game, although mass picking apple trees is not a bug I want them to fix yet given that canned food seems to be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to find sometimes. The zombies are a nightmare because upon collision your character will be pushed around at incredible speeds and launch you through walls and off ledges because of the new player control that is present in the zombies but not the actual players for some reason. Why they separated the installation of this change I have no idea.
Now, this game has been plagued by a lot of bad publicity, the long dev cycle, the fiasco that is all the bugs and game breaking problems that have arisen throughout this cycle, the hackers. Bohemia also decided to release this game on, essentially, the absolutely broken engine that plagued Arma II and decided to implement most of the features they want to have in the game. Then over 2 years down the line they decided to release a new engine for it, that is just slightly less broken but does have much better performance. However now they have to rework all the mechanics that they have implemented because of the change in the engine. They decided to make this game in the most♥♥♥♥♥backwards way that I can imagine. However, if you want the same type of game that I mentioned above in my wants of a survival game section, then this game is definitely for you. If you want a survival game that has a base building focus with, in my opinion, child-like shooting mechanics then pick up H1Z1 or Rust. Miscreated is also a game that I can highly recommend, that game finds a good middle ground actually.

There's plenty to complain about in DayZ. You can spend your early hours with the game just wandering through the woods or searching empty houses for supplies. The game offers very little in the way of guidance when you start. Once you finally get some decent gear, you can lose it in a flash if you're caught by surprise by a couple zombies or a trigger happy player.
Still, the loose and harsh nature that many people hate about DayZ is also why people love it. Yes, finding fresh food or water so you won't die can be annoying. On the other hand, it forces players to converge on the supply-rich towns where the zombies are most concentrated. The hunt for scarce resources and ease of death forces players to either band together, hunt each other, or become sneaky hermits. You can make the game into a co-op shooter, survival horror, deathmatch, or somewhere in between. The game's what you make of it.
